sourceIssues.locator: §3.2, proof of Proposition 3.2.1 (injectivity when 𝒳 is proper), p. 13 (author version, 17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: Author version p. 13, checked on the rendered page: "Take a normal proper formal model 𝔛 of 𝒳 such that the sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛. We can obtain such a model as follows. By Raynaud's theory, we can find a model 𝔛′ of 𝒳 which admits an affinoid covering 𝔘′ whose generic fiber refines 𝒰. We can replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation 𝔛 in 𝒳. This is still a formal model. The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛′. By [52], lemma 2.6, this model is automatically proper. Let 𝔙 be an affine covering of 𝔛 and 𝒱 be its generic fiber. ... The cohomology Ȟⁱ_𝒱(𝒳, ℱ⁺) is identified with the cohomology Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ) and it is a finite 𝒪_k-module since 𝔛 is proper."
sourceIssues.correction: "The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛", where 𝔛 is the normalisation of 𝔛′ in 𝒳. This matches the paragraph's opening sentence ("a normal proper formal model 𝔛 ... a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛") and the later use of Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ).
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed text is exactly as quoted. The symbol is a fraktur X with a prime (𝔛′), so this is not a text-layer artefact. Four points support a misprint.

(1) It contradicts the framing sentence of the same paragraph, which asks for a normal model 𝔛 with ℱ⁺ coming from a locally free ℱ on 𝔛. The rest of the proof uses ℱ on 𝔛: the affine covering 𝔙 of 𝔛, Ȟⁱ_𝒱(𝒳, ℱ⁺) = Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ), and finiteness because 𝔛 is proper.

(2) As mathematics, the claim on 𝔛′ is false in the sense the proof needs, which is ℱ(𝔙) = ℱ⁺(𝔙_η), i.e. sp_*ℱ⁺ = ℱ. On an affine piece Spf A of a model with reduced generic fiber, O⁺(Spf A_η) = A°, the integral closure of A in A[1/p]. This equals A exactly when A is integrally closed there. So on a non-normal 𝔛′ we get sp_*O⁺ = ν_*O_𝔛 ≠ O_𝔛′. This is not even invertible. Suppose A° = A·a. Since 1 ∈ A°, we have 1 = ba with b ∈ A, and a² = ca with c ∈ A. Cancelling the unit a gives a = c ∈ A, so A° = A. Already for ℱ⁺ = O⁺, the sheaf on 𝔛′ is therefore not locally free. On the normal 𝔛, O_𝔛(𝔙) = O⁺(𝔙_η). So the gluing matrices in GL_r(O⁺) descend, and ℱ is locally free on 𝔛. This is why the normalisation is taken.

(3) HAL v3 (p. 11) had the sentences in the other order and without "locally free": "The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a sheaf ℱ on 𝔛′. We can then replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation 𝔛 in 𝒳. This is still a formal model." The 2019 revision moved the sentence after the normalisation step and added "locally free", but did not change 𝔛′ to 𝔛. That is a leftover from editing.

(4) The intended argument is correct once 𝔛 is read, so no gap remains. The only later use I found, in the construction of the map "ext" ("by proposition 3.2.1, this defines the map ext", p. 100), relies on the statement of Proposition 3.2.1, which is unaffected.

By Raynaud's theory, we can find a model 𝔛′ of 𝒳 which admits an affinoid covering 𝔘′ whose generic fiber refines 𝒰. We can replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation 𝔛 in 𝒳. This is still a formal model. [...] The cohomology Ȟ^i_𝒱(𝒳,𝓕^+) is identified with the cohomology H^i(𝔛,F) and it is a finite O_k-module since 𝔛 is proper." sourceIssues.correction:
The proof as written needs k to be discretely valued, or k to be algebraically closed (more generally, stable with divisible value group, by the Grauert–Remmert finiteness theorem). Under those hypotheses the normalisation of an admissible formal model is again admissible. The paper's only use of the result is over C_p, where this holds.

For arbitrary k, replace the claim "finite type plus torsion" by boundedness, which is all that is needed:
- 𝒳 is reduced, so the Čech complex Č(𝒰, ℱ^+) is termwise bounded in the Banach complex Č(𝒰, ℱ).
- H^i(𝒳, ℱ) is finite-dimensional, so B^i is closed. Hence the image of Ȟ^i_𝒰(𝒳, ℱ^+) in H^i(𝒳, ℱ) is bounded.
- By Lemma 3.2.2, c·Im(H^i(𝒳, ℱ^+) → H^i(𝒳, ℱ)) lies inside that bounded image.
- Therefore ∩_n p^n Im = 0, which gives injectivity.

This is the argument the paper itself uses in Lemma 14.7.1. There "lattice" just means "bounded".

Two further remarks:
1. The application is over C_p, not Q_p (§12.1: "the base ring for our constructions is O the ring of integers of C_p"; the space 𝒳_Kli(p) lives over Spa(C_p, O)).
2. Stability of k alone, without a divisible value group, does not seem enough: the obstruction already appears for a tame extension without defect in which |L*| is not contained in |k*| and |k*| is dense.

A separate small slip: "locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛'" should read "on 𝔛".
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 13 at 220 dpi and transcribed the passage. The field k is an arbitrary complete non-archimedean field (§3.1, p. 11), and Proposition 3.2.1 is stated for all i ≥ 0.

Counterexample to the intermediate claim, for i = 0:
- Take p odd, k the completion of Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), with value group Γ_k = Z[1/p]. Since 1/2 ∉ Z[1/p], √p ∉ k, so L = k(√p) has degree 2.
- 𝒳 = Spa(L, O_L) = Spa(k⟨T⟩/(T²−p)) is finite étale over Spa(k, O_k). So it is of finite type, smooth, separated and proper. Take 𝓕 = O_𝒳 and 𝓕^+ = O_𝒳^+.
- For a, b ∈ k, v(a + b√p) = min(v(a), v(b) + 1/2), because the two values lie in different cosets of Z[1/p]. So O_L = O_k ⊕ I·√p with I = {b ∈ k : v(b) > −1/2}.
- Finitely generated submodules of k over the valuation ring O_k are principal. I is not principal, because −1/2 ∉ Γ_k and I has no element of minimal valuation. So H^0(𝒳, 𝓕^+) = O_L is torsion-free and not finitely generated. It is therefore not "the sum of a finite type O_k-module and a torsion group", since any torsion part inside O_L is 0.
- The step "We can replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation … This is still a formal model" also fails. For the model 𝔛′ = Spf O_k⟨T⟩/(T²−p), the normalisation is Spf O_L. If O_L were topologically of finite type, the images t_i of the variables would generate a finite free O_k-submodule M = O_k[t_i]. M is closed in L because all norms on L are equivalent. Then the image of O_k⟨T⟩ would be M, so O_L would be finitely generated, which is false. In fact 𝒳 has no normal formal model of finite type at all.

The proposition's conclusion still holds here: ∩ p^n O_L = 0, and L → lim_n L/p^nO_L is an isomorphism because L is complete. It also holds in general, by the Banach/Čech boundedness argument given in the correction. So only the proof is affected, not the stated result.

I classify this as an "error" rather than a "gap": the printed intermediate claims are false for general k, not just left unproved.

The proposition is applied over C_p, not Q_p. Part III works over Spa(C_p, O) (p. 73: "the associated analytic adic space over Spa(Cp, O)"), and the proposition is used in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (pp. 99–100). C_p is algebraically closed, so the normalisation there is of finite type, and the finiteness of H^i(𝔛,F) for proper admissible 𝔛 holds. The paper's application is therefore unaffected. I checked the page image. §3.1 lets k be any complete non-archimedean field, and §3.2 only fixes p as a topologically nilpotent unit of k. With that generality the step "replace 𝔛' by its normalisation 𝔛 … This is still a formal model" can fail, and so can the claim that H^i(𝒳, ℱ^+) is "finite type + torsion".

**Counterexample.** Let p be odd, let k be the completion of Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), and let L = k(√p).
- The value group of k is Z[1/p], and 1/2 is not in it, so [L:k] = 2, e = 2, f = 1.
- Since v(a) and v(b) + 1/2 can never be equal, v(a + b√p) = min(v(a), v(b) + 1/2). Hence O_L = O_k ⊕ J·√p, where J = {b : v(b) > −1/2}.
- J is not finitely generated, because Z[1/p] ∩ (−1/2, ∞) has no least element. So O_L is not finitely generated over O_k.
- Equivalently: m_k O_L = m_L, so O_L/m_k O_L = F_p has dimension 1, whereas a free module of rank 2 would give dimension 2.

Take 𝒳 = Spa(L, O_L), which is finite étale over Spa(k, O_k), hence smooth, proper and separated. Take ℱ = O and ℱ^+ = O^+, and i = 0.
- H^0(𝒳, O^+) = O_L. It is torsion-free and not of finite type, so the intermediate claim is false.
- Any normal formal model is Spf A with O_L ⊆ A ⊆ L° = O_L, so A = O_L.
- O_L is not topologically of finite type. If O_L/p were a finitely generated O_k/p-algebra, it would be finite (it is integral), and topological Nakayama would make O_L finitely generated. So no normal formal model exists, and "This is still a formal model" fails.

The proposition itself still holds here: lim_n L/p^n O_L = L.

**Defence tried and rejected.** The author version says "k-vector space" (HAL v3 said "Q_p-vector space"), so general k really is intended. No nearby statement restricts k.

**Consequences.** Proposition 3.2.1 is cited only once, in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 99, continued "by proposition 3.2.1" at the top of p. 100), for the proper space 𝒳_Kli(p) over Spa(C_p, O). C_p is algebraically closed, so the Grauert–Remmert theorem makes the normalisation admissible. Coherent cohomology of proper admissible formal schemes over O_{C_p} is finitely presented. The paper's argument therefore works there.

Even over C_p, the proof literally shows only that c·H^i(𝒳, ℱ^+) lies in a finitely generated submodule. That is not quite "finite type + torsion" over a non-noetherian O, but it gives the needed boundedness.

The boundedness argument above proves Proposition 3.2.1 for every k. So no stated result changes: only the proof, in the generality stated in §3, is wrong. I classify this as an error rather than a gap, because a concrete counterexample shows the intermediate assertions are false, not merely unproved.

sourceIssues.printed: Proof. We first observe that the result holds true after inverting p by classical results on toroidal embeddings (see [40], coro. 1 on page 44) and the comparison theorem stated in [70], thm. 9.1. It follows easily that O^{++}_{T^an_Σ} ≃ f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}} and we are left to prove that R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}} = 0 for all i > 0. It suffices to show that R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p = 0 for all i > 0 since this will imply that multiplication by p is surjective on R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}} for all i > 0 and we know that this sheaf is torsion.
sourceIssues.correction:
What the argument actually needs is that O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p → Rf_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) is a quasi-isomorphism, including in degree 0. Then multiplication by p is bijective on R^i f_⋆O^{++} for every i > 0, and a torsion sheaf on which p is injective is 0.

- For i ≥ 2 the printed vanishing is already enough: R^{i−1}f_⋆(O^{++}/p) = 0 makes p injective on R^i f_⋆O^{++}.
- For i = 1 one must add the degree-0 step f_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) = O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p. Together with f_⋆O^{++} = O^{++}, this makes f_⋆O^{++} → f_⋆(O^{++}/p) surjective. That surjectivity is equivalent to p being injective on R^1 f_⋆O^{++}.
- Alternatively, a bound on the p-power torsion of R^1 f_⋆O^{++} would do, but the paper proves none.

sourceIssues.printed: (p. 20, checked on the page image) "We make the following choice of positive roots {e1 − e2, −2e1 + e3, −e1 − e2 + e3, −2e2 + e3}. Set α1 = e1 − e2 and α2 = −2e2 + e3. The simple positive roots are ∆ = {α1, α2}. The compact root is α1. We let ρ = (−1, −2; 0) be half the sum of the positive roots. This choice of positive roots is related to the Shimura datum (see remark 5.2.1.1). [...] The coroot of α1 is α1^∨ = f1 − f2 and the coroot of α2 is α2^∨ = f2. We let ∆^∨ = {α1^∨, α2^∨}. [...] By [65], lemma 2.3.1 there is an isomorphism of roots datum between (X*(T), ∆, X_*(T), ∆^∨) and (X_*(T), ∆^∨, X*(T), ∆). It is given by a map i : X*(T) → X_*(T) whose matrix in the basis e1, e2, e3 and f1, f2, f3 is (1 1 1 / 1 0 1 / 1 1 2)". Earlier on the page: e1 = (1,0;1), e2 = (0,1;1), e3 = (0,0;2); f1 = (1,0;0), f2 = (0,1;0), f3 = (−1/2,−1/2;1/2).
sourceIssues.reason:
I redid the computation. A character (a1,a2;c) pairs with a cocharacter (b1,b2;d) as a1b1 + a2b2 + cd, and I checked that the f_i are dual to the e_i.

**Positive roots and ρ.** In (t1,t2)-exponents the printed positive roots are t1/t2, t1^−2, (t1t2)^−1 and t2^−2. They form a positive system; λ = (−1,−2) is regular dominant for it. Half their sum is (−1,−2;0), so ρ is right.

**The printed ∆ is wrong.**
- −e1−e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−2e1+e3), and −2e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−e1−e2+e3). So −2e2+e3 is a sum of two positive roots and is not simple.
- The coroot of −2e2+e3 = (0,−2;0) is −f2, not f2: ⟨−2e2+e3, f2⟩ = −2.
- ⟨ρ, −f2⟩ = 2, which is its height. The simple coroots f1−f2 and −f1 both pair with ρ to give 1.
- ⟨e1−e2, −f2⟩ = +1 > 0, so {e1−e2, −2e2+e3} is not a base of any positive system.

**The printed matrix.** It is symmetric, so rows and columns read the same way. It gives i(e1) = f1+f2+f3, i(e2) = f1+f3, i(e3) = f1+f2+2f3. So i(e1−e2) = f2, which is the printed α2^∨ but a negative coroot for the printed positive system. And i(−2e2+e3) = f2−f1, which is not in the printed ∆^∨. For the correct base, i(−2e1+e3) = −f1−f2. So the printed i is not a based isomorphism for the author-version choices.

**Images in ∆^∨.** The image f2 does lie in the printed ∆^∨ (it is the printed α2^∨); only f2−f1 does not. Neither image lies in the correct ∆^∨ = {f1−f2, −f1}. This does not change the conclusion.

**HAL v3.** HAL v3 had the upper-triangular positive system on printed p. 17 (PDF p. 18): positive roots {e1−e2, 2e1−e3, e1+e2−e3, 2e2−e3}, α2 = 2e2−e3 and α2^∨ = f2. The same matrix is on printed p. 18 (PDF p. 19). There everything is consistent: i(e1−e2) = f2 = α2^∨ and i(2e2−e3) = f1−f2 = α1^∨. HAL v3 has a different typo, e2 = (1,0;1). The revision negated the three non-compact roots and added ρ, but left ∆, the coroot of α2 and i as they were. So the inconsistency was introduced by the revision; HAL v3 itself was consistent (its matrix is on printed p. 18).

**Affects nothing.** ∆, α1, α2, α2^∨ and ∆^∨ appear only in §5.1.1; I grepped the whole text. The printed i still sends every root to a coroot and satisfies the transpose condition, so it is an unbased root-datum isomorphism, and a based one for the upper-triangular Borel. The identification of the dual group with GSp4(C) is therefore still valid. It is used only through semisimple conjugacy classes c_Θ in §5.1.3 and §5.1.5, which do not depend on the choice of base. ρ and 'our choice of positive roots' are used later (§5.1.6), and both are printed correctly. I checked this by hand and by direct computation. The pairing is (a1,a2;c)·(b1,b2;d) = a1b1 + a2b2 + cd, and the f_i are dual to the e_i.

**No reading makes the printed §5.1.1 consistent.**
- The printed Δ = {e1−e2, −2e2+e3} is not a base of any positive system: ⟨e1−e2, (−2e2+e3)^∨⟩ = ⟨(1,−1), (0,−1)⟩ = +1 > 0.
- In the printed list, −2e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−e1−e2+e3), so it is not simple. The simple roots of the printed list are e1−e2 and −2e1+e3.
- α2^∨ = f2 is wrong in every system: ⟨−2e2+e3, f2⟩ = −2, so the coroot is −f2.
- The printed i sends α1 to f2 and α2 to f2 − f1. The pair {f2, f2 − f1} is not the printed Δ^∨ = {f1−f2, f2}. So the stated based isomorphism fails for the printed data.

**Defence attempt.** The printed list and ρ = (−1,−2;0) do agree with each other, and Remark 5.1.2.1 holds for them. But the paper's only later uses of "our choice of positive roots" require e2−e1 to be positive:
- §5.1.6 (p. 22) says: "0 ≥ λ2 > λ1 and C is the dominant chamber corresponding to our choice of positive roots". The same range for holomorphic λ appears on p. 24, and the embedding into H^0(Ω^(λ2−λ1−1, 2−λ2)) gives λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; ·).
- For λ = (−5, −2), λ pairs with the coroots of the printed positive roots as (−3, 5, 7, 2). The signs are mixed, so λ is neither dominant nor antidominant under either sign convention.
- For the lower-Borel system the same pairings are (3, 5, 7, 2), all positive.
- The normalizing region "−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1" in §5.1.6 lies in the half-plane λ2 ≥ λ1, where e2−e1 is non-negative on λ.
- In §15.2.1 (λ2 = 0 > λ1), both chambers positive for λ contain e2−e1. For λ = (−5, 0) the printed pairings are (−5, 5, 5, 0). So the printed chamber is not one of the "two choices for C", and π(λ)^h would be ill-defined as written.
- The printed α2 = −2e2+e3 and the printed matrix are exactly right for the lower-Borel system.
- On the other side, §15.2.2 says "(−λ1+1, 2; −c) is dominant for the Levi M_Si". That is the standard upper-Borel convention for GL2 highest weights, and the same phrase appears in HAL v3. It does not refer to "our choice".
So no charitable reading rescues the printed list.

**How the error arose.** HAL v3 used upper-triangular conventions throughout, with holomorphic λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0. The revision negated λ but updated §5.1.1 only in part: it negated the non-compact roots, kept e1−e2, computed ρ from that mixed list, and kept the old α1^∨, α2^∨ and matrix.

**Consequences.** Δ, Δ^∨ and i only fix the identification of the dual group with GSp4(C). That identification is used only through semisimple conjugacy classes (c_Θ in §5.1.3 and §5.1.5), which do not depend on the base. In §5.1.6 and §15.2.1 the intended holomorphic chamber is clear from the stated range of λ. No stated result or proof changes once the correction is made, so this affects nothing downstream.

**On §5.1.6.** The statement in the "Affects nothing" paragraph that ρ and 'our choice of positive roots' are used later (§5.1.6) and both are printed correctly is wrong for §5.1.6. The correct §5.3 formula is λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; k+2r). The main text on p. 24 actually prints (1−k+r, …), which is a separate slip; the correct form appears in Remark 5.3.1.

review.reason: Confirmed, and I checked the root system by hand rather than taking the finding's word for it. Page 20 prints `We make the following choice of positive roots $\{e_1-e_2,-2e_1+e_3,-e_1-e_2+e_3,-2e_2+e_3\}$. Set $\alpha_1=e_1-e_2$ and $\alpha_2=-2e_2+e_3$. The simple positive roots are $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\alpha_2\}$.' Writing the other two in that basis gives $-e_1-e_2+e_3=-\alpha_1+\alpha_2$ and $-2e_1+e_3=-2\alpha_1+\alpha_2$: two of the four declared positive roots have a negative $\alpha_1$-coefficient, so $\{\alpha_1,\alpha_2\}$ is not a base of the declared positive system and the system is internally inconsistent. Taking the opposite system, as the correction does, makes $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ simple.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1.2 (Parabolic subgroups), p. 20 (author version). HAL v3 has the same text (§5.1.2).
sourceIssues.printed: If W ⊂ V is a totally isotropic direct factor, we let P_W be the parabolic subgroup of GSp_4 which stabilizes P_W.
sourceIssues.correction: … the parabolic subgroup of GSp_4 which stabilizes W.
sourceIssues.reason: A subgroup defined as the stabilizer of itself is circular. The paper later recalls the intended definition on p. 27, §6.1.5.2: 'Recall from section 5.1.2 that P_W is the parabolic subgroup which is the stabilizer of W'. The next lines are also consistent with this: W = ⟨e1⟩ gives the Klingen parabolic and W = ⟨e1,e2⟩ the Siegel parabolic, with M_{W,l} = GL(W).

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1.6 (Discrete series), first sentence, p. 22 of the author version (17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: 5.1.6. Discrete series. — Given λ = (λ1, λ2; c) ∈ X⋆(T) + (−1, −2; 0) ⊂ X⋆(T)_C which satisfies −λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1 and a Weyl chamber C positive for λ we have a (limit of) discrete series π(λ, C) (see [28], 3.3). [...] If λ2 ≠ 0 and λ2 ≠ −λ1, λ determines uniquely C and π(λ, C) is a discrete series. It is natural to normalize the central character c by c = −λ1 − λ2 + 3. If 0 ≥ λ2 > λ1 and C is the dominant chamber corresponding to our choice of positive roots, then π(λ, C) is called a holomorphic (limit of) discrete series.
sourceIssues.correction: Read '−λ1 ≥ λ2 > λ1', making the inequality strict on the compact wall λ1 = λ2. This is exactly v3's 'λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1' after the sign change. The one-symbol fix repairs both sentences: once λ2 > λ1, the only root walls left in the region are λ2 = 0 and λ2 = −λ1. An alternative correction instead adds 'λ2 ≠ λ1' to the uniqueness sentence. That also works but is less minimal, because it leaves the first sentence claiming that a (limit of) discrete series exists for λ1 = λ2. That claim holds only if one lets the zero coherent continuation count as a 'limit', which the text does not do.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked on page images (pdftoppm at 300 dpi, crop of p. 22): the printed text is '−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1', with both signs non-strict. The holomorphic condition two sentences later is '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1', which is strict.

Conventions (§5.1.1, pp. 20–21): (a1, a2; c) = a1e1 + a2e2 + ((c−a1−a2)/2)e3, and f1, f2 are dual to e1, e2. So a weight λ = (λ1, λ2; c) pairs with the coroot α1∨ = f1 − f2 of the compact root α1 = e1 − e2 to give λ1 − λ2. The line λ1 = λ2 is therefore the compact wall, whichever sign convention is used for positivity.

The set of admissible λ modulo the order-4 group {id, s_α1, −1, −s_α1} is cut out by λ2 ≥ λ1 and λ1 + λ2 ≤ 0. That is the printed inequality. But a (limit of) discrete series needs λ to be regular for the compact root. The next sentence confirms this: it lists only the non-compact walls λ2 = 0 and λ2 = −λ1 as the limit cases. So the equality λ2 = λ1 has to be excluded.

Counterexample: take λ = (−1, −1; 5). Then λ − (−1, −2; 0) = (0, 1; 5), and 5 ≡ 0 + 1 (mod 2), so λ is in X⋆(T) + ρ. Also c = 5 = −λ1 − λ2 + 3 matches the paper's normalization. The inequality holds: 1 ≥ −1 ≥ −1. And λ2 = −1 ≠ 0, λ2 ≠ −λ1 = 1. So as printed, λ 'determines uniquely C' and gives a discrete series. In fact λ lies on the wall between two chambers, and no (limit of) discrete series has this parameter.

HAL v3 (§5.1.4, printed p. 18, checked on the page image) has 'λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1' with shift (2, 1; 0) and a strict compact inequality. The author version changed conventions by negation. v3 holomorphic 'λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0' becomes '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1', exactly as printed, but the strict sign in the region was lost. So this is not an artefact of the text layer.

Side notes, not part of this item:
- §15.2.1 on p. 107 prints '−λ1 ≥ λ2 > −λ1', which describes an empty set, together with the stale shift (2, 1; 0). This is a separate misprint, probably meant to read the same as the corrected §5.1.6.
- The stated positive system {e1−e2, −2e1+e3, −e1−e2+e3, −2e2+e3} with ρ = (−1, −2; 0) has dominant chamber 0 ≥ λ1 ≥ λ2. Its simple roots are e1−e2 and −2e1+e3, not −2e2+e3. That does not match '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1, C dominant'. This separate sign problem does not affect the correction, because the compact wall is λ1 = λ2 in every convention.

The published Duke version could not be checked. Printed text, checked on a 300 dpi crop of p. 22: '−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1', with both inequalities non-strict. The holomorphic condition on the same page, '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1', is strict.

The walls are convention-independent. §5.1.1 (p. 20) writes (a1, a2; c) = a1e1 + a2e2 + ((c−a1−a2)/2)e3, with f1, f2, f3 dual to e1, e2, e3. The coroots of the roots e1−e2, −2e1+e3, −2e2+e3 and −e1−e2+e3 are proportional to f1−f2, f1, f2 and f1+f2. So the walls in the λ-plane are λ1 = λ2, λ1 = 0, λ2 = 0 and λ1 + λ2 = 0. The compact root is α1 = e1−e2, so its wall is λ1 = λ2. This holds under any sign convention for positivity.

A separate sign inconsistency in §5.1.1 does not change this. The stated coroots α1∨ = f1−f2 and α2∨ = f2 are left over from v3, and the dominant chamber of the stated positive system is 0 > λ1 > λ2, which does not match '0 ≥ λ2 > λ1'.

Strongest defence tried: in the Knapp–Zuckerman / Harris [28] §3.3 framework, a (limit of) discrete series needs λ to be nonsingular for the compact roots. When λ is singular for a compact root, the coherent continuation is 0, not a representation. So the printed sentence 'we have a (limit of) discrete series π(λ, C)' fails for λ1 = λ2. The later sentence is false outright: λ then lies on the wall between two chambers exchanged by s_α1, so C is not unique, and there is no discrete series. The defence fails.

These points are attainable in the paper's lattice. For any a < 0, λ = (a, a; −2a+3) satisfies λ − (−1, −2; 0) = (a+1, a+2; −2a+3), and the parity condition c ≡ a1 + a2 (mod 2) holds. So λ ∈ X⋆(T) + ρ, and it has the paper's normalized c.
- Example λ = (−1, −1; 5): 1 ≥ −1 ≥ −1 holds, λ2 ≠ 0 and λ2 ≠ −λ1 = 1, so the printed text calls π(λ, C) a discrete series.
- Another example, (−2, −2; 1), also checks: (−1, 0; 1) ∈ X⋆(T) since 1 ≡ −1 (mod 2).
- Cross-check: Theorem 5.1.7.1(3) would give Hodge–Tate weights (0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2) = (0, 1, 1, 2), which are not distinct. This fits with no discrete series existing there.

The intended meaning is clear from context:
- v3 has the strict sign.
- The next sentence lists only the non-compact walls λ2 = 0 and λ2 = −λ1 as the degenerate cases.
- The holomorphic condition is strict.
So this is a misprint rather than a mathematical error.

Consequences: nothing later in the paper uses the case λ1 = λ2.
- Theorem 5.1.7.1 assumes π∞ is in the discrete series, which forces λ to be regular.
- §5.3 (pp. 24–25) uses holomorphic λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; ...) with k ≥ 0, so λ2 − λ1 = k + 1 > 0, strictly.
- §15.2.1–15.2.2 (p. 107) use λ2 = 0 > λ1, which lies inside the corrected region.
§15.2.1 has its own misprint, the empty region '−λ1 ≥ λ2 > −λ1' with the stale shift (2, 1; 0), and should read like the corrected §5.1.6. That is a separate item. No explicit cross-reference to §5.1.6 was found.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1.5, unnumbered paragraph between Proposition 5.1.5.1 and Proposition 5.1.5.2, p. 22 (author version, 17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: Let π_ℓ be an irreducible complex smooth admissible representation of GSp_4(Q_ℓ) and assume that π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)} ≠ 0. Then there is a quadruple (α, β, γ, δ) ∈ C^4 satisfying αβ = γδ such that π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)} ≠ 0 contains an eigenvector for U_{Kli(ℓ),0}, U_{Kli(ℓ),1} and U_{Kli(ℓ),2} with eigenvalues ℓ^{−3}αδ, ℓ^{−1}αβ, α + β. The W-orbit of (α, β, γ, δ) ∈ C^4 is still called the Hecke parameters of π_ℓ.
sourceIssues.correction: "satisfying αδ = βγ" in place of "satisfying αβ = γδ". The rest of the sentence, including the eigenvalues ℓ^{−3}αδ, ℓ^{−1}αβ, α+β, stays as printed.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the printed text on a 250 dpi render of p. 22, and it does read "αβ = γδ". This does not fit the paper's own conventions:

(1) The maximal torus. §5.1.1 (p. 20) defines it as diag(st1, st2, st2^{-1}, st1^{-1}), so diag(a,b,c,d) lies in GSp4 exactly when ad = bc. §5.1.5 (p. 21) matches this: it orders the Hecke parameters "in such a way that αδ = βγ, so that diag(α,β,γ,δ) represents the semi-simple conjugacy class". The Weyl group W acts on quadruples by keeping αδ = βγ. It does not keep αβ = γδ: for example, swapping α and δ turns it into δβ = γα.

(2) Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} ↦ ℓ^{−3}αδ, T_{ℓ,1} ↦ ℓ^{−1}(αβ+αγ+αδ+βδ+γδ) − ℓ^{−3}αδ, T_{ℓ,2} ↦ α+β+γ+δ). I checked it against the Hecke polynomial Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T2X + ℓ(T1+(ℓ²+1)T0)X² − ℓ³T2T0X³ + ℓ⁶T0²X⁴ = ∏(1−ξX), both by hand and numerically. The formulas hold only under αδ = βγ, which makes αδ the similitude and gives αβγδ = (ℓ³T0)².

(3) Proposition 5.1.5.1 (p. 22) gives the eigenvalues as the W-orbit of ℓ^{−3}αδ, ℓ^{−1}αβ, α+β. The central eigenvalue ℓ^{−3}αδ stays the same across the orbit only because αδ = βγ. The orbit {αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ} is the 4-element set that appears in Lemma 5.1.5.2.

(4) Proposition 5.1.5.2 concludes that π_ℓ is generic spherical "with Hecke parameters (α,β,γ,δ)". By the definition on p. 21, such parameters must satisfy αδ = βγ. So the Klingen-level parameters must be normalised the same way.

(5) Later use. In the proof of Lemma 14.8.3 (p. 102), Corollary 14.9.1 is invoked for the Klingen-level Hecke parameters of this paragraph, together with Proposition 5.1.5.2 and Lemma 5.1.5.2. Corollary 14.9.1 (p. 102) says those parameters have valuations (0,0,k+1,k+1). That is impossible under αβ = γδ: the unit ℓ^{−1}αβ would force Σv = 2v(αβ) = 0. It holds under αδ = βγ, where αβ is a unit and v(αδ) = v(βγ) = k+1.

Also, "αβ = γδ" does not occur anywhere else in the text. HAL v3 has no such passage: its §5.1 goes straight from the spherical Hecke algebra to discrete series, and its §5.1.5 is about Galois representations. Where HAL v3 orders Hecke parameters (printed p. 57), it uses "α_p δ_p = β_p γ_p". The slip was therefore introduced in the revision. As a bare existence claim the printed sentence is not false, because the quadruple is underdetermined. But the "Hecke parameters" it defines are the wrong ones for every later use, so this is a genuine misprint rather than an artefact of the text layer.

review.reason: Confirmed, and the paper's own torus settles it. The sentence prints `there is a quadruple $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)\in\C^4$ satisfying $\alpha\beta=\gamma\delta$', with eigenvalues $\ell^{-3}\alpha\delta$, $\ell^{-1}\alpha\beta$, $\alpha+\beta$. Page 20 defines the maximal torus by $\mathrm{diag}(st_1,st_2,st_2^{-1},st_1^{-1})$, so a diagonal matrix $\mathrm{diag}(a,b,c,d)$ lies in $\GSp_4$ exactly when $ad=bc$; the similitude relation among the Hecke parameters is therefore $\alpha\delta=\beta\gamma$, which is also what makes $\ell^{-3}\alpha\delta$ the similitude eigenvalue.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1.6 (Discrete series), p. 22 (author version). HAL v3 §5.1.4 has the same statement: 'By Harris-Chandra isomorphism (recalled in [16], p. 229 for instance), Z ≃ C[Y(T)]^W'.
sourceIssues.printed: Let ℨ be the center of the enveloping algebra U(𝔤). By Harish-Chandra isomorphism (recalled in [18], p. 229 for instance), ℨ ≃ ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W where W is the Weyl group. The infinitesimal character of π(λ, C) is the Weyl group orbit of λ.
sourceIssues.correction: ℨ ≅ Sym(X_⋆(T) ⊗ ℂ)^W = S(𝔥)^W, i.e. the W-invariant polynomial functions on X^⋆(T)_ℂ = 𝔥^*.
sourceIssues.reason: One paragraph earlier (§5.1.3, p. 21) ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W is the target of the twisted Satake isomorphism, so it denotes the W-invariants of the group algebra of the cocharacter lattice, i.e. regular functions on the dual torus. With that meaning the displayed isomorphism is false. ℨ is a polynomial algebra with only constant units. ℂ[X_⋆(T)]^W contains the non-constant unit given by the similitude ν^{±1} of the dual GSp_4. The Harish-Chandra isomorphism is ℨ ≅ S(𝔥)^W with 𝔥 = X_⋆(T) ⊗ ℂ. Its characters are W-orbits in 𝔥^* = X^⋆(T)_ℂ, which is what the next sentence uses: the orbit of λ ∈ X^⋆(T)_ℂ. The intended meaning is clear and nothing depends on the notation. The misprint is milder if one reads ℂ[X_⋆(T)] loosely as the polynomial algebra on the lattice, but that clashes with the paper's own notation.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1.7, footnote 4 (on 'general type' in the paragraph after Remark 5.1.7.1), p. 23 of the author version. HAL v3 does not have this footnote: its §5.1.5 only lists 'general type, Yoshida type, Saito-Kurokawa type' and never defines general type.
sourceIssues.printed: 4. π is of general type if it has a base change to a cuspidal automorphic representation on GL4.
sourceIssues.correction: π is of general type if its transfer (functorial lift) to GL4, along the natural 4-dimensional representation of the dual group GSp4(C), is a cuspidal automorphic representation.
sourceIssues.reason: Checked on the 130 dpi render; the footnote text is exactly as quoted. In standard usage 'base change' means changing the base field (GL_n over F to GL_n over E, or Res_{E/F}). What is meant here is the endoscopic or functorial transfer from GSp4 to GL4 over Q, the notion in Arthur's classification that the paragraph invokes. The mathematics as intended is right: general type means the transfer to GL4 is cuspidal. So this is only the wrong name for the operation, and the meaning is clear from context. Confidence is low because this is a wording issue that some readers would accept as loose usage rather than a mistake.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed: footnote 4 on p. 23 reads `$\pi$ is of general type if it has a base change to a cuspidal automorphic representation on GL4.' In standard usage base change means changing the base field, whereas what Arthur's classification calls general type is that the functorial transfer to GL$_4$ along the standard four-dimensional representation of the dual group is cuspidal — an endoscopic transfer over $\Q$, not a base change. The mathematics intended is right and the paragraph that the footnote annotates makes it clear, so this is a wording slip and nothing downstream depends on the phrase. The finding's own low confidence is appropriate, and I record it as confirmed on the terminology rather than on any mathematical content.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1.7, Theorem 5.1.7.1, item 5, p. 23 (with Remark 5.1.7.1, p. 23). HAL v3: Theorem 5.1.5.1, item 5, printed p. 19 (PDF p. 20).
sourceIssues.printed: Thm 5.1.7.1, item 3 (p. 23, from the page image): "The representation ρ_{π,λ} is de Rham at p with Hodge-Tate weights (0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2)." Item 5: "ρ_{π,λ} ≃ ρ^∨_{π,λ} ⊗ χ_p^{−λ1−λ2} ω_{π,λ} for some finite character ω_{π,λ} and the cyclotomic character χ_p." Remark 5.1.7.1: "We use geometric Frobenii, the Artin reciprocity law is normalized by sending p to the geometric Frobenius at p, and the Hodge-Tate weight of the cyclotomic character is −1. [...] The Hodge cocharacter is given by t ↦ diag(1, t^{−λ1}, t^{−λ2}, t^{−λ1−λ2}). The central character of π ⊗ |ν|^{−3/2} is |.|^{−λ1−λ2} ⊗ ω_π for some finite character ω_π."
sourceIssues.correction: Item 5 should read ρ_{π,λ} ≃ ρ^∨_{π,λ} ⊗ χ_p^{λ1+λ2} ω_{π,λ}. Equivalently, ν∘ρ_{π,λ} = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}·(finite), which is χ_p^{3−k−2r}·(finite) for λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; k+2r). This is the minimal fix: it keeps item 3, the Hodge cocharacter, geometric Frobenius and HT(χ_p) = −1. The Remark's sentence "central character of π⊗|ν|^{−3/2} is |.|^{−λ1−λ2}⊗ω_π" is tied to item 5. The link goes through Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−3}αδ), item 2 and the stated reciprocity normalisation, where |·|_A corresponds to χ_p. For consistency that sentence must also change, to |.|^{λ1+λ2}⊗ω_π (or ω_{π,λ} must be matched with ω_π^{−1}). This second change is right under the standard convention that T_{ℓ,0} acts by π_ℓ(ℓ). It is less certain than the fix to item 5, because the author version's automorphic-side central normalisation (c = −λ1−λ2+3) is itself hard to reconcile with §5.3.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 23 at 200 dpi and read it off the image. The exponent in item 5 is −λ1−λ2 as quoted, so this is not a text-layer artefact.

(1) Hodge-Tate weights. If ρ ≃ ρ^∨⊗χ_p^m⊗(finite) and HT(χ_p) = −1, then the multiset {h_i} must equal {−h_i − m}. With h = (0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2), pairing the largest weight with the smallest forces m = λ1+λ2. The printed m = −λ1−λ2 would need λ1+λ2 = 0, which the theorem's discrete-series hypothesis excludes (λ2 ≠ −λ1). The Hodge cocharacter has similitude t^{−λ1−λ2}. Under the paper's own map i (p. 20), i(λ1,λ2;−λ1−λ2) = diag(1, t^{−λ2}, t^{−λ1}, t^{−λ1−λ2}), which gives the same answer.

(2) Frobenius check, which does not depend on the HT convention. Lemma 5.1.5.1 gives T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−3}αδ. In §5.3, T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−6}T′_{ℓ,0}, where T′_{ℓ,0} is the differential of the isogeny [ℓ] acting on Sym^k⊗det^r ω, i.e. ℓ^{k+2r}. So T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{k+2r−6} and αδ = ℓ^{k+2r−3} = ℓ^{−λ1−λ2}, using λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; k+2r) from the proof of Thm 5.3.1. Thus ν(ρ(Frob_geom)) = ℓ^{−λ1−λ2} up to a root of unity. Since χ_p(Frob_geom) = ℓ^{−1}, this gives ν∘ρ = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}·(finite). The printed character would give ℓ^{λ1+λ2} instead. This agrees with item 4 and with Remark 5.3.2: slopes 0, r−2, k+r−1, k+2r−3, so v_p(αδ) = k+2r−3.

(3) Abelian surface. Take (k,r) = (0,2), so λ = (−1,0). Item 3 gives weights (0,0,1,1), which is H^1(A), and αδ = ℓ. The Weil pairing gives H^1 ≅ (H^1)^∨ ⊗ χ_p^{−1} = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}. The printed formula gives χ_p^{+1}, which is right for V_pA = H_1, not for H^1.

HAL v3 prints the same formula χ_p^{−λ1−λ2}, with no convention remark. But v3 uses the opposite λ: holomorphic means λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0 and λ = (k+r−1, r−2; −k−2r+6). There χ_p^{−λ1−λ2} = χ_p^{3−k−2r}, which is correct, and it is the same character as the corrected author-version χ_p^{λ1+λ2}. So the error came in when the author version negated λ (and made HT(χ_p) = −1 explicit) without flipping the sign in item 5. The new Remark's |.|^{−λ1−λ2} carries the same leftover sign.

Impact: this is a false statement inside a theorem quoted from the literature. Nothing later uses item 5. Theorem 5.3.1 uses only the Frobenius characteristic polynomials (item 2), and §15 uses only Θ_m(Q_ℓ(X)). The correction above is right. Its supporting numbers αδ = ℓ^{k+2r−3} and T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{k+2r−6} check out. I checked the text on the rendered page images (author pp. 20–26 and 38; v3 PDF pp. 19–22), not only in the text layer. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) HT check, independent of the Frobenius convention. Item 3 gives weights {0, −λ2, −λ1, −λ1−λ2}. For a GSp4-valued ρ we have ρ ≅ ρ^∨⊗(ν∘ρ), and the weights pair to the weight of ν∘ρ. Other pairings would force λ1 = 0 or λ2 = 0, which the discrete-series hypothesis excludes. So HT(ν∘ρ) = −λ1−λ2, which is also the similitude t^{−λ1−λ2} of the stated Hodge cocharacter. With HT(χ_p) = −1 this gives ν∘ρ = χ_p^{λ1+λ2}·(finite). The printed χ_p^{−λ1−λ2} would need λ1+λ2 = 0, i.e. λ2 = −λ1, and that is excluded.

(2) Crystalline check, independent of both the Frobenius and the HT conventions. D_crys(χ_p^n) has φ = p^{−n}. By item 4, φ on D_crys(ν∘ρ) is α_pδ_p. §5.3 (p. 25) sets T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−6}T'_{ℓ,0}, where T' is the differential of the isogeny [ℓ] acting on Sym^k⊗det^r ω, so T' = ℓ^{k+2r}. Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} = ℓ^{−3}αδ) then gives αδ = ℓ^{k+2r−3} = ℓ^{−λ1−λ2}. This agrees with Remark 5.3.2 and p. 38, where the Hodge slopes are 0, r−2, k+r−1, k+2r−3 with the same endpoints, so v_p(α_pδ_p) = k+2r−3. The printed character gives slope λ1+λ2 = 3−k−2r instead. The ℓ-adic check with geometric Frobenius (χ_p(Frob_ℓ) = ℓ^{−1}) gives the same exponent, λ1+λ2.

(3) Small cases, checked by direct computation over λ = (1−k−r, 2−r). For (k,r) = (0,3), λ = (−2,−1), the weights are (0,1,2,3). The HT, Frobenius and crystalline routes all give ν = χ_p^{−3}; the printed formula gives χ_p^{3}. For (0,2), H^1 of an abelian surface: the Weil pairing gives χ_p^{−1}; the printed formula gives χ_p^{+1}.

Defences tried:
(a) The HT convention is the misprint. Flipping it breaks check (2).
(b) "Geometric" should read "arithmetic". Then item 5 would agree with item 2 and §5.3, but it would still contradict item 3 (check (1)) and item 4 (check (2)).
(c) Cited sources. The printed exponent k+2r−3 = k1+k2−3 is the twist in the arithmetic-Frobenius statement of the cited literature (Weissauer/Taylor style), so it does not fit the geometric normalisation this paper declares. That attribution is from memory: I did not check the cited papers.
(d) HAL v3 prints the same formula. Its value there is χ_p^{3−k−2r}, and it is consistent with v3's non-positive weights under HT(χ_p) = +1.

So the error entered in revision. The author negated λ and flipped the HT sign convention, which keeps item 3 describing the same representation. Item 5 was not updated, and the new Remark was written to match item 5.

Uses later in the paper: none. Theorem 5.3.1 uses only item 2 (Frobenius characteristic polynomials). p. 38 uses Remark 5.3.2's weights and slopes. §15 uses Arthur's classification and reducibility. No later passage cites ρ^∨, the twist, or ω_π. The false statement is therefore confined to item 5 of the recalled theorem (and the matching Remark sentence), so 'affects' is "a stated result" with no downstream consequence. One could record 'nothing' because nothing downstream uses item 5; I use 'a stated result' because item 5 itself is false as printed.

Item 3 prints Hodge\u2013Tate weights $(0,-\lambda_2,-\lambda_1,-\lambda_1-\lambda_2)$ and item 5 prints $\rho_{\pi,\lambda}\simeq\rho^\vee_{\pi,\lambda}\otimes\chi_p^{-\lambda_1-\lambda_2}\omega_{\pi,\lambda}$, with Remark 5.1.7.1 fixing $\mathrm{HT}(\chi_p)=-1$. sourceIssues.printed: where π_f runs through the set of admissible representations of GSp4(A_f) such that π(λ, C) ⊗ π_f is cuspidal automorphic for λ = (1 − k + r, 2 − r; k + 2r) and π(λ, C) the holomorphic (limit) of discrete series.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page 24 image at 250 dpi. It reads "λ = (1 − k + r, 2 − r; k + 2r)" with a plus sign before r, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The paragraph just above sets the convention: "λ = (λ1, λ2; −λ1 − λ2 + 3) (and hence 0 ≥ λ2 > λ1)", with the embedding π_f^K ↪ H^0(S^tor_{K,Σ}, Ω^(λ2−λ1−1, 2−λ2)(−D)). Section 5.1.6 on p. 23 gives the same convention: holomorphic means 0 ≥ λ2 > λ1, and c = −λ1 − λ2 + 3.

Redoing the computation: set k = λ2 − λ1 − 1 and r = 2 − λ2. Then λ2 = 2 − r, λ1 = 1 − k − r and c = −(1−k−r) − (2−r) + 3 = k + 2r. For k ≥ 0 and r ≥ 2 this satisfies 0 ≥ λ2 > λ1 and −λ1 ≥ λ2 (because k + 2r ≥ 3). It is a limit of discrete series exactly when r = 2, which is the singular weight (k, 2) case.

The printed triple is inconsistent in two ways:
- It breaks 0 ≥ λ2 > λ1 whenever k ≤ 2r − 1. For example, (k, r) = (0, 2) gives λ1 = 3 > λ2 = 0.
- It breaks the stated normalization of c: −(1−k+r) − (2−r) + 3 = k, not k + 2r.

Page 25 prints the corrected value twice (checked on the image):
- Remark 5.3.1: Ω^(k,r) has highest weight (k+r, r; −k−2r), "therefore the automorphic forms contributing to the cohomology have infinitesimal character (1 − k − r, 2 − r; k + 2r)".
- Proof of Theorem 5.3.1: "λ = (1 − k − r, 2 − r; k + 2r)".

Remark 5.3.2 gives Hodge–Tate weights (0, r−2, r+k−1, k+2r−3), which also matches the corrected value.

HAL v3 (printed p. 20, PDF p. 21) does not have this error. It uses the opposite sign convention: "λ = (λ1, λ2; c) (and hence λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0)", embedding into Ω^(λ1−λ2−1, λ2+2)(−D), and "λ = (k + r − 1, r − 2; −k − 2r + 6)" both in this sentence and in the proof. That is correct in its own convention. So the misprint arrived with the 2019 switch to negated weights: negating k + r − 1 correctly gives 1 − k − r, but only k was negated. The Duke text could not be checked.

Why it affects nothing: this is an unnumbered descriptive sentence. The proof of Theorem 5.3.1 restates the formula correctly, and the remarks that follow use the correct weights. No later result depends on the wrong sign.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.3, Remark 5.3.1, p. 25 of the author version. HAL v3 has no Remark 5.3.1 and no normalisation of the Hecke operators.
sourceIssues.printed: We introduce a twist to fix the infinitesimal character to be (1 − k − r, 2 − r; k + 2r − 3) because when r is greater than 2, this twist optimizes the integral properties of the operator T_{ℓ,2} (it makes it integral on q-expansions) and normalizes the greater Hodge-Tate weight to be 0.
sourceIssues.correction: … and normalizes the smallest Hodge–Tate weight to be 0. The weights are (0, r − 2, r + k − 1, k + 2r − 3), and 0 is the least of them for r ≥ 2.
sourceIssues.reason: Remark 5.1.7.1 fixes the conventions: geometric Frobenius, and the cyclotomic character has HT weight −1. Theorem 5.1.7.1(3) gives HT weights (0, −λ_2, −λ_1, −λ_1 − λ_2). With λ = (1 − k − r, 2 − r) this is (0, r − 2, k + r − 1, k + 2r − 3), and Remark 5.3.2 on the same page states exactly these weights. For r ≥ 2 and k ≥ 0, 0 is the minimum. The twist confirms this. T_{ℓ,2} = ℓ^{−3}T'_{ℓ,2} amounts to tensoring with χ_p^3, since χ_p(Frob_ℓ) = ℓ^{−1} for geometric Frobenius. That lowers every weight by 3, taking (3, r+1, k+r+2, k+2r) to (0, …), so it is the smallest weight that is brought to 0. 'Greater' would be right only with the opposite sign convention (cyclotomic weight +1), which the paper explicitly rejects. The remark is purely explanatory and nothing depends on it.

review.reason: Confirmed. Remark 5.3.1 prints `normalizes the greater Hodge-Tate weight to be 0', and Remark 5.3.2 on the same page lists the weights as $(0,r-2,r+k-1,k+2r-3)$. For $r\geq2$ and $k\geq0$ every one of the last three is $\geq0$, so $0$ is the least of the four, not the greatest; at $r=2$ the list is $(0,0,k+1,k+1)$, which is also the quadruple Corollary 14.9.1 uses. The twist itself points the same way, since shifting the infinitesimal character by $3$ moves the Hodge–Tate weights down to start at $0$. The word `greater' should be `smallest', and nothing else in the remark changes.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed: `Taking the tensor product we get a cohomological correspondence $T'_{\ell,i}:p_2^\star\Omega^{(k,r)}\to p_1^!\mathcal O_{S^{\mathrm{tor}}_{K,\Sigma}}$.' The two ingredients named in the preceding sentences are the fundamental class $p_1^\star\mathcal O\to p_1^!\mathcal O$ and the differential $p_2^\star\Omega^{(k,r)}\to p_1^\star\Omega^{(k,r)}$; tensoring the first with $\Omega^{(k,r)}$ and using the projection formula of Proposition 4.1.2.1 turns it into $p_1^\star\Omega^{(k,r)}\to p_1^!\Omega^{(k,r)}$, so the composite lands in $p_1^!\Omega^{(k,r)}$. sourceIssues.correction: Replace "dimension rank_ℤW" and "genus rank_ℤW" with "dimension (genus) 2 − rank_ℤW" (= ½ rank_ℤ(W^⊥/W)) in all four places. In the last sentence, replace "ℬ_{W,γ,par} is an abelian scheme over Y_{W,γ}" with "... over Y_{W,γ,par}", as the diagram on p. 27 already has it. No other change is needed.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered pp. 27–28 at 110 and 220 dpi and confirmed the printed text above. Under the paper's own conventions the printed genus is wrong except when rank W = 1:
(1) W is a totally isotropic direct factor of V ≅ Z^4. The torus is isogenous to Sym^2(V/W^⊥)⊗G_m and has rank r(r+1)/2, with r = rank W. The Levi M_W = M_{W,l} × M_{W,h}, and §5.1.2 (p. 20) defines M_{W,h} as "the group of symplectic similitudes of W^⊥/W (with the convention that when W = W^⊥, this group is G_m)". So the abelian part of the 1-motive has dimension g' = rank(W^⊥/W)/2 = 2 − r.
(2) Dimension check, which I redid. The base has relative dimension g'(g'+1)/2, ℬ adds r·g', and the torus adds r(r+1)/2. The total is (r+g')(r+g'+1)/2, which equals 3 (the chart dimension) only if g' = 2 − r. With the printed g' = r, the r = 2 case gives Y = a Siegel threefold plus a rank-3 torus, so dimension ≥ 6 (10 if ℬ had relative dimension r·g'). For r = 1 both formulas give 1, which is a coincidence. For r = 0 the printed formula gives 0 instead of 2, since that stratum is Y_K itself.
(3) Other parts of the paper confirm the correct genus. On p. 24, S_K^(0) = P_Si(Q)\H^(0)×G(A_f)/K is 0-dimensional (the cusps), so the Siegel parabolic, W of rank 2, has no abelian part. §12.9.2 (pp. 82–83) says "The case W = {0} corresponds to the open and dense stratum". For one-dimensional W it has an elliptic curve ℬ_W over a modular curve with a G_m-torsor. For two-dimensional W it has a T_W-torsor with T_W isogenous to Hom(Sym^2 V/W^⊥, G_m) and no abelian part. That gives genus 2, 1, 0, i.e. 2 − rank W. The proof of Thm 6.1.5.1(4) also invokes "our knowledge of modular curves".
(4) The paramodular sentence names the base Y_{W,γ}, but the diagram shows ℬ_{W,γ,par} → Y_{W,γ,par}. Its second alternative (polarization degree a multiple of p^2) cannot be Y_{W,γ}, whose polarization has prime-to-p degree. So the subscript "par" was dropped.
HAL v3 has the identical wording on printed pp. 22–23, with ℬ_{W,γ,p} "over Y_{W,γ}". I rendered pp. 27–28 of the author version and pp. 23–24 of HAL v3 (PDF pages) and confirmed that the text is exactly as quoted.

Defence attempted and failed. In this section, W is explicitly "a totally isotropic direct factor W ⊂ V" with V ≅ ℤ^4. The torus T_{W,γ} is isogenous to Sym²(V/W^⊥)⊗G_m. V/W^⊥ ≅ W^∨ has rank r = rank W, so the toric part of the 1-motive has rank r and its abelian part has dimension 2 − r. I found no convention in the paper under which "rank_ℤW" means anything else. The paper's own definitions confirm the correct value:
- §5.1.2 (p. 20) defines M_{W,h} as "the group of symplectic similitudes of W^⊥/W (with the convention that when W = W^⊥, this group is G_m)". It gives M_{Kli,h} ≃ GL_2 for W = ⟨e1⟩ and M_{Si,h} ≃ G_m for W = ⟨e1,e2⟩. That is genus 1 and genus 0.
- p. 24: S_K^(0) for the Siegel parabolic is "the union of cusps".
- §12.9.2 (pp. 82–83): W = {0} is the open stratum. One-dimensional W gives an elliptic curve ℬ_W over a modular curve with a G_m-torsor. Two-dimensional W gives only a T_W-torsor, with T_W isogenous to Hom(Sym²V/W^⊥, G_m), and no abelian part.
- Dimension count: the chart has dimension (r+g')(r+g'+1)/2, which is 3 only if g' = 2 − r. With the printed g' = r, the case r = 2 would give dimension ≥ 6. The case r = 0 would give genus 0 for what is really Y_K itself. The two formulas agree only when r = 1.

The "over Y_{W,γ}" in the paramodular sentence is also a dropped subscript. The diagram shows Y_{W,γ,par}. The sentence's own second alternative (polarization degree a multiple of p²) cannot describe Y_{W,γ}, whose polarizations have prime-to-p degree, at least when W = 0.

The intended meaning is clear from the torus Sym²(V/W^⊥), from §5.1.2 and from the cited sources ([74] sect. 1, [48] sect. 6.2, [50] thm. 6.1). So this is a misprint, not a mathematical error. The label "error" would fit the literal falsity of the printed sentence, but PROTOCOL §18 counts a slip whose intended meaning is recoverable as a misprint.

Consequences: nothing depends on the wrong genus.
- Theorem 6.1.5.1 is quoted as "a special case of [50], thm. 6.1". Its part (4) is proved from "the description of the local charts, proposition 6.1.4.1 and our knowledge of modular curves". That proof matches the correct genus: W = 0 gives Y itself, rank 1 gives modular curves, rank 2 gives points.
- The other later uses rely only on rank-one W, where the printed and correct genus agree, or not on the genus at all:
  - p. 61, "smoothness of the modular curves of level Γ0(p)" at the boundary;
  - p. 94, the local charts M_{σ∩Σ'} → M_σ;
  - §12.9.2, which re-describes the strata correctly and independently.

The proposed correction is right and minimal.

review.reason: Confirmed, and the genus is decidable from the paper's own conventions. The four sentences are printed as quoted: `of dimension $\mathrm{rank}_{\Z}W$' on p. 27 and `of genus $\mathrm{rank}_{\Z}W$' three times on p. 28. Here $W\subset V\cong\Z^4$ is a totally isotropic direct factor of rank $r\in\{0,1,2\}$, and §5.1.2 defines $M_{W,h}$ as the group of symplectic similitudes of $W^\perp/W$, a lattice of rank $4-2r$; the abelian schemes parametrised by $Y_{W,\gamma}$ therefore have dimension $2-r$, not $r$. The two agree only at $r=1$, which is presumably why the slip survived. The torus rank printed in the same paragraph is consistent with this reading, $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V/W^\perp)\otimes\G_m$ having rank $r(r+1)/2$. The last of the four sentences also names the wrong base, which E37 records separately; the two findings agree.

sourceIssues.printed: Author version p. 28 (§6.1.5.3), checked on the 300 dpi page image: "Let us fix a ℤ-lattice L_W ⊂ Sym²(V/W^⊥) ⊗_ℤ ℚ. Then the cone is called smooth with respect to L_W if the s_i's can be taken to be part of a ℤ-basis of Hom(L_W, ℤ)." ... "For all (W, γ) ∈ 𝕮 × GSp_4(𝔸_f^p)/K^p we have integral structures X_⋆(T_{W,γ}), X_⋆(T_{W,γ,par}) and X_⋆(T_{W,γ,Kli(p)}) ⊂ Sym²(V/W^⊥) ⊗_ℤ ℚ. We say that a rational polyhedral cone decomposition Σ is smooth with respect to one of these integral structures if each cone σ ∈ Σ is smooth." p. 29, condition 3: "If H is Γ (resp. Γ_par, resp. Γ_{Kli}(p))-admissible, the decomposition is smooth with respect to the integral structure given by X_⋆(T_{W,γ}), (resp. X_⋆(T_{W,γ,par}), resp. X_⋆(T_{W,γ,Kli(p)}))." In every case the star is a subscript (X_⋆). Earlier on the same page the cone generators are "s_i : V/W^⊥ × V/W^⊥ → ℚ".
sourceIssues.correction: Change the three lattices in Sym²(V/W^⊥) ⊗_ℤ ℚ to the character groups X^⋆(T_{W,γ}), X^⋆(T_{W,γ,par}) and X^⋆(T_{W,γ,Kli(p)}). Put L_W = X^⋆(T) in the smoothness definition, so that the s_i form part of a ℤ-basis of Hom(X^⋆(T), ℤ) = X_⋆(T). Make the same change in condition 3 if it is read through the L_W definition. An equivalent fix keeps X_⋆ but replaces "⊂ Sym²(V/W^⊥) ⊗_ℤ ℚ" by "⊂ Hom(Sym²(V/W^⊥), ℚ)", the space of symmetric bilinear forms on V/W^⊥ that contains C(V/W^⊥). Smoothness then means the s_i form part of a ℤ-basis of X_⋆(T). Read this way, condition 3's phrase "smooth with respect to the integral structure given by X_⋆(T)" is correct as printed; this is Lan's phrasing with S_Φ^∨. This correction applies to both the author version and HAL v3.
sourceIssues.reason:
1. The paper's own conventions. On p. 20: "The character group X^⋆(T)" and "The cocharacter group X_⋆(T) is the dual of X^⋆(T)". On p. 14: "Let X_⋆(T) denote the group of cocharacters of T. Let Σ be a rational polyhedral cone in X_⋆(T). Let T → T_Σ be the associated toric embedding." So in this paper the cones that define the affine toroidal embeddings T_{W,γ} → T_{W,γ,σ} on p. 28 lie in X_⋆(T)_ℝ.

2. Where the cones actually lie. They are made of symmetric pairings: p. 27 describes C(V/W^⊥) as positive symmetric bilinear forms, and p. 28 has s_i : V/W^⊥ × V/W^⊥ → ℚ. These are elements of Hom(Sym²(V/W^⊥), ℚ). The printed definition matches this: L_W ⊂ Sym²(V/W^⊥)⊗ℚ and s_i ∈ Hom(L_W, ℤ).

3. The clash. Taking L_W = X_⋆(T), as the text does, gives Hom(L_W, ℤ) = X^⋆(T). The s_i would then be characters, contradicting p. 14. No identification can repair this, because Hom(X_⋆(T), ℤ) is always X^⋆(T).

4. The geometry agrees with the correction. In the Faltings–Chai and Lan setup the torus is E = Hom(S, G_m) with S ⊗ ℚ ≅ Sym²X. Here X is the character group of the toric part, which the paper says is V/W^⊥ (V_1/W^⊥ in the par case). So X^⋆(T) is a lattice in Sym²(V/W^⊥)⊗ℚ and X_⋆(T) is a lattice in the space of forms. I checked this on the Tate curve (V = ℤ², W = W^⊥ = ℤe_1, X = ℤ): E = Hom(Sym²X, G_m) has coordinate q, the positive ray lies in X_⋆(E)_ℝ, and E_σ = Spec ℤ[q].

5. Probable source of the slip. The paper describes T as "isogenous to Sym²(V/W^⊥) ⊗ G_m", which would give X_⋆ = Sym². Any two split tori of equal rank are isomorphic, so that phrase is vacuous and not itself wrong; the canonical, equivariant form is Hom(Sym²(V/W^⊥), G_m). With that description the cones of forms still do not lie in X_⋆(T)_ℝ, so the inconsistency stands either way.

6. HAL v3 (printed p. 23) has the same text: L_W ⊂ Sym²V/W^⊥ ⊗_ℤ ℚ, and X_⋆(T_{W,γ}), X_⋆(T_{W,γ,p}), X_⋆(T_{W,γ,Kli(p)}) ⊂ Sym²V/W^⊥ ⊗_ℤ ℚ, all subscript stars, with the same condition 3. The only differences are notation: Γ_p instead of Γ_par, and no parentheses.

7. Effect: none. Theorem 6.1.5.1 is quoted from Lan [50, thm. 6.1] and Faltings–Chai, where the conventions are correct. Later uses (§14.2, Proposition 14.4.1.1 and its proof, p. 95 "smooth polyhedral decompositions Σ and Σ' (for different integral structures)") only need smooth decompositions to exist and never compute with these lattices. The intended meaning (T_{W,γ,σ} smooth) is clear.

review.reason: Confirmed as a type slip, and the finding's primary repair is the one that restores consistency with the rest of the paper. Page 28 prints `integral structures $X_\star(T_{W,\gamma}),X_\star(T_{W,\gamma,\mathrm{par}})$ and $X_\star(T_{W,\gamma,\mathrm{Kli}(p)})\subset\mathrm{Sym}^2(V/W^\perp)\otimes_{\Z}\Q$'. The cones in play are spanned by symmetric pairings $s_i:V/W^\perp\times V/W^\perp\to\Q$, i.e.\ by elements of $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Sym}^2(V/W^\perp),\Q)$, and §3.4 puts the cone defining a toric embedding in $X_\star(T)_\R$; together these force $X_\star(T)\subset\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Sym}^2(V/W^\perp),\Q)$ and hence $X^\star(T)\subset\mathrm{Sym}^2(V/W^\perp)\otimes\Q$, which is the finding's correction. With $L_W=X^\star(T)$ the smoothness definition on the same page also reads correctly, since $\mathrm{Hom}(L_W,\Z)=X_\star(T)$ is exactly where the $s_i$ live. The alternative repair the finding records, keeping $X_\star$ and changing the ambient space, is self-consistent too; either way the printed pair of symbols cannot both stand. E38 records a separate wording slip in the same condition 3.

sourceIssues.printed: 2. If Σ′ ⊂ Σ is a refinement, then there are projective maps π_{Σ′,Σ} : X_{K,Σ′} → X_{K,Σ} and (Rπ_{Σ′,Σ})_⋆𝒪_{X_{K,Σ′}} = 𝒪_{X_{K,Σ}}. sourceIssues.correction: Replace "π^⋆_{Σ′,Σ}𝓘_{X_{K,Σ}} = 𝓘_{X_{K,Σ′}}" with "(Rπ_{Σ′,Σ})_⋆𝓘_{X_{K,Σ′}} = 𝓘_{X_{K,Σ}}", i.e. Rπ_⋆𝒪(−D′) = 𝒪(−D). Make the same change for X_par and X_Kli(p). In general there is only an inclusion π^⋆𝓘_{X_{K,Σ}} ⊂ 𝓘_{X_{K,Σ′}}, and it is an equality only when Σ′ = Σ. The corrected identity is the minimal fix. It is the form found in the literature: Boxer, arXiv:1507.05922, Prop. 3.3.4, gives R^i[1]_⋆I_D = 0 and [1]_⋆I_{D_Σ} = I_{D_{Σ′}}, citing the proof of Lan's book, Lemma 7.1.1.4. With the projection formula it gives RΓ(X_Σ, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)) ≅ RΓ(X_{Σ′}, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D′)), which is what the rest of the paper needs.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 29 at 300 dpi. The printed text reads π^⋆ with the star as a superscript, i.e. pull-back; the push-forward (Rπ)_⋆ earlier in the same sentence has a subscript star. Point 1 of the theorem defines the boundary as the reduced complement of Y_K, so 𝓘 is the ideal of a reduced divisor.

My own computation. By point 1 and the good-cone condition, the completion near the stratum of a smooth cone σ = ⟨s_1,…,s_r⟩ is toric. Locally D = {x_1⋯x_r = 0}. A nontrivial refinement of smooth fans must add a primitive ray u in the relative interior of some cone σ with dim σ ≥ 2; refining a simplicial cone using only its own rays is impossible. Write u = Σ a_i s_i with integers a_i ≥ 1. The new ray gives a boundary divisor E of X_Σ′, and ord_E π^⋆(x_1⋯x_r) = ⟨Σ s_i^*, u⟩ = Σ a_i ≥ 2. So π^⋆𝓘_D = 𝓘_{D′}(−Σ(Σa_i − 1)E) ≠ 𝓘_{D′}.

Explicit case: σ = ⟨s_1, s_2⟩ with the ray s_1+s_2 added is the blow-up. In the chart for the cone ⟨s_1+s_2, s_2⟩, with dual basis s_1^*, s_2^* − s_1^*, we have x_1 = a and x_2 = ab. Then π^⋆(x_1x_2) = a²b, while the reduced boundary has ideal (ab).

At GSp4 0-dimensional cusps the cones have dimension up to 3, so nontrivial refinements occur. The printed identity therefore fails for every Σ′ ≠ Σ. The corrected identity holds: toric ω = 𝒪(−boundary), π^⋆ω_X = ω_{X′}(−E), and Rπ_⋆𝒪(E) = 𝒪.

Downstream, nothing breaks.
- §6.2.1 (p. 30) cites point 2 only for the non-cuspidal sheaves Ω^{(k,r)}. That needs only Rπ_⋆𝒪 = 𝒪 and π^⋆Ω = Ω′, which are correct. So §6.2.1 is not about cuspidal cohomology.
- Prop. 7.2.1 (p. 40) uses t^⋆ on Ω^{(k,r)} only.
- The only place that could rely on the false identity is Lemma 7.3.1(3) (p. 41), whose cuspidal functoriality is 'proved exactly in the same way', and the corrected identity repairs it.
- Lemma 4.2.4.1 separately requires D_X → f^{-1}(D_Y) to be a homeomorphism only, which suggests the author is aware of non-reducedness.

HAL v3 has identical wording but no §6.2.1 'Definition' paragraph. The theorem attributes point 2 to Lan [50], thm. 6.1 and prop. 7.5, which I could not consult. So the false assertion is a stated result, but no later result depends on it in a way the correct statement does not cover. Printed text. I rendered p. 29 at 300 dpi. The identity has π^⋆_{Σ′,Σ} with a superscript star, so it is a pull-back. The preceding (Rπ_{Σ′,Σ})_⋆ has a subscript star. Point 1 says "The boundary is the reduced complement of Y_K in X_{K,Σ} … This is a relative Cartier divisor", so 𝓘 = 𝒪(−D) with D reduced.

Why the pull-back identity is false. By point 1, the completion along a stratum Z_σ is the completion of the affine torus embedding M̄_σ. Prop. 14.4.1.1 of the paper puts this as: M_{σ∩Σ′} → M_σ is locally T_{Σ′}×B → T_σ×B. So D is locally the toric boundary {x_1⋯x_r = 0} of a smooth cone σ = ⟨s_1,…,s_r⟩. A nontrivial refinement of smooth fans has to add a primitive ray u = Σa_i s_i, with a_i ≥ 1, in the relative interior of a face of dimension ≥ 2. A simplicial cone cannot be subdivided using only its own rays. Then ord_{E_u} π^⋆(x_1⋯x_r) = ⟨Σs_i^*, u⟩ = Σa_i ≥ 2, but E_u has multiplicity 1 in the reduced D′.

Explicit case: blow up A² at the origin (add s_1+s_2). In the chart x_1 = u, x_2 = uv, the reduced boundary {v = 0} ∪ {u = 0} has ideal (uv), while π^⋆(x_1x_2) = u²v. Such refinements exist for GSp4, since the cones at 0-dimensional cusps are 3-dimensional, and the paper itself says any two decompositions have a common refinement (p. 28). So the printed identity fails for every Σ′ ≠ Σ. The same argument applies to X_par and X_Kli(p).

Defence tried and rejected:
(a) Reading 𝓘 as 𝒪(D) or as the inverse-image ideal does not help, since π^⋆D ≠ D′.
(b) Calling it a misprint: the printed statement is a coherent, well-typed claim that is false. The intended push-forward version needs the direction reversed and R added. The context does not make this evident, although the paper's own Lemma 4.2.4.1 (which only asks for a homeomorphism D_X → f^{-1}(D_Y)) and Prop. 14.4.1.1 suggest the author knows the correct form.
(c) The cited source [50] (Lan, IMRN 2017, thm. 6.1 and prop. 7.5): I could not get it (the author's server returned 403). Boxer's account of Lan's results states the push-forward form.

The corrected statement holds: toric ω = 𝒪(−boundary), and Rπ_⋆𝒪(−D′) = 𝒪(−D) torically over any base.

Consequences:
- §6.2.1 (p. 30; this passage is absent from HAL v3's §6.4.1) cites point 2 only for Ω^{(k,r)}. That uses Rπ_⋆𝒪 = 𝒪 and π^⋆Ω = Ω′, which are correct.
- Prop. 7.2.1 uses t^⋆ on Ω^{(k,r)} only.
- The only place that implicitly needs the boundary identity is Lemma 7.3.1(3), the cuspidal analogue of 7.2.1, "proved exactly in the same way". The corrected identity covers it: t^⋆Ω(−D_Σ) ⊂ Ω(−D_Λ) is a quasi-isomorphism on RΓ.
- The independence of cuspidal cohomology from Σ (p. 24, attributed to Harris [30], prop. 2.4) is likewise true with the corrected identity.

So a stated part of Theorem 6.1.5.1 is false, but no later result in the paper fails. HAL v3 has the identical statement.

We suppose that the generic étale rank and multiplicative rank of G over S are equal to one. We let S' be the dense open subscheme of S where G has étale rank and multiplicative rank one. We moreover assume that over S, the Hasse-Witt map V⋆ : ω_G → ω_G^(p) has rank 1 : this means that Ker V⋆ is an invertible sheaf and locally a direct factor of ω_G." p. 33: "Lemma 6.3.3.3. — The maps V⋆_H and W vanish on the complement of S'. Moreover, they have the same order of vanishing. Proof. Let x be a generic point of one component of S \ S'. We work over the discrete valuation ring O_{S,x}. [...] The matrix of V⋆ in this basis has the form (0 a; 0 b) where b ∈ m_{S,x} and a ∈ O^×_{S,x} since V⋆_H vanishes at x and V⋆ has rank one. The claim is now obvious." "Lemma 6.3.3.5. — This section is regular and vanishes precisely over S \ S'. Proof. This follows from lemma 6.3.3.3 since p + 1 > p − 1."
sourceIssues.correction:
Minimal fix, keeping S' and Proposition 6.3.3.1 unchanged. In Lemmas 6.3.3.3 and 6.3.3.5, replace "the complement of S'" and "S∖S'" with "the closed subset where G has multiplicative rank 0". That subset is exactly where H is not multiplicative, and therefore exactly where V⋆_H vanishes. This is the missing justification: H_y = V(G_y[F]^{(p)}), which equals G_y^m (≅ μ_p) when the multiplicative rank is 1, and is α_p-like otherwise. By duality, B vanishes exactly on the locus of étale rank 0. V⋆ has rank 1 on ω_G and, by Lemma 6.3.3.1, on ω_{G^D}. So both ranks are at most 1, and S∖S' is the union of these two loci. Proposition 6.3.3.1 then holds as stated, with the same proof: A⊗B vanishes exactly on S∖S'.

An alternative correction also works: add the hypothesis that étale rank equals multiplicative rank at every point. This holds in Lemma 6.4.2, because G is the p-torsion of an abelian surface with a prime-to-p or paramodular polarization, and p-rank(A) = p-rank(A^t). Quasi-polarizability is not needed.

A second option (redefine S' as the locus of multiplicative rank 1) is not suitable for Prop. 6.3.3.1. The invariant Ha'(G) is only defined where both ranks are 1.

I rendered pp. 29–34 and read them; the transcription above matches the page. The hypotheses of §6.3.3 bound the ranks only at the generic points, and they allow a point with étale rank 0 but multiplicative rank 1. The proof asserts without justification that "V⋆_H vanishes at x", and that is exactly the step that fails.

Counterexample. Let S = Spec F̄_p[[t]], which is normal and reduced. Take the Lubin–Tate deformation of the height-3 formal group over F̄_p[[u1,u2]] and restrict it to the curve u1=0, u2=t. This gives a connected p-divisible group G_1 over S of height 3 and dimension 1 (Tate). Its formal height is 2 at the generic point, so G_1 there has an étale part of height 1 and a local-local part of height 2. At the closed point its formal height is 3, so it is local-local. Set G = μ_p × G_1[p]. This is a BT_1 of height 4 and dimension 2.

1. The generic étale rank and multiplicative rank are both 1, so S' is the generic point. At the closed point the étale rank is 0 and the multiplicative rank is 1.
2. V⋆ has rank 1 everywhere. It is an isomorphism on ω_{μ_p}. It is zero on ω_{G_1}, because [p](x)=V(x^p) and the formal height is ≥2, so the coefficient of x^p vanishes. So Ker V⋆ = ω_{G_1} is an invertible direct factor. All hypotheses hold.
3. The construction of Lemma 6.3.3.2 gives H = μ_p on all of S. V is an isomorphism on μ_p^(p) and zero on G_1[F]^(p), so K = G_1[F]^(p) and H = G[F]^(p)/K = μ_p. It is also the unique finite flat extension of G^m_{S'} = μ_p.
4. Hence V⋆_H = V⋆_{μ_p} is an isomorphism at the closed point. So is W: ω^(p)_{G_1} → (ω^(p)_{μ_p}⊕ω^(p)_{G_1})/ω^(p)_{μ_p}. Lemma 6.3.3.3 therefore fails.
5. Z is pointwise an isomorphism. It is induced by V on E/(ω_G + Ker V) → Im V/V(ω_G) = ω_G^(p)/V⋆ω_G, using Ker V = Im F⋆. So A = (V⋆_H)^{p+1}⊗(W^{-1}∘Z)^{p-1} is nowhere zero, and Lemma 6.3.3.5 ("vanishes precisely over S∖S'") fails too.

The damage is contained. The dual section B does vanish at the closed point, because G^D has multiplicative rank 0 there. So Prop. 6.3.3.1 still holds in this example, and its proof can be repaired as described in the correction. Its application in Lemma 6.4.2 is unaffected. This is an error, not a gap, because the two lemmas are false under the paper's stated hypotheses. The counterexample holds up. Take S = Spec F̄_p[[t]] and G = μ_p × X[p]. Here X is the restriction of the Lubin–Tate family of the height-3, dimension-1 formal group to the curve u_1 = 0, u_2 = t. Generically X is étale of rank 1 times a local-local group of height 2; at the closed point x it is local-local of height 3. G is a BT_1 of height 4 and dimension 2.

Checking the hypotheses:
- X[p] has multiplicative rank 0 everywhere, so V⋆ is 0 on the line bundle ω_{X[p]}. On ω_{μ_p}, V⋆ is an isomorphism. So V⋆ on ω_G has rank 1 everywhere, and its kernel ω_{X[p]} is a direct factor.
- The generic ranks are (étale, multiplicative) = (1, 1). At x they are (0, 1). So S' = {η} and S∖S' = {x}.

What Lemma 6.3.3.2 constructs here:
- V is 0 on X[F]^{(p)}: it vanishes at every point and S is reduced. So K = X[F]^{(p)} and H = μ_p on all of S.
- So V⋆_H is an isomorphism at x.
- ω_{G[F]/H} = ω_{X[p]} and V⋆(ω_G) = ω_{μ_p}^{(p)}, so W is the identity of ω_{X[p]}^{(p)}.
- Z is always an isomorphism, since V⋆(E) = Ker F⋆ = ω_G^{(p)} pointwise and both sides are line bundles.
- So A = (V⋆_H)^{p+1}⊗(W^{-1}Z)^{p-1} is nowhere zero. Lemma 6.3.3.3 (first sentence) and Lemma 6.3.3.5 ("vanishes precisely over S∖S'") are false as stated.

The proof simply assumes that V⋆_H vanishes at x. No convention or nearby statement supplies this: §6.3.3 never requires the two ranks to agree pointwise, and HAL v3 is even looser.

The "same order" part of Lemma 6.3.3.3 is sound once b ∈ m. For the matrix (0 a; 0 b) with (a, b) unimodular: if b is a unit, then V⋆_H and W are both isomorphisms. If b ∈ m, then a is a unit and W(f_1) = −(b/a)f_2. So A is always regular and is, locally, b^2 times a unit.

Consequences:
- Proposition 6.3.3.1 survives. A vanishes exactly on the locus of multiplicative rank 0 and B exactly on the locus of étale rank 0. Their union is S∖S', because rank 2 is excluded by V⋆ having rank 1 on ω_G and ω_{G^D}. In the counterexample, B vanishes at x, since L_x ⊂ X^D[p]_x is local-local, so Ha'(G) still vanishes there.
- The only uses are Prop. 6.3.3.1 (p. 33), Lemma 6.4.2 (p. 36) and Remark 6.4.1 (p. 37). In all of them G is the p-torsion of a polarized abelian surface, so étale rank = multiplicative rank = p-rank. The lemmas hold there as printed.
- Two intermediate lemmas are false in the generality stated. Nothing later in the paper is affected.

sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 35 at 110 and 250 dpi. The superscripts are clearly ≤r and ≥r, and the words are "less than r" and "greater than r". HAL v3 (PDF pp. 29–30) has word-for-word the same two items.

In English, "less than" and "greater than" are strict. Read that way, the definitions contradict the paper itself:
(1) The next sentence says "X_n^{=r} is dense open in X_n^{≤r}". This is impossible if X^{≤r} means rank < r, because then X^{=r} and X^{<r} are disjoint.
(2) p. 35 defines X_1^{≤1} as the vanishing locus of Ha(G), which is the non-ordinary locus (rank ≤ 1). The strict reading would give the rank-0 locus.
(3) p. 5 says X^{≥2}_{Kli(p)K} "is the ordinary locus". The strict reading makes X^{≥2} empty, since rank > 2 never occurs.
(4) Lemma 6.4.2 and p. 37 use X_1^{≤0}, defined as the vanishing locus of Ha'(G) (the p-rank 0 locus), which is non-empty. The strict reading makes it empty.
(5) p. 3 and §9.2 (p. 51) describe X^{≥1} as where the p-rank or multiplicative rank "is at least 1".

The paper has no convention that "less than" means ≤. §13.1.1 carefully writes "less or equal to h" and "strictly greater than h". The wording is a Gallicism ("inférieur à"), and it recurs in §14.7 ("cocycles of slope less than h" for (M•)^{≤h}). The symbols and every later use are unambiguous, so no statement or proof depends on the strict reading. Affects: nothing.

Side observation, not part of this entry: the same paragraph says X^{=r} and X^{≤r} "are of dimension 3 − r (see [57])". By Norman–Oort [57], for g = 2 the rank-r stratum has codimension 2 − r, so its dimension is r + 1. Footnote 11 (p. 48) itself says X_1^{=0} has dimension 1, and the ordinary stratum r = 2 is dense in the threefold. So "3 − r" looks like a separate misprint for "r + 1" (it agrees only when r = 1). HAL v3 prints the same "3 − r (see [53])".

sourceIssues.reason: I read the rendered p. 34 at 250 dpi; the formula is exactly as quoted. The paper itself says ω is contravariant (λ^⋆ : ω_{G′} → ω_G). The character group of G = T ⊗ μ_{p^∞} is T^∨, so ω_G = T^∨ ⊗ ω_μ. Test case: T = Z_p^h, G = μ_{p^∞}^h. Then ω_G = ω_μ^{⊕h} and det ω_G = ω_μ^{⊗h}, not ω_μ. T also enters through its dual. If det λ_0 = p^r u with u a unit, the literal reading gives u^{−1} where the correct map is u = p^{−r}det λ^⋆. The paper needs the latter, since it later says this is the same normalization as the cohomological correspondence (Prop. 7.4.1.1). The intended construction is clear, and it works once the formula is corrected. The Hasse-invariant compatibility is unaffected either way: the canonical trivialisations of (det T/pT)^{p−1} kill the difference, because ū^{p−1} = 1 in F_p. For the same reason the next sentence should strictly read Ha(G) = 1⊗Ha(μ_{p^∞})^{⊗h}. That is part of the same slip.

sourceIssues.locator: §6.4 (Stratification of the special fiber), p. 35, the paragraph right after the definitions of X_n^{=r}, X_n^{≤r}, X_n^{≥r}, author version of 17 June 2019. [57] is Norman–Oort, "Moduli of abelian varieties". HAL v3 has the same text on printed p. 29 (PDF p. 30), in the notation X_{p,n} and citing [53], which is Norman–Oort in that bibliography.
sourceIssues.printed: We define similarly X^{=r}_{par,n}, X^{≤r}_{par,n} and X^{≥r}_{par,n}. We recall that X^{=r}_n is dense open in X^{≤r}_n, that X^{=r}_{par,n} is dense open in X^{≤r}_{par,n} and they are of dimension 3 − r (see [57]).
sourceIssues.correction: "... and they are of dimension r + 1", which is codimension 2 − r in the 3-dimensional X_n or X_{par,n}. An equally minimal fix is "of codimension 3 − r in X": X is 4-dimensional over Z_p, so 3 − r is exactly the codimension of the stratum there. The reading "dimension r + 1 (codimension 2 − r in the 3-dimensional X_n)" is right and minimal.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page image at 200 dpi; the printed text is exactly as quoted. HAL v3 (image checked) has the same sentence.

1. Setting. X is a toroidal compactification of Y_K, which Prop. 6.1.4.1 says is smooth over Z_p. So X_n has the underlying space of X_1, a 3-dimensional F_p-scheme. r is the multiplicative rank, which is the p-rank, and r = 2 is the ordinary locus.

2. r = 2 fails. The sentence itself says X_n^{=2} is dense open in X_n^{≤2} = X_n, so its dimension is 3, not 3 − 2 = 1.

3. r = 0 fails, even inside the paper. X_1^{≤1} is defined as the vanishing locus of Ha(G), a section of the invertible sheaf ω^{p−1} on the smooth 3-fold X_1. So it has dimension 2, and X^{≤0} ⊂ X^{≤1} cannot have dimension 3. By Norman–Oort, the p-rank ≤ r locus has codimension g − r = 2 − r in a 3-dimensional space, so its dimension is 1 + r (3, 2, 1 for r = 2, 1, 0). Only r = 1 happens to agree with 3 − r.

4. Paramodular case (pp. 36–37). Away from the finite set SS, X^{≤1}_{par,1} is locally Spec F_p[a,b,c]/(ab), and X^{=1}_{par,1} is the part where a ≠ 0 or b ≠ 0. So X^{=0}_{par,1} \ SS lies in {a = b = 0}, which has dimension ≤ 1.

5. The paper elsewhere uses the correct values:
- Footnote 11, p. 48: "The p-rank 0 locus X_1^{=0} is of dimension 1".
- Lemma 7.4.2.5, p. 48: "the p-rank 0 locus has codimension 1" in X_Kli(p)_1 ×_{X_1} X_1^{≤1}.
- Proof of Prop. 8.2.1, p. 53: "Since X_1^{=0} is of codimension 2 in X_1".
- p. 38: the non-ordinary locus has codimension 2 in X_Kli(p).

The corrected reading is right. It is a slip, not a substantive error: 3 − r is exactly the codimension of the stratum in the 4-dimensional X, and the intended values are clear from context. Nothing depends on the wrong values:
- The proofs of Lemmas 6.4.1 and 6.4.2 use only the density claims (which are correct) and the r = 1 case, where both formulas give 2.
- Every later argument (§7.4, Prop. 8.2.1, §11, Lemma 14.9.2) states the dimension or codimension it needs directly and does not cite this sentence.
- The sentence restates Norman–Oort; it is not a result of the paper.

So 'affects' is 'nothing', not 'a stated result'. A separate slip in the same passage, not part of this item: the definitions say "less than r" and "greater than r" where they mean ≤ r and ≥ r. I tried to defend the text and could not. As printed, the sentence is false.

(1) Setting. Prop. 6.1.4.1 (p. 26) says Y_K is smooth over Z_p. X is its toroidal compactification, a Siegel threefold. So X_n has the underlying space of X_1, which is 3-dimensional. r is the multiplicative rank of G, which equals the p-rank, so r = 2 is the ordinary locus. No convention in the paper makes "dimension 3 − r" come out right: r is not a corank, and "dimension" does not mean codimension anywhere else in the paper.

(2) The sentence contradicts itself at r = 2. It says X_n^{=2} is dense open in X_n^{≤2} = X_n, so X_n^{=2} has dimension 3, not 3 − 2 = 1.

(3) At r = 0 it contradicts the construction that follows. On p. 35, X_1^{≤1} is the vanishing locus of Ha(G), a nonzero section of the line bundle ω^{p−1} on the smooth 3-fold X_1, so it has dimension 2. On p. 37, X_1^{≤0} is the vanishing locus of Ha' inside X_1^{≤1}. So X^{=0} cannot have dimension 3. Norman–Oort says the p-rank ≤ f locus has codimension g − f; with g = 2 that gives dimension r + 1, i.e. 3, 2, 1 for r = 2, 1, 0. Only r = 1 happens to give the same value under both formulas.

(4) The paramodular case agrees with r + 1. On pp. 36–37, away from the finite set SS, X^{≤1}_{par,1} is locally Spec F_p[a,b,c]/(ab), which is 2-dimensional, and X^{=1}_{par,1} is where a ≠ 0 or b ≠ 0. So X^{=0}_{par,1} has dimension ≤ 1, and exactly 1 because it is cut out by Ha' inside a 2-dimensional scheme.

(5) The paper itself uses the correct values elsewhere:
- footnote 11, p. 48: "The p-rank 0 locus X_1^{=0} is of dimension 1";
- Lemma 7.4.2.5, p. 48: "the p-rank 0 locus has codimension 1" in X_{Kli(p),1} ×_{X_1} X_1^{≤1};
- proof of Prop. 8.2.1, p. 53: "Since X_1^{=0} is of codimension 2 in X_1".

So the intended content is clear from context: a standard Norman–Oort fact that the paper states correctly elsewhere. That makes it a misprint rather than a substantive error.

Consequences. Nothing downstream relies on the wrong numbers.
- The proof of Lemma 6.4.1 uses only that X^{=1} is dense in X^{≤1}, which is correct: it works at the generic points of the non-ordinary locus.
- The proof of Lemma 6.4.2 uses only that X^{≤1} is Cohen–Macaulay and that the finite set SS has codimension ≥ 2 in it. That holds because X^{≤1} is 2-dimensional, which is the r = 1 case, where both formulas agree.
- Every later dimension argument states the value it needs directly and does not cite this sentence: footnote 11 and Lemma 7.4.2.5; Prop. 8.2.1; the codimension-2 claims on p. 38 and in Lemma 10.5.2.2; and the codimension-2 claims for X^{≥1} on pp. 71 and 103.
- The sentence only recalls a result from [57]; it is not a result of the paper.

So affects = nothing, not "a stated result".

sourceIssues.printed: Author version p. 35, checked on the rendered page: "The contravariant Dieudonné module D of H is isomorphic to the 4-dimensional free W(k)-module with canonical basis (e1, e2, e3, e4) and with Frobenius matrix given by : (p 0 0 0 ; 0 0 1 0 ; 0 p 0 0 ; 0 0 0 1) It is the sum of three direct factors W(k)e1 ⊕ (W(k)e2 ⊕ W(k)e3) ⊕ W(k)e4, corresponding to the multiplicative-biconnected-étale decomposition. We find that the Hodge filtration is given by Ker(F) = ⟨ē1, ē2⟩ ⊂ D/pD. [...] The matrix of F in the basis ē3, ē4 of D ⊗ R/Fil is: (−Y 0 ; −Z 1). [...] There is a unique principal polarization on D, induced by the symplectic form of matrix J (see section 5.1). In the principally polarized case, the tangent space at x is given by the subspace where the filtration is isotropic with respect to this polarization. This condition writes X = Z." Section 5.1 (p. 19) defines J = (0 A ; −A 0), where A is the 2x2 anti-diagonal matrix with entries 1. So ⟨e1,e4⟩ = ⟨e2,e3⟩ = 1.
sourceIssues.correction:
The minimal fix is to change the (3,2) entry of the Frobenius matrix from p to −p, so that F e2 = −p e3 and F e3 = e2. This keeps Ker F = ⟨ē1,ē2⟩, the displayed matrix (−Y 0; −Z 1), the isotropy condition X = Z, the Fil^⊥ display, and the paramodular forms J·diag(1,p,p,1) and J·diag(p,1,1,p) with their conditions Z = 0 and X = 0. All of these then become correct.

An alternative correction takes F e3 = −e2 instead. That is also valid, but the displayed matrix then becomes (Y 0; Z 1).

Another proposed reading is wrong: keeping F and taking ⟨e1,e4⟩ = 1, ⟨e2,e3⟩ = −1 is not compatible either. With the printed F, the compatible principal forms are exactly ⟨e1,e4⟩ = a with a ∈ Z_p^× and ⟨e2,e3⟩ = c with c ∈ W(k)^× and σ(c) = −c. The isotropy condition is then aZ = c̄X, as in HAL v3.

Also, "unique" should read "unique up to isomorphism".

A principal quasi-polarization must satisfy ⟨Fx,Fy⟩ = pσ⟨x,y⟩ (equivalently ⟨Fx,y⟩ = σ⟨x,Vy⟩). With J integral this means MᵀJM = pJ. Directly: ⟨Fe2,Fe3⟩ = ⟨pe3,e2⟩ = −p, while pσ⟨e2,e3⟩ = p.

That version is consistent, because a compatible form with ⟨e2,e3⟩ = c, σ(c) = −c exists over W(k) for k algebraically closed. So the inconsistency came in with the 2019 rewrite.
