The conclusion is unaffected. With any consistent fix the tangent condition is linear in X and Z only, and the Hasse invariant ±Y is a nonzero linear form on it. The paramodular conditions Z = 0 and X = 0 on p. 36 do not depend on the sign. Lemma 6.4.1 is not cited by number anywhere later in the text. 1. Reading the matrix. Its columns are the images of the basis vectors: F e1 = p e1, F e2 = p e3, F e3 = e2, F e4 = e4. This is the only reading that gives the printed Ker(F) = ⟨ē1,ē2⟩; reading rows as images gives ⟨ē1,ē3⟩. 3. The fix is right. With F e2 = −p e3 (or with F e3 = −e2), MᵀJM = pJ, and the paramodular forms are compatible too (checked numerically).

4. The other claims check out. The isotropy of Fil is ⟨f1,f2⟩ = Z⟨e1,e4⟩ + X⟨e3,e2⟩ = Z − X under J. The p. 36 Fil^⊥ is exactly the J-orthogonal of Fil. For a general compatible form (a, c), Fil^⊥ = ⟨(1,0,(a/c)Z,W), (0,1,Y,(c/a)X)⟩, and the paramodular conditions are still Z = 0 and X = 0.

5. The other readings. The reading c = −1 fails: with the printed F, ⟨Fe2,Fe3⟩ = p, but pσ(−1) = −p. Compatible forms with the printed F do exist. For p odd, take c to be the Teichmüller lift of a root of ζ^{p−1} = −1; for p = 2, use Lang's theorem on W(k)^×. The choice u^{p−1} = −1 works only for p odd, but no restriction to p odd is needed.

So the only false step is choosing a basis that is standard for F and for J at the same time. That is a one-sign slip, which PROTOCOL §18 lists as a misprint ("an index, a sign, a name").

Lemma 6.4.1 is not cited by number anywhere later in the paper. Its content is used implicitly: the scheme structures X_1^{≤1} and X_par,1^{≤1} feed Lemma 6.4.2 and §6.4 onward. Those uses depend only on the statement, which is unaffected.

The Frobenius matrix is printed with rows $(p,0,0,0)$, $(0,0,1,0)$, $(0,p,0,0)$, $(0,0,0,1)$, so reading columns as images $Fe_1=pe_1$, $Fe_2=pe_3$, $Fe_3=e_2$, $Fe_4=e_4$; that is the reading which gives the printed $\ker F=\langle\bar e_1,\bar e_2\rangle$ and the printed matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-Y&0\\-Z&1\end{pmatrix}$ of $F$ on $\bar e_3,\bar e_4$. I rendered p. 36 at 110 and 250 dpi. The page prints "λ^t : (G′)^t → G." with an unprimed G, and the text layer reads the same way. The same sentence appears word for word in HAL v3 (Lemma 6.3.2, PDF p. 31, rendered and checked).

Why the target must be G′, under the paper's own conventions:
(1) In §6.1.3, λ′ : G′ → (G′)^t is a polarization of degree p^2, so K(λ) has order p^2. The dual polarization of (G′)^t is the isogeny λ^t : (G′)^t → G′ with λ^t ∘ λ = p. Its kernel is λ(G′[p]) ≅ G′[p]/K(λ), which has order p^4/p^2 = p^2. That fits the proof's own claim that K(λ^t) is a BT_1 of height 2. A polarization of (G′)^t lands in (G′)^{tt} = G′ in any case.
(2) G = G′/H is only defined in the next sentence. Any map (G′)^t → G′/H along the chain is (G′)^t → G′′ → G′ → G, which has degree p^3. That cannot be a polarization whose kernel has height 2.
(3) The printed chain itself contains "→ G′′ → G′ → G". So the map G′′ → G′ is the one induced by λ^t, which factors through (G′)^t/H′ because H′ ⊂ K(λ^t).
(4) The same structure appears elsewhere in the paper. §14.9.2, p. 104, speaks of "the universal chain G → (G′)^t → G′ → G (where the first map has degree p, the second p^2, the third p ...)", so there the degree-p^2 map (G′)^t → G′ targets G′. §6.1.2–6.1.3 give the Klingen chain G → G/H → G/H^⊥ → G, with G′ = G/H^⊥ and (G′)^t ≅ G/H.

Degree check: G′→G has degree |H| = p; G→(G′)^t has degree |K(λ)/H| = p; (G′)^t→G′′ has degree |H′| = p; G′′→G′ has degree |K(λ^t)/H′| = p. The total is p^4 = deg[p] on an abelian surface, which is consistent.

So the unprimed G is a dropped prime. It is not a text-layer artefact, and no convention in the paper makes it correct. This correction is right.

Effect: the argument only uses K(λ^t), H′ and G′′ to embed X^{≤1}_{par,1} \ SS into the Iwahori-level moduli space and to read off the local model from [62]. With the obvious reading that the target is G′, all of this goes through unchanged. Nothing later depends on the wrong target: Lemma 6.4.2, the definition of X^{≤0}_{par,1}, and later uses of the chain (e.g. p. 104) all use the correct (G′)^t → G′.

sourceIssues.locator: §7.1, proof of Lemma 7.1.1, last paragraph, p. 39 of the author version. HAL v3, p. 32, has the same text.
sourceIssues.printed: On the components where G → G′ has kernel a group of p-rank two, the map p_2^⋆Ω^{(k,r)} → p_1^⋆Ω^{(k,r)} factors through p^{(k+2r)}p_1^⋆Ω^{(k,r)} and the map p_1^⋆Ω^{(k,r)} → p_1^!Ω^{(k,r)} is an isomorphism.
sourceIssues.correction: "On the components where G → G′ has kernel a group of étale rank one (equivalently, of multiplicative rank two), …"
sourceIssues.reason: I read the rendered p. 39 at 250 dpi. The kernel L of G → G′ has order p^3 and lies in G[p], which at an ordinary point is μ_p^2 × (Z/p)^2. So there are two cases: étale rank 2 with multiplicative rank 1, or étale rank 1 with multiplicative rank 2. The proof handles the first case first ("components where G → G′ has kernel a group of étale rank two", p. 38), where it gets divisibility by p^r and a fundamental class divisible by p^2. In standard usage the p-rank is the étale rank, so "p-rank two" names that first case again, with a contradictory conclusion. The stated conclusion fits only the second case. There L ⊇ G[p]^m, so λ restricted to G^m is [p] up to an isomorphism, and λ^⋆ on ω = ω_{G^m} is p times an isomorphism. That gives p^k·p^{2r} on Sym^k ⊗ det^r. Also, subgroups L ⊇ G[p]^m correspond to lines in G[p]^{et}, so p_1 is étale there and the fundamental class is an isomorphism. The proof of Prop. 7.4.1.1 (p. 42) describes these components correctly as "of étale rank 1 and thus of multiplicative rank 2". One caveat: the paper calls X^{=r} (multiplicative rank of G equal to r) the "p-rank r locus". A reader who carries over "p-rank = multiplicative rank" to L would read the sentence correctly. That is why confidence is medium, not high.

This is a trivial labelling slip with clear intended meaning, which is why confidence is only medium: some readers would call it harmless abuse of notation.

sourceIssues.locator: §7.4.2, proof of Lemma 7.4.2.3, p. 45 (first sentence of the proof)
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. Over X^{=1,oo}_{par,1} we consider K(λ) the kernel of the quasi-polarization G′[p^∞] → (G′)^t[p^∞]. If G′ is an abelian scheme, this group is either a connected BT_1 of height 2 and dimension 1 or an extension of an étale by a multiplicative group. We consider the group KerF : K(λ) → K(λ)^{(p)}. This is a rank p group either of multiplicative type or locally isomorphic to α_p. We can apply lemma 7.4.2.1.
sourceIssues.correction: Replace "Over X^{=1,oo}_{par,1}" with "Over X^{=1}_{par,1}". The lemma statement and the rest of the proof stay as they are.
sourceIssues.reason: I rendered p. 45 at 150 and 300 dpi. The superscript is clearly "=1,oo", so this is not a text-layer artefact. Lemma 7.4.2.3 says that X^{=1}_{par,1} is the union of two kinds of open and closed pieces, X^{=1,oo}_{par,1} and X^{=1,m−et}_{par,1}. Neither piece is defined before this lemma: grep finds no earlier "=1,oo" or "=1,m−et", and the pieces are only named later in Lemma 7.4.2.4 and the T_1/T_2 split. So the proof has to work over all of X^{=1}_{par,1}. The proof itself shows this. Its next sentence covers both cases, K(λ) a connected BT_1 of height 2 and dimension 1 (biconnected) or an extension of étale by multiplicative. Then Lemma 7.4.2.1 is applied to the order-p group Ker F on K(λ), which is multiplicative or locally α_p. That gives S = S^m ⊔ S^oo, with S^et empty because Ker F is connected. These two pieces are exactly the two in the lemma. Starting the proof on the oo-piece is circular and would never reach the m−et case, so the "oo" is a stray superscript. The intended reading is obvious and the argument is correct once it is fixed. Later results use only the statement of Lemma 7.4.2.3, which is unaffected: Lemma 7.4.2.4, the decompositions T_1 = T_1^m + T_1^et + T_1^oo and T_2 = T_2^m + T_2^et + T_2^oo, and Proposition 7.4.2.1. So affects = nothing. HAL v3 (printed p. 37, PDF p. 38; image checked) has the same sentence, "Proof. Over X^{=1,oo}_{p,1} we consider K(λ) …". The only difference is that HAL v3 writes X_{p,1} where the author version writes X_{par,1}. So the misprint was carried over between versions. The published Duke version could not be checked.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed: the proof of Lemma 7.4.2.3 opens `Over $X^{=1,oo}_{\mathrm{par},1}$ we consider $K(\lambda)$ the kernel of the quasi-polarization'. The lemma is the statement that $X^{=1}_{\mathrm{par},1}$ decomposes into the two kinds of components $X^{=1,oo}_{\mathrm{par},1}$ and $X^{=1,m-et}_{\mathrm{par},1}$, so those pieces are its conclusion and cannot be the domain its proof starts from; neither symbol occurs earlier in the paper. The argument that follows — classify $K(\lambda)$, then $\ker F$ inside it, then apply Lemma 7.4.2.1 — is exactly an argument over all of $X^{=1}_{\mathrm{par},1}$. E58 records a separate gap in the same proof, about the semi-abelian case at the boundary; the two findings are about different clauses and do not conflict.

sourceIssues.locator: §7.4.2, proof of Lemma 7.4.2.3 (and the proof of Lemma 7.4.2.4 below it), p. 45 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same text at Lemma 7.4.2.3, with X_{p,1} in place of X_{par,1} (PDF p. 38, printed p. 37).
sourceIssues.printed: Proof of Lemma 7.4.2.3: "Over X^{=1,oo}_{par,1} we consider K(λ) the kernel of the quasi-polarization G'[p^∞] → (G')^t[p^∞]. If G' is an abelian scheme, this group is either a connected BT_1 of height 2 and dimension 1 or an extension of an étale by a multiplicative group. We consider the group KerF : K(λ) → K(λ)^{(p)}. This is a rank p group either of multiplicative type or locally isomorphic to α_p. We can apply lemma 7.4.2.1." Proof of Lemma 7.4.2.4: "The group Ker(G' → G) is a closed subgroup of K(λ) and therefore it determines its type : it is étale or multiplicative if K(λ) contains a mutliplicative group, and it is biconnected if K(λ) is."
sourceIssues.correction: Add a treatment of the boundary. X^{=1}_{par,1} meets the boundary D exactly at torus-rank-1 points whose abelian part E' is supersingular; torus-rank-2 points are ordinary. §6.1.5.2 lists two kinds of torus-rank-1 charts for X_par. (a) B_{W,γ,par} lies over elliptic curves with a polarization of prime-to-p degree. Then the p-part of λ sits on the torus, λ restricted to the torus has kernel μ_p, and so ker λ contains μ_p: the m−et type. (b) The polarization of E' has degree p^2 times a prime-to-p integer. Then λ is an isomorphism on the torus and on the character group, and K(λ) sits inside the finite flat G̃[p] of Mumford's construction, where G̃[p] has constant ranks (multiplicative 1, étale 0 on this locus). There K(λ) ≅ E'[p], which is biconnected: the oo type. Apply Lemma 7.4.2.1 to H = Ker F|_{K(λ)} ⊂ G̃[p] over the formal completion along each chart, as in the paper's own footnote 13 on G̃. Then the type is constant on a neighbourhood of every boundary point, so the open–closed decomposition of the interior extends to all of X^{=1}_{par,1}, "by the description of the local charts" as in Lemma 7.4.2.2. This correction is right and minimal. Separately, the first words of the proof, "Over X^{=1,oo}_{par,1}", should read "Over X^{=1}_{par,1}": this is a slip, since that set is being defined.
sourceIssues.reason:
(1) Boundary points exist in X^{=1}_{par,1}. §6.4 defines X^{=r}_{par,n} on the toroidal compactification using the multiplicative rank of the semi-abelian G'. §6.1.5.2 (pp. 28-29) says that each rank-1 boundary stratum of X_par is fibred over the universal elliptic curve, with polarization either prime to p or of degree a prime-to-p multiple of p^2. Over supersingular points of these modular curves, the semi-abelian G' = extension of a supersingular E by G_m has multiplicative rank exactly 1. This gives a 1-dimensional boundary divisor inside the 2-dimensional X^{=1}_{par,1}. The paper knows these points exist: p. 36 says "The construction applies to the open subscheme of X^{=1} ... where the semi-abelian scheme is an abelian scheme. We check that the second Hasse invariant extends to the boundary." The decomposition is also used with Ω(−D) on p. 45, i.e. H^*(X^{=1,oo}_{par,1}, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)). (2) The proof as printed covers only the abelian locus. The case analysis of K(λ) is stated only "If G' is an abelian scheme". The final step applies Lemma 7.4.2.1, which requires the subgroup to lie in a truncated Barsotti-Tate group of level N with constant étale and multiplicative ranks. At a boundary point G'[p] is quasi-finite and not finite, so that hypothesis fails, and nothing else in the proof handles these points. Compare Lemma 7.4.2.2 just above, whose proof explicitly says "This decomposition extends to X_Kli(p)|X^{=1}_{par,1} by the description of the local charts". Footnote 13 (p. 54) likewise replaces G[p^m] by G̃[p^m] at the boundary. Lemma 7.4.2.3 has no such step. (3) The stated result is still true. At the boundary, K(λ) is either E[p] with E supersingular (biconnected, KerF ≅ α_p) or μ_p (KerF = μ_p). Near the boundary, X^{=1}_{par,1} is locally the product of a supersingular point, the elliptic fibre and the toric line, so each local component lies entirely in one type and the decomposition extends. The omission is therefore a routine, fillable gap in the proof, not an error in the statement. The HAL v3 text is identical. Defence attempts, and why they fail.
(1) Does the lemma really concern boundary points? Yes. §6.4 defines X^{=r} using the multiplicative rank of the semi-abelian G'. Torus-rank-1 points with supersingular abelian part have rank 1 and Ha = 0. §6.4 itself treats the boundary of X^{=1} ("We check that the second Hasse invariant extends to the boundary"). The cohomology on p. 45 is H^*(X^{=1,oo}_{par,1}, Ω(−D)) ⊕ H^*(X^{=1,m−et}_{par,1}, Ω(−D)), and the twist by the boundary divisor only matters because the boundary meets the stratum.
(2) Does the proof cover those points? No. It says "If G' is an abelian scheme, this group is either…" and gives no other case. Lemma 7.4.2.1 needs a truncated BT group with constant ranks, and G'[p] is not one at the boundary, where it is only quasi-finite. Compare Lemma 7.4.2.2 just above, which states the interior-only step and then adds "extends … by the description of the local charts". §10.2 hedges the same way: "When G' is an abelian scheme, this group is…".
(3) Is density enough? Not on its own. Closures of two disjoint open–closed pieces of the interior can meet at a boundary point. To rule this out you need either normality or smoothness of X^{=1}_{par,1} at the boundary, or a chart analysis, and the paper gives neither here. The density reduction used in the proof of Proposition 7.4.2.1 works for identities of maps, not for open–closed decompositions.
(4) Is the statement still true? Yes, by the chart analysis in the correction. The two kinds of torus-rank-1 charts in §6.1.5.2 give K(λ) ⊇ μ_p (m−et) and K(λ) ≅ E'[p] with E' supersingular (oo), so the type is locally constant near the boundary.

Downstream use. Lemma 7.4.2.4: once 7.4.2.3 holds everywhere, it follows by density of the interior. The paired cohomology maps on p. 45. Most importantly, Corollary 7.4.2.1 (T = T1∘T2 = T1^et∘T2^et for r ≥ p+1). Its proof cites only T1^m = T1^oo = T2^m = 0, but it also needs the cross term T1^et∘T2^oo to vanish, and Remark 7.4.2.1 says T2^oo ≠ 0 at r = p+1. That cross term vanishes because p2 sends the oo components into X^{=1,oo}_{par,1} and the et components into X^{=1,m−et}_{par,1}, which are disjoint open–closed pieces, and this uses Lemmas 7.4.2.3 and 7.4.2.4 on the whole compactified stratum. The corollary then feeds §8 (Proposition 8.1.1 and the ordinary-part results). Since the lemma's statement is true and the missing step is routine, no stated result changes. Only the proof is incomplete.

sourceIssues.printed: Let A = Y^{=1}_{par,1} and Â be the completion of Y_{par,1} along this locally closed subscheme. Let B = Y^{=1}_1 and B̂ be the completion of Y_1 along B. The ideal of definition of Â and B̂ are (p, Ha.ω^{(1−p)}). sourceIssues.correction: Â should be the completion of Y_par (the Z_p-scheme) along A = Y^{=1}_{par,1}, and B̂ the completion of Y (over Z_p) along B = Y^{=1}_1. Equivalently, drop the subscript 1 on the schemes being completed, while A and B keep theirs. sourceIssues.reason: I checked the page image at 150 and 300 dpi; the text above is exactly what is printed. Notation (§6.4, p. 34): "we let X_n → Spec Z/p^nZ be the mod p^n reduction of X and X_{par,n} the reduction modulo p^n of X_par". Y is the interior, so Y_1 and Y_{par,1} are special fibres over F_p. The level subscript K (Y_{par,K}, §6.1.3) is dropped in §7 and K is never 1, so the '1' can only mean mod p. With that reading, the proof as printed does not work. (1) Ĉ is "the completion of X_{Kli}(p)", not of X_{Kli}(p)_1. It is flat over Z_p, so it cannot map to Â or B̂ if these are completions of F_p-schemes; that would force p = 0 on Ĉ. (2) On p. 47, "The non-normalized map p_2^⋆ω → p_1^⋆ω can be normalized by p^{-1}" and "The fundamental class p_1^⋆O_B̂ → p_1^!O_B̂ is divisible by p^2" only make sense on p-torsion-free objects. In characteristic p, divisibility by p^2 would make the fundamental class zero. (3) The ideal of definition (p, Ha.ω^{(1−p)}) and "C = V(p, p_1^⋆Ha.p_1^⋆ω^{1−p}) ↪ Ĉ" are only meaningful when p ≠ 0 on these formal schemes. The Z_p reading is therefore forced. It also fits the regularity and miracle-flatness remark: Y is smooth over Z_p, X_{Kli}(p) is regular (Prop. 6.1.4.1), and both sides have dimension 4. So the subscript 1 on Y_{par,1} and Y_1 (as the objects being completed) is a notational slip, probably carried over from A = Y^{=1}_{par,1}. The claim that this is only a misprint is correct. HAL v3 has the same slip in its older notation: "Let A = X^{=1}_{p,1} and Â be the completion of X_{p,1} along this locally closed subscheme. Let B = X^{=1}_1 and B̂ be the completion of X_1 along B." The subscript 1 is there too, with X and X_{p,1} in place of Y and Y_{par,1}. Effect: the intended argument goes through unchanged with the correction. Nothing stated changes, including Proposition 7.4.2.1 and the results that depend on it (Corollary 7.4.2.1, Lemma 7.4.2.5 and later uses of T = T_1^{et}∘T_2^{et} and of commutation with Ha'). So 'nothing' is right.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed: `Let $A=Y^{=1}_{\mathrm{par},1}$ and $\hat A$ be the completion of $Y_{\mathrm{par},1}$ along this locally closed subscheme. Let $B=Y^{=1}_1$ and $\hat B$ be the completion of $Y_1$ along $B$. The ideal of definition of $\hat A$ and $\hat B$ are $(p,\mathrm{Ha}.\omega^{(1-p)})$.' By the notation of §6.4 the subscript 1 is reduction mod $p$, so $Y_1$ and $Y_{\mathrm{par},1}$ are $\F_p$-schemes on which $p$ is already zero and the printed ideal of definition makes no sense; and the proof goes on to use that $\hat B$ is regular and $p_1$ finite flat onto it, which is a statement about the $p$-adic formal completion of the $\Z_p$-scheme. Completing $Y_{\mathrm{par}}$ and $Y$ instead, as the finding proposes, makes both the ideal and the flatness argument correct and changes nothing else.

Then  μ′ : ℂ² →^{ψ⊗1} e⋆Ω¹_Ã ⊗ ℂ →^{dξ^{−1}} e⋆Ω¹_{Ã/L} ⊗ ℂ  where ξ : Ã → Ã/L is the isogeny." (checked on the page image rendered at 110 and 300 dpi. sourceIssues.reason:
This is a real leftover-notation misprint, not something the text layer introduced. Evidence:

(1) The page image shows 'ψ⊗1'. The sentence just before it defines μ : W(l)² ≃ e⋆Ω¹_Ã as 'the' isomorphism in the formula T_1^{00} f(Ã,μ) = p^{−2−r} Σ f(Ã/L, μ′). So the only trivialization that can go ℂ² → e⋆Ω¹_Ã ⊗ ℂ here is μ⊗1.

(2) ψ is never defined as a trivialization of e⋆Ω¹. I searched every ψ in the author text. Apart from this display, ψ appears only as: the K^p-level structure in the moduli triples (G,λ,ψ) of §6.1.1 (p. 26); the map ψ_T : G̃^D[p^m]|_T → H_m^D in a deformation argument; and the universal trivialization ψ : Z/p^n → H_n^D in a later section. None of these can map ℂ² to e⋆Ω¹_Ã.

(3) HAL v3 shows the history. On its printed p. 40 it has the same display (with B for Ã): 'μ′ : ℂ² →^{ψ⊗1} e⋆Ω¹_B ⊗ ℂ →^{dξ^{−1}} e⋆Ω¹_{B/L} ⊗ ℂ'. Its conclusion also uses ψ: 'T_1^{oo} f(A, ψ mod p) = 0'. The 2019 author version changed that conclusion to 'T_1^{oo} f(Ã, μ) mod p = 0' but left ψ⊗1 in the display. So ψ is an older name for μ that was not fully replaced. HAL v3 has the same error.

(4) I redid the estimate. From §6.2.1 (p. 30), Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω ⊗ det^r ω. (dξ)^* : e⋆Ω¹_{Ã/L} → e⋆Ω¹_Ã has elementary divisors (p, ϖ) with v(ϖ) = 1/(p+1). Write μ′ = μ₀∘g, where μ₀ is an integral trivialization of ω_{Ã/L}. Then f(Ã/L, μ′) = ρ(g^{−1}) f(Ã/L, μ₀), and g^{−1} has elementary divisors (p, ϖ). The weights of Sym^k⊗det^r at diag(p,ϖ) are p^i ϖ^{k−i}(pϖ)^r for 0≤i≤k. The smallest valuation is r + (k+r)/(p+1), at i=0. So p^{−2−r} f(Ã/L, μ′) lies in 𝔪_{O_ℂ} as soon as (k+r)/(p+1) > 2, i.e. k+r > 2(p+1). This matches the paper's condition. The argument works for any integral trivialization, so the correction does not change it.

The paper gives k+r > 2(p+1) only as a sufficient condition ('If r+k > 2(p+1) then ...'; Remark 7.4.2.1(2) says it is not optimal), not as an 'iff'.

Unrelated misprints in the same passage, noted but not part of this issue: 'T_1^{00}' is printed with zeros instead of oo, and the parenthesis opened in '(actually one sees that T_1^m is zero ... proposition 7.4.1.1.' is never closed.

sourceIssues.reason: §6.4 (pp. 34–35) defines X_n^{=r} only as 'the locally closed subset … where the multiplicative rank of G is exactly r'. The schematic structure it then specifies is for X^{≤1} (vanishing of Ha) and, on p. 37, for X^{≤0} (vanishing of Ha′). The correspondence on p. 48 is obtained 'by proposition 7.4.2.1 and proposition 4.1.2.1', i.e. by restricting along the vanishing of Ha′, so its natural domain is X^{≤0}. The proof of 7.4.2.2 in fact uses the ideal (p, Ha, Ha′), which is exactly X_1^{≤0} as a scheme. Proposition 8.1.1 needs the vanishing on the third column of its diagram, which is written X^{≤0}. That column is non-reduced, since by Remark 6.4.1 Ha′(G) vanishes to order 2 along the rank 0 locus. So the vanishing is needed on X^{≤0}, not on the reduced p-rank 0 locus. The mathematics is consistent once one identifies X^{=0} (with the ideal given in the proof of 7.4.2.2) with X^{≤0}. The inconsistency is purely notational. Confidence is medium because one could read the proof of 7.4.2.2 as defining the scheme structure on X^{=0} in place.

sourceIssues.reason: Lemma 7.1.1 (p. 38) states: 'The map T_1′ factors through p^{2+r}p_1^!Ω^{(k,r)} if k + 2r ≥ 2 + r.' On p. 39 the paper normalizes T_1 = p^{−2−r}T_1′ 'Under the assumption k + 2r ≥ 2 + r (which holds if r ≥ 2)'. The proof of Lemma 7.1.1 gives two bounds. On components where G → G′ has kernel of étale rank 2, the divisibility is p^r·p^2. On components where the kernel has multiplicative rank 2, it is p^{k+2r}, and there the fundamental class is an isomorphism. So the proof yields exactly p^{min(r+2, k+2r)}. For (k,r) = (0,1) this is p^2, not p^3, so 'when r ≥ 1' misstates the lemma's hypothesis. It fails only at (0,1). In Proposition 7.4.2.2, however, r ≥ p^2 + p and k ≥ C, so the correct hypothesis holds and the argument is unaffected. It is a mis-citation of a hypothesis whose intended meaning ('the hypothesis of Lemma 7.1.1 holds') is clear.

The displayed inclusion should then be read as being about Θ_{k,r}∘Ψ_{k,r}(Sym^k M_2 ⊗ det^r M_2) = Θ_{k,r}∘Ψ_{k,r}(p_2^⋆Ω^{(k,r)}(Spec A)), which lies in p^{2+r}M_1 ∩ (∩_i p^r 𝔭_i^k)M_1. Index the minimal primes as 𝔭_1, …, 𝔭_s so that r stays the weight. Also, 'when r ≥ 1' should be 'when k+r ≥ 2 (e.g. r ≥ 2)', which is Lemma 7.1.1's hypothesis k+2r ≥ 2+r. sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the printed text on a 300 dpi render of p. 49 and it matches the quote above. Paper's convention (§6.2.1, p. 30): Ω^1 := ω_G, the rank-2 bundle, and Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G.

Two slips are genuine and not artefacts of the text layer:
(1) M_1 = p_1^!Ω^1(Spec A) is used only as the target of Θ_{k,r}: p_1^⋆Ω^{(k,r)} → p_1^!Ω^{(k,r)}, in 'p^{2+r}M_1' and 'p^{2+r}IM_1'. It has to be p_1^!Ω^{(k,r)}.
(2) 'Let 𝔭_1, ⋯, 𝔭_r' reuses r, which in the next display is the weight in p^r and p^{2+r}.

Not all three modules should become sections of Ω^{(k,r)}-bundles: M_2 and M_3 have to stay Ω^1, because dΨ(M_2) ⊂ 𝔭_i M_3 is a statement about dΨ on Ω^1. HAL v3 even writes dΨ_{1,0}(M_2), making the (1,0) weight explicit. Only M_1 is wrong; Ψ_{k,r}(M_2) is an abuse for Ψ_{k,r}(Sym^k M_2 ⊗ det^r M_2).

On 'r ≥ 1': Lemma 7.1.1 (p. 38) needs k+2r ≥ 2+r, i.e. k+r ≥ 2, and p. 39 says this 'holds if r ≥ 2'. For k=0, r=1 it fails, so 'r ≥ 1' is loose. It is irrelevant here because the proposition assumes r ≥ p²+p.

I redid the argument:
- Ψ_{0,1} factors through p·p_1^⋆ω^1, so det^r gives a factor p^r. Sym^k(dΨ) sends Sym^k M_2 into 𝔭_i^k Sym^k M_3. So Ψ_{k,r}(p_2^⋆Ω^{(k,r)}) ⊂ p^r 𝔭_i^k p_1^⋆Ω^{(k,r)}, and Θ_{k,r} is linear. Together with Lemma 7.1.1 this gives the displayed inclusion.
- Shrink Spec A so that M_1 is free (p_1^!O_X is invertible). X_Kli(p) is flat over Z_p, so p is a non-zero-divisor, and x = p^r y with y ∈ p²A ∩ ∩_i 𝔭_i^k, coordinatewise.
- Artin–Rees applied to each 𝔭_i and the submodule p²A: p²A ∩ 𝔭_i^n ⊂ p²𝔭_i^{n−c}. Then z ∈ ∩_i 𝔭_i^{n−c} whenever p²z ∈ ∩_i 𝔭_i^n.
- ∩_i 𝔭_i^N ⊂ I for N large. Every associated prime 𝔮 of I contains some 𝔭_i, and a 𝔮-primary component Q satisfies 𝔭_i^N ⊂ 𝔮^N ⊂ Q.
- So p²A ∩ ∩_i 𝔭_i^{C(A)} ⊂ p²I holds, and C(A) depends only on A, I and the 𝔭_i, not on r. This matches 'all r ≥ p²+p' in the statement.

The statement of Proposition 7.4.2.2 is unchanged. Its later uses (Prop. 8.1.1, Prop. 8.2.1, pp. 50–51) rely only on the statement. HAL v3 has the same text, with the same Ω^1 definitions, the same 𝔭_1,⋯,𝔭_r and the same 'r ≥ 1'; the only difference is dΨ_{1,0}(M_2) instead of dΨ(M_2).

sourceIssues.correction: Replace (p^2−1)n with (p−1)n in both places: "the support of colim_{n,×Ha}Ω^{(k,r+(p−1)n)}(−D) is the rank 2 locus … The support of colim_nΩ^{(k,r+(p−1)n)}(−D)/(Ha)^n is the rank 1 locus". These are exactly the two sheaves in the resolution displayed just above.
sourceIssues.reason: These are the paper's own conventions. §6.2.1, p. 30 (as already in §5.3, p. 24): Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G. §6.4: ω = det ω_G and Ha(G) ∈ H^0(X_1, ω^{p−1}). So multiplying by Ha sends Ω^{(k,s)} to Ω^{(k,s+p−1)}. The weight p^2−1 belongs to the second Hasse invariant Ha′ ∈ H^0(X_1^{≤1}, ω^{p^2−1}) (§6.3.2, Lemma 6.4.2). Ha′ is what the proof of Prop 8.1.x uses on the same page, which probably explains the slip. With the printed exponent the transition maps "×Ha" send Ω^{(k,r+(p^2−1)n)} to Ω^{(k,r+(p^2−1)n+p−1)}, not to Ω^{(k,r+(p^2−1)(n+1))}, because (p^2−1)−(p−1) = p(p−1) ≠ 0. So the colimit as written does not make sense. The same proof uses weight p−1 for Ha everywhere else. It is in the displayed resolution and the complex just after (both (p−1)n). It is also in "H^0(X_1^{=2},Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)) = colim_n H^0(X_1,Ω^{(k,r+n(p−1))}(−D)) where the transition maps are given by multiplication by Ha", and in the final exact sequence. So under the paper's own notation, (p^2−1) is an inconsistent slip for (p−1), not an artefact of the text layer: the rendered page clearly shows p^2 in both places. HAL v3 has word-for-word the same text, with p^2−1 in both places, on printed p. 43 (PDF p. 44). The only difference there is that it cites "thm 6.4.2.1". The slip does not affect the argument. The sentence only claims where the two sheaves of the displayed resolution are supported (the ordinary, rank 2, locus and the rank 1 locus, both with affine image in the minimal compactification), and those sheaves are the (p−1)n ones. One could read the printed objects with transition maps ×Ha^{p+1}, which have weight p^2−1. On that reading they give cofinal versions of the same localisation and torsion sheaves anyway, so the support claims hold either way. Lemma 8.2.1 and what uses it (Prop 8.2.1) do not depend on the misprinted exponent.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed, and the weight is decidable. The resolution displayed at the head of the proof uses $\Omega^{(k,r+(p-1)n)}$, and the complex derived from it three lines later uses $\Omega^{(k,r+(p-1)n)}$ again, but the two sentences in between print $\mathrm{colim}_{n,\times\mathrm{Ha}}\Omega^{(k,r+(p^2-1)n)}(-D)$ and $\mathrm{colim}_n\Omega^{(k,r+(p^2-1)n)}(-D)/(\mathrm{Ha})^n$. Since $\mathrm{Ha}(G)\in H^0(X_1,\omega^{p-1})$, multiplication by $\mathrm{Ha}$ raises the weight by $p-1$; $p^2-1$ is the weight of the second Hasse invariant $\mathrm{Ha}'$, which is not the section used in this colimit. So the two middle sentences carry the wrong exponent, as the finding says.

sourceIssues.locator: §9.1.1, proof of Lemma 9.1.1.1, pp. 54–55 (both slips are on p. 55; ψ_T is defined on p. 54)
sourceIssues.printed: p. 55, top lines (checked on page images rendered at 110 and 250 dpi): "H^D_m|_{T′} over T′ and the data of h′ provides a deformation G̃[p^m]_{T′} to T′ of G̃^D[p^n]|_T. By Illusie's deformation theory ([37], thm VII, 4.2.5) , the map ψ_T admits a unique extension ψ_{T′} : G̃^D[p^m]|_{T′} → H^D_m|_{T′}." Earlier, on p. 54: "To the map g is associated a surjective map ψ_T : G̃^D[p^m]|_T → H^D_m|_T over T where H^D_m|_T is an étale group scheme, locally isomorphic to Z/p^mZ." Later on p. 55: "…provides a section s ∈ H^0(Z′, L^{(p−1)}). The non vanishing locus of this section is the open subscheme (Z′)^m of Z where C/H_{m−1} is of multiplicative type. The map (Z′)^m → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1 is affine as the composite of the affine open immersion (Z′)^m ↪ Z′ and the finite map Z′ → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1."
sourceIssues.correction: Replace "a deformation G̃[p^m]_{T′} to T′ of G̃^D[p^n]|_T" with "a deformation G̃^D[p^m]|_{T′} to T′ of G̃^D[p^m]|_T". This is the Cartier dual of the deformation G̃[p^m]_{T′} of G̃[p^m]|_T. The essential fix is p^n → p^m, with the dual used consistently. The second change is optional: "the open subscheme (Z′)^m of Z" could read "of Z′", which is what the argument proves and what the next sentence uses. The printed "of Z" is not actually false, though.
sourceIssues.reason:
First part: a genuine misprint. The map being deformed is ψ_T : G̃^D[p^m]|_T → H^D_m|_T (p. 54), and its extension is ψ_{T′} : G̃^D[p^m]|_{T′} → H^D_m|_{T′}. So Illusie's theorem needs a deformation of the source G̃^D[p^m]|_T. Here n is the p-adic truncation level of X_n and has nothing to do with m. As printed, G̃[p^m]_{T′} (order p^{4m} away from the boundary) cannot be a deformation of G̃^D[p^n]|_T (order p^{4n}) when n ≠ m, and the dual is used on one side only.

HAL v3 (PDF p. 46, printed p. 45) shows where the slip came from. There p^n appears throughout: "ψ_R : G̃^D[p^n]|_R → H^D_m|_R", "a deformation of G̃[p^n]_{R′} to R′ of G̃^D[p^n]|_R", and "ψ_{R′} : G̃^D[p^n]|_{R′} → H^D_m|_{R′}". The author version changed ψ_T, ψ_{T′} and the first group to p^m but left G̃^D[p^n]|_T. So the revision was incomplete. This correction is right.

Second part: this is at most a wording slip, not an error. It is true that s lives on Z′, so the reason given only makes (Z′)^m open in Z′, and the next sentence uses the open immersion (Z′)^m ↪ Z′. But the printed claim is also literally true. Points of (Z′)^m have C an extension of multiplicative groups by multiplicative groups, so C is multiplicative, and that locus U is open in Z. On U, the order of C[p^{m−1}] is locally constant. Both C[p^{m−1}] and H_{m−1} lie in the finite flat group G[F^{m−1}]. By Cartier duality, the condition C[p^{m−1}] ⊂ H_{m−1} says that a homomorphism from a finite flat group to an étale group vanishes, and that condition is open and closed. So Z′ is open and closed in Z near (Z′)^m, and (Z′)^m is open in Z. HAL v3 has the same "(Z′)^m of Z" wording.

Neither slip affects the logic. The proof works once the obvious indices are read in. Nothing downstream depends on the wording: Remark 9.1.1.2, §9.1.2, §9.2, and Lemma 9.5.1 ("Similar to the proof of lemma 9.1.1.1") use only the statement "étale and affine". Separately, the author version gives the number 9.1.1.1 to both a Remark and this Lemma.

The map being deformed is $\psi_T:\tilde G^D[p^m]|_T\to H^D_m|_T$, introduced on the previous page, and the extension produced is $\psi_{T'}:\tilde G^D[p^m]|_{T'}\to H^D_m|_{T'}$, so what Illusie's theorem needs is a deformation of $\tilde G^D[p^m]|_T$; the printed phrase names a deformation of one object as a deformation of a different one, and the exponent $n$ is the truncation level of $X^{\geq1}_n$, unrelated to $m$. The section is $s\in H^0(Z',\mathcal L^{(p-1)})$, constructed on $Z'$, the closed subscheme of $Z$ where $C[p^{m-1}]=H_{m-1}$, so its non-vanishing locus is open in $Z'$ and only locally closed in $Z$. sourceIssues.locator: §9.1.1, proof of Lemma 9.1.1.1 (the affineness part, case n = 1), p. 55 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same text on printed pp. 45–46 (PDF p. 46), where "Verschiebung" is misspelt "Vershiebung".
sourceIssues.printed: "Let us denote by Z′ the closed subscheme of Z where C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}. The group scheme C/H_{m−1} is connected of order p over Z′. Its co-normal sheaf is ℒ, an invertible sheaf over Z′ and the differential of the Verschiebung map V : (C/H_{m−1})^{(p)} → C/H_{m−1} provides a section s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{(p−1)}). The non vanishing locus of this section is the open subscheme (Z′)^m of Z where C/H_{m−1} is of multiplicative type. The map (Z′)^m → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1 is affine as the composite of the affine open immersion (Z′)^m ↪ Z′ and the finite map Z′ → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1."
sourceIssues.correction:
For m ≥ 2, replace the definition of Z′. In all cases, give the reason why ℒ is invertible. (It is enough to treat n = 1, as the paper does.)

m = 1. Here H_0 = 0, so Z′ = Z. C ⊂ G[F] is killed by F. So locally C ≅ Spec R[x]/(x^p − ax) with a = 0, and ℒ ≅ R/aR = R is invertible. With this sentence added, the printed argument is correct.

m ≥ 2. Let Z′ be the closed subscheme of Z where H_{m−1} ⊂ C and F kills C/H_{m−1}; in Oort–Tate terms, a = 0. Both conditions are closed, so Z′ is finite over X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1. On Z′ the conormal sheaf ℒ of C/H_{m−1} is ≅ R/aR = R, so it is invertible. The differential of V gives s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{⊗(p−1)}), and its non-vanishing locus (Z′)^m is where C/H_{m−1} is multiplicative. So (Z′)^m → Z′ → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine.

The map H_m ↦ C = H_m embeds X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 in Z, because μ_{p^m} is killed by F^m. The image lies in (Z′)^m: C/H_{m−1} ≅ H_{m−1}[p] is multiplicative, hence killed by F. On (Z′)^m, C is multiplicative of order p^m. There, the three conditions "C is étale-locally μ_{p^m}", "C[p] has order p" and "C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}" are equivalent, and they cut out an open and closed subscheme. That subscheme is X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1, since both represent the subgroups H_m with H_m[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}. So the map X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine.

Two alternative fixes:
- Keep Z′ = {H_{m−1} ⊂ C}, write C/H_{m−1} = G^L_{a,b} in Oort–Tate form, and replace s by the section b of L^{⊗(1−p)}. Its non-vanishing locus is the multiplicative locus, and a = 0 there.
- Replace {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} by its reduction. On a reduced base, a connected group of order p has a nilpotent, hence a = 0. X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is reduced, being étale over the smooth X^{≥1}_1, so it lies in the reduction.

The same change repairs the proof of Lemma 9.5.1.
sourceIssues.reason:
What the step claims. The affineness half of Lemma 9.1.1.1 is reduced to n = 1. Z → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is the finite scheme of subgroups C ⊂ G[F^m] of order p^m. Z′ is defined as "the closed subscheme of Z where C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}". The proof then makes two claims.
(a) Z′ is closed in Z, so Z′ is finite over X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1.
(b) C/H_{m−1} is connected of order p over Z′, and its conormal sheaf ℒ is invertible; no other reason is given. The differential of V then gives s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{⊗(p−1)}), whose non-vanishing locus (Z′)^m is the multiplicative locus.
From these, (Z′)^m → Z′ → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine, and X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is open and closed in (Z′)^m.
Connectedness is true: H_{m−1} ⊂ G[F^{m−1}] ⊂ G[F^m], and G[F^m] is infinitesimal. So C and C/H_{m−1} are connected wherever H_{m−1} ⊂ C.

Why "connected of order p" gives no reason. Over an F_p-algebra R, a group of order p is locally Oort–Tate: Spec R[x]/(x^p − ax) with ab = 0. Its conormal module is I/I² = Rx/(ax) ≅ R/aR. Connectedness says only that a vanishes at every point, i.e. that a is nilpotent. If a is nilpotent and non-zero, R/aR is not invertible. Such a group is still killed by F^m once a^{1+p+⋯+p^{m−1}} = 0. The paper knows only that Z is finite over a smooth base; it does not claim Z is reduced. Invertibility holds exactly where a = 0, i.e. where F kills the group. On a reduced base, connectedness does imply a = 0.

m = 1. Here H_0 = 0, so Z′ = Z under any reading. C ⊂ G[F] is killed by F, so a = 0 and ℒ is invertible. The step is correct and only the reason is missing.

m ≥ 2, literal reading. Suppose C_T[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1,T}. Since C ⊂ G[F^m] ⊂ G[p^m], multiplication by p^{m−1} induces a monomorphism C/H_{m−1} ↪ H_{m−1}[p]. Both are finite flat of order p, so C/H_{m−1} ≅ H_{m−1}[p] is multiplicative. Then C is multiplicative with C[p] of order p, so C is étale-locally μ_{p^m}. Conversely, every H_m gives such a C. So the literal locus is X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 itself. On it, ℒ is invertible, s is nowhere zero, and (Z′)^m = Z′.

This locus is not closed in Z; Remark 9.1.1.2 itself says it is not finite over the base. The usual argument that equality of two finite flat subgroups of the same order is a closed condition does not apply here. The reason is that C[p^{m−1}] is not flat over Z: the literal condition is the closed condition H_{m−1} ⊂ C together with the open condition that C[p^{m−1}] has order p^{m−1}.

Suppose the locus were closed. Then it would be finite over the base. The map is étale (first half of the lemma), so it would be finite locally free of locally constant rank. But the rank is p at ordinary points: the lifts of a cyclic H_{m−1} ⊂ μ_{p^m}² are the p points of P¹(Z/p^m) over a point of P¹(Z/p^{m−1}). The rank is 1 at points of p-rank 1, where the multiplicative part is μ_{p^m} (Remark 9.1.1.2). The ordinary locus is dense, being the complement of the Hasse divisor in a scheme étale over the smooth X^{≥1}_1. This is a contradiction.

The missing points can be identified. Let x be a geometric point of X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 of p-rank 1, over k. Write E for the local-local p-divisible group of height 2 and dimension 1 at x. Then G_x[F^m] = μ_{p^m} × E[F^m] and H_{m−1} = μ_{p^{m−1}} × 0. Over k, the only order-p subgroups of G_x[F^m]/H_{m−1} = μ_p × E[F^m] are μ_p × 0 and 0 × E[F]. Indeed, such a subgroup is μ_p or α_p. Hom(μ_p, E[F^m]) = 0 and Hom(α_p, μ_p) = 0. And E[F] is the only subgroup of order p of E[F^m], since E is one-dimensional. So {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} has two points over x.
- C = μ_{p^m} lies in the literal locus.
- C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F] is killed by p^{m−1}, so it does not.
The literal locus is open in {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} and étale over the base. Hence, along a trait from an ordinary point to x, at most one of the p lifts can specialise into it. The others specialise to μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F].
So under the literal reading, claim (a) is false, and the step assumes the finiteness it was meant to supply.

m ≥ 2, closed reading. The last sentence of the proof ("X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is the open and closed subscheme of (Z′)^m where C ≅ μ_{p^m}") only has content if (Z′)^m can be strictly larger than X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1. That holds for Z″ = {H_{m−1} ⊂ C}. For example, take H_{m−1} = μ_{p^{m−1}} × 0 and C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × μ_p at an ordinary point. Z″ is closed and finite, but ℒ is not invertible on it.

Counterexample. Take x as above, and let E_0 be a supersingular elliptic curve over k, so that E ≅ E_0[p^∞]. Let Spec A be the scheme of order-p subgroups of E[p]. This is the fibre over E_0 of the finite flat degree-(p+1) Γ_0(p) map of Katz–Mazur. Its only k-point is E[F]. So A is Artin local with residue field k and length p+1. Let D ⊂ E[p]_A be the universal subgroup, D ≅ Spec A[t]/(t^p − at). The locus V(a) where F kills D is where D = E[F]_A, which is the closed point. So aA = m_A ≠ 0, and ω_D ≅ A/aA = k is not free over A. Since E[p] = E[F²] ⊂ E[F^m], the group C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × D ⊂ G_x[F^m]_A is flat of order p^m, contains H_{m−1}, and has C/H_{m−1} ≅ D. The conormal sheaf commutes with base change. So the conormal sheaf of C/H_{m−1} on Z″ is not invertible at C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F]. Under this reading, claim (b) is false.

Conclusion. For m ≥ 2 the printed step fails under both readings. The literal Z′ is not finite over the base, and the closed Z′ does not carry an invertible ℒ. The argument works as written only on a closed subscheme the text does not define. Examples are the locus where F also kills C/H_{m−1}, or the closure of X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 in Z, which is reduced. So this is an error in the proof. The lemma itself is still true, with the fix given in the correction.

What is affected. Lemma 9.5.1 (p. 57) is proved as "Similar to the proof of lemma 9.1.1.1", for G′ over X_par. Its p-rank-1 points have the same shape, so it has the same flaw, and the same fix repairs it. The affineness is used in three places:
- in §9.1.2, where the vertical maps are "étale and affine";
- in §9.2, to form 𝔛^{≥1}_Kli(p^∞) ("It exists because the transition maps are affine");
- in Remark 9.3.1.
All of these still hold. No stated result changes.

sourceIssues.reason: Printed text confirmed on pp. 55 and 111. The chapter placement was checked from outside sources. Springer's contents for LNM 283 list the chapters "Cohomologie de diagrammes", "Déformations équivariantes de G-schémas et déformations de schémas en groupes" and "Catégories formelles, complexes de de Rham et cohomologie cristalline". The alternative argument works: H^D_m|_{T'} is étale and G̃^D[p^m]|_T ↪ G̃^D[p^m]|_{T'} is a nilpotent thickening. So ψ_T lifts uniquely to a T'-morphism, and by the same uniqueness applied to G×G the lift is a homomorphism. The result stands; only the bibliographic pointer is wrong.

sourceIssues.printed: Let ℭ_𝔜(p^m) be the moduli over 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) of triples (G, H_m, L) where L ⊂ G[p²] is totally isotropic, L[p] is of rank p³ and L∩H_m = {0}. We recall that H_1 = H_m[p]. In the following lemma the orthogonal is taken for the Weil pairing inside G[p].
sourceIssues.correction: "... of triples (G, H_m, L) where L ⊂ G[p^2] is a totally isotropic subgroup of rank p^4 (that is, a Lagrangian of G[p^2]), L[p] is of rank p^3 and L ∩ H_m = {0}." The extra clause "étale-locally ≅ (Z/pZ)^2 ⊕ Z/p^2Z" of an alternative correction should not go into this definition over 𝔜, where p is nilpotent. sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the rendered p. 57, and the text matches the quote above, with the symbol ℭ_𝔜 (fraktur C). The definition does not bound the order of L.

In detail:
(1) Every subgroup of G[p] is totally isotropic in G[p²]. Take x, y ∈ G[p] and write x = p·x̃. Then e_{p²}(x, y) = e_{p²}(x̃, y)^p = e_{p²}(x̃, py) = 1.
(2) Suppose L is totally isotropic with |L[p]| = p³. Then |L| = p³·|pL| ≤ p⁴, so |L| is p³ or p⁴. Order is locally constant for finite flat L, so the literal ℭ_𝔜(p^m) has an extra open and closed piece where L ⊂ G[p] has order p³.
(3) This piece is not empty. Take an ordinary point with G[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f, where a pairs with e and b pairs with f. Let H_1 = μ_p a and L = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f. Then L ∩ H_m ⊂ L ∩ H_1 = 0. Also H_1^⊥ = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f, so L ∩ H_1^⊥ = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f. That gives L/(L ∩ H_1^⊥) ≅ Z/p, not Z/p², so the second claim of Lemma 10.1.1 fails. More generally, L ∩ H_1 = 0 forces L ≠ H_1^⊥, so the quotient always has order p on this piece.
(4) The proof of Lemma 10.1.1 needs |L| = p⁴ for "pL = L[p]^⊥". The inclusion pL ⊂ L[p]^⊥ always holds, and |L[p]^⊥| = p, so equality holds exactly when |pL| = p.
(5) Proposition 10.2.1 fails literally. Its proof needs "the kernel of G/L[p] → G/L is étale of order p". Also, ℭ(p^m) = ℭ² ×_{𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m)} ℭ¹ only parametrises isogenies G → G' → G'' of degree p³·p = p⁴, while on the extra piece G → G/L has degree p³.

The intended meaning is clear from the paper itself. Footnote 16 on p. 60 (in the proof of Lemma 10.3.2) says "the universal rank p⁴ subgroup L". The proof of Proposition 10.2.1 uses an étale kernel of order p for G/L[p] → G/L. The parallel definitions on p. 44 (§7, the correspondence D: "an extension of an étale group scheme locally isomorphic to Z/pZ ⊕ Z/p²Z by ... µ_p") and in §13.2.1 ("locally ... isomorphic to (Z/pZ)² ⊕ Z/p²Z") both state the isomorphism type. So this is an omitted condition, not a real mathematical error.

Effect: ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is only used on pp. 57–60. It appears in Lemma 10.1.1, Proposition 10.2.1 and Lemmas 10.3.1–10.3.2, where the 1/p³ trace normalisation and the deformation computation assume |L| = p⁴. As literally stated, Lemma 10.1.1 and Proposition 10.2.1 are false. The U-operator itself is built from ℭ(p^m) via ℭ¹ and ℭ², which never mention L, so the operator and everything after §10.3 are unaffected once the obvious correction is made.

HAL v3 (p. 47, §10.1) has different text: "Let ℭ_𝔜(p^m) be the moduli over 𝔜_{Kli}(p^m) of triples (G, H_m, L) where L ⊂ G[p²] is totally isotropic L ∩ H_m = {0}, and pL ∩ H_m^⊥ = {0}", with the matrix diag(1,p,p,p²). That definition also has no order condition. It is even weaker, since L = {0} satisfies it. So the defect was already there in v3, in a different form. Defence attempted and failed.
(a) The paper's own convention does not make "totally isotropic" mean Lagrangian. §5.1.2 calls W = <e1> a "totally isotropic direct factor". §6.1.4 says "totally isotropic direct factors L ⊂ V1 of rank 2", giving the rank separately. In §6.1.5.2 the set C contains isotropic factors of every rank.
(b) The conditions do not force the order. For x ∈ L and y ∈ L[p], e_p(px, y) = e_{p^2}(x, y) = 1, so pL ⊂ L[p]^⊥, which has order p. Hence |L| is p^3 or p^4, and every subgroup of G[p] is isotropic for e_{p^2}. The case |L| = p^3 (L = L[p]) does occur. Take an ordinary point with G[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f, H_m = μ_{p^m} a and L = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f. Then L ∩ H_m ⊂ L ∩ H_1 = 0.
(c) Brute force for p = 2 on (Z/4)^4 with the standard symplectic form and H_1 = <2a>, by a short computer enumeration. There are 16 = p^4 subgroups of order p^4, each with L/(L∩H_1^⊥) ≅ Z/4. There are also 8 = p^3 extra subgroups of order p^3, each with quotient of order p.
(d) On this extra piece the literal statement of Lemma 10.1.1 fails, because the quotient has order p and is not Z/p^2. Its proof uses "pL = L[p]^⊥", which needs |pL| = p. Worse, G/L = G/H^⊥ with H = L^⊥ is the paramodular quotient of the Klingen chain in §6.1.2–6.1.3. The polarization descended from p^2λ has degree p^2, so t_2(G, H_m, L) = (G/L, ...) does not lie in 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m). In fact this piece is just ℭ^1(p^m)|_𝔜. Proposition 10.2.1 is also false as printed: ℭ(p^m) = ℭ^2 ×_{𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}} ℭ^1 only gives composite isogenies of degree p^3·p = p^4.

So the literal definition is wrong. The intended meaning is still clear from the context:
- U is "associated to the matrix diag(p^2,p,p,1)", which is U_{Kli(p),1} of §5.1.4.
- The statement of Lemma 10.1.1 forces |L| = p^4.
- The proof of Proposition 10.2.1 factors G → G/L[p] → G/L, where the second map has an étale kernel of order p.
- Footnote 16 on p. 60 speaks of "the universal rank p^4 subgroup L".
- The parallel definitions state the type: D in §11.1.1 (p. 67; the "p. 44, §7" given above is a wrong locator), Lemma 11.1.1.4 on p. 68 (L_n of type Z/p^n ⊕ Z/p^{2n} by μ_{p^n}), and §13.2.1 on p. 85.
This is an omitted condition in a definition, not a step asserted without proof, so "misprint" fits better than "gap".

Consequences: ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is used only on pp. 57–60, in Lemma 10.1.1, the maps t_1 and t_2, Proposition 10.2.1, and Lemmas 10.3.1–10.3.2. All of these hold once the definition is corrected. The operator U = U_1 ∘ U_2 of §10.4 is built from ℭ^1 and ℭ^2 and the traces of Lemmas 10.3.3–10.3.4, which never mention L. §11.1.1 and §13.2.1 state the kernel type again explicitly. So no later result depends on the defective wording. Following PROTOCOL §18 ("nothing (the mathematics is right as intended)"), I set affects = nothing. If the register records printed statements that are literally false, it should instead say "a stated result": Lemma 10.1.1 and Proposition 10.2.1 are false as printed.

review.reason: Confirmed, and the omission lets in objects the paper does not intend. The definition prints `$L\subset G[p^2]$ is totally isotropic, $L[p]$ is of rank $p^3$ and $L\cap H_m=\{0\}$', with no bound on the order of $L$. Every subgroup of $G[p]$ is totally isotropic in $G[p^2]$ for the $p^2$-Weil pairing, since for $x=p\tilde x\in G[p]$ and $y\in G[p]$ one has $e_{p^2}(x,y)=e_{p^2}(\tilde x,y)^p=e_{p^2}(\tilde x,py)=1$; so an $L\subset G[p]$ of order $p^3$ complementary to $H_1$ satisfies all three printed conditions and is not what is wanted. Lemma 10.1.1, immediately below, decomposes $L$ into a $\mathrm{BT}_1$ of height 2 and an \u00e9tale part locally $\Z/p^2$, giving order $p^4$, and footnote 16 on p.\u202f60 calls it `the universal rank $p^4$ subgroup'. So the Lagrangian condition is meant and is missing. The finding is also right to keep the $L[p]$ condition, which excludes the Lagrangians of type $(\Z/p^2)^2$, and to keep the \u00e9tale-local description out of a definition over a base where $p$ is nilpotent.

sourceIssues.locator: §10.1, proof of Lemma 10.1.1 (the 'classical fact' paragraph), p. 57 of the author version (17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. We start by recalling the following classical fact^(14). Let S be a scheme over which p is nilpotent, and let M → S be a finite flat group scheme. Then M → S is a truncated Barsotti-Tate group scheme of level n if and only if M is killed by p^n and for all s ∈ S, M_s → s is a truncated Barsotti-Tate group scheme of level n. We give the argument when n = 1 (a similar argument works for arbitrary n). By definition, we can suppose that S is a scheme over Spec F_p. By assumption, G is killed by p and it follows that the Frobenius map F : G → G^(p) factors into a map G → Ker(V : G^(p) → G). We have to prove that the morphism G → Ker(V : G^(p) → G) is faithfully flat. By assumption, it is surjective. By the criterion for flatness by fiber it is flat.
sourceIssues.correction: Write M for G in the two sentences that prove the classical fact: "By assumption, M is killed by p and it follows that the Frobenius map F : M → M^(p) factors into a map M → Ker(V : M^(p) → M). We have to prove that the morphism M → Ker(V : M^(p) → M) is faithfully flat." That is all nine occurrences of G/G^(p) in those two sentences. "Throughout" must stop there. In the next paragraph of the same proof ("L[p] ⊕ H1 = G[p]"), G correctly means the universal abelian surface and should stay as it is.
sourceIssues.reason: I rendered p. 57 at 150 dpi, and the page image confirms the printed text word for word. The paragraph states the fact for an arbitrary finite flat M → S, but the proof then says "G is killed by p" and works with F : G → G^(p), V : G^(p) → G. In §10.1, G is the abelian scheme in the triples (G, H_m, L) with L ⊂ G[p^2]. That abelian surface is not killed by p. It is also not the object the fact is about: the fact is applied to L and its subquotients to reduce Lemma 10.1.1 to geometric points. The same proof uses G for the abelian surface again a few lines later (G[p]). So the letter G here is a slip for M. With M in place of G I redid the argument and it is correct. If M is killed by p, then V∘F = [p] = 0, so F factors through Ker V. Surjectivity onto Ker V is a fiberwise statement: fibers of a BT_1 satisfy Im F = Ker V, and taking kernels commutes with base change. Faithful flatness then follows because M is flat and finitely presented over S and each fiber map M_s → (Ker V)_s is a surjective homomorphism of finite group schemes over a field, hence flat (fiberwise flatness criterion, EGA IV 11.3.10). The proof of the other half, Ker F = Im V, is left to "a similar argument" in the paper and is not considered here. Nothing downstream uses the letter G in this paragraph, so the statement and logic of Lemma 10.1.1 and everything built on it (the U-correspondence in §10.2 onwards) are unaffected. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018, §10.1, pp. 48–49) does not have this text. There the exact sequences are stated inline with no proof, and the 'classical fact' / footnote-to-Fargues paragraph does not appear, so it was added between v3 and the June 2019 version. The published Duke text (revised 15 Oct 2019) could not be checked.

sourceIssues.locator: §10.2, definition of ℭ^2(p^m), p. 59 of the author version. HAL v3 does not have this sentence: its p. 49 only says Ker(G' → G) is a subgroup of the kernel of the polarization G' → (G')^t. The slip is new in the author version.
sourceIssues.printed: By definition Ker(G' → G) is a subgroup of the kernel K(λ') of the polarization λ' : G' → (G')^t which contains a unique multiplicative subgroup of order p, K(λ')^m. Therefore the condition defining ℭ^2(p^m) is that Ker(G' → G)∩K(λ)^m = {0}.
sourceIssues.reason: Confirmed on a 250 dpi crop: the preceding sentence has K(λ') and K(λ')^m, while the defining condition has an unprimed K(λ)^m. On 𝔛_par the polarization of G' is λ' (the moduli description on p. 33 writes triples (G', λ', ψ)). The polarization λ of G on 𝔛 is principal, so K(λ) = 0 and the condition would be empty. In §7 the paper did write K(λ) for the kernel of G' → (G')^t, so the intended object is clear. But inside this paragraph, having just named λ' and K(λ')^m, the unprimed λ is an inconsistency, and the correction is right.

sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 10.3.1. — The map t_1 : ℭ_𝔜(p^m) → 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is finite flat. Proof. The map is proper. The quasi-finiteness follows from the fact that an abelian surface over a field of characteristic p and of p-rank at least 1 has only finitely many subgroups of order p. Therefore the map is finite. We prove the flatness. The formal scheme 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is regular and ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is Cohen-Macaulay by lemma 10.2.2. Flatness follows from [53], chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1.  [The cited lemma, p. 59: "Lemma 10.2.2. — The structural morphisms ℭ^i(p^m) → Spf Z_p for i ∈ {1, 2} are local complete intersection morphisms^(15). Proof. The morphism 𝔛_Kli(p) → Spf Z_p is a local complete intersection morphism. There are étale morphisms ℭ^i(p^m) → 𝔛_Kli(p) by construction. So the proposition follows."]
sourceIssues.correction:
Add one step saying why ℭ(p^m) (and hence ℭ_𝔜(p^m)) is lci. The shortest fix keeps the proof of Lemma 10.2.2.

(a) The map q'_2 : ℭ(p^m) → ℭ^2(p^m) is the base change of q_2 : ℭ^1(p^m) → 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m), and q_2 is étale. The reason: on ℭ^1, Ker(G'→G) is the image of H_1, so it equals K(λ')^m. On that open-closed piece, p_2 : 𝔛_{Kli}(p) → 𝔛_par is an isomorphism onto 𝔛^{m-et}_par, since G = G'/K(λ')^m. So ℭ^1 and 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m) are both étale over 𝔛^{m-et}_par. It follows that the composite ℭ(p^m) → ℭ^2(p^m) → 𝔛_{Kli}(p) is étale. The argument of Lemma 10.2.2 then gives: ℭ(p^m) is lci over Spf Z_p, so ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is Cohen–Macaulay.

(b) Another route, the one HAL v3 takes, also works. Over the interior, r_1 is finite flat of degree p: its fibre is the set of order-p subgroups C ⊂ K(λ') with C ∩ K(λ')^m = 0, which is a torsor under Hom(K^et, K^m), locally μ_p. So r'_1 : ℭ → ℭ^1 is finite flat with lci fibres, and ℭ_𝔜 is lci by Lemma 10.2.2 for i = 1.

An alternative correction gets r_1 flat by miracle flatness. That needs 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m) to be regular, which the paper never establishes, so the direct torsor description is preferable.

The statement of Lemma 10.3.1 is unchanged.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page images for pp. 58–61 of the author version. The text layer matches the page.

As printed, the justification is inadequate. Lemma 10.2.2 is stated and proved only for ℭ¹(p^m) and ℭ²(p^m). ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is the restriction of the fibre product ℭ² ×_{r_1,q_2} ℭ¹ (Prop. 10.2.1). A fibre product of lci formal schemes is not lci in general unless one of the two maps is flat or étale. The author version never proves the step that is needed: it states neither that r_1 is flat nor that q_2 is étale. That makes this a gap in the sense of PROTOCOL §18: a step asserted without an adequate proof.

The conclusion is true, and I redid it both ways. Along the way I recomputed the fibres.
- r_1 has degree p: its fibre is the splittings torsor.
- q_1 has degree p^3: it parametrizes hyperplanes H^⊥ ⊂ F_p^4 not containing H_1, and there are p^3+p^2+p+1−(p^2+p+1) = p^3 of them.
- So t_1 has degree p^4. This agrees with the rank p^3 of each Serre–Tate component on p. 60 times the p components counted in footnote 16. On the ordinary locus it also agrees with t_2 being étale.

One might think CM needs an extra flatness step, because the composite is not étale over ℭ¹. But ℭ(p^m) is étale over ℭ²(p^m), since q_2 is étale. So the lemma's own "étale over 𝔛_Kli(p)" argument extends directly, and flatness of r_1 is one sufficient fix, not a necessary one. The flatness route (b) of the correction is still mathematically valid.

HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3, pp. 49–50) does not have this text. It has no Lemma 10.2.2, and its proof of Lemma 10.3.1 argues instead that "This boils down to the flatness of the maps r_1 and q_1 over the interior". It proves r_1 finite flat as "a standard fact". Its q_1 step has a weakness: it deduces flatness from "the fiber is flat". So the gap was introduced by the rewrite into the miracle-flatness argument (Matsumura, CRT Thm 23.1, printed as "chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1"). The published Duke text could not be compared.

Dependence: Lemma 10.3.1 is used only in Lemma 10.3.2 (the normalized trace (1/p^3)Tr_{t_1} over the interior). Neither lemma is cited later by number. The U-operator is built from Lemmas 10.3.3 and 10.3.4, which use Lemma 10.2.2 only for ℭ^i. So only this proof is affected.

Side observation, outside this issue and not fully checked: q_2 is étale but seems not finite. Over the open-closed locus {H'_1 = K(λ')^m}, for m = 1 its fibres have p points at ordinary points and 1 point at p-rank-1 points. That suggests the parenthetical "q_2 and q_1 are proper" (p. 58) is wrong for q_2. U_1 does not need q_2 to be proper. I checked the page images for pp. 57–61 of the author version and pp. 49–50 of HAL v3. The text layer matches the pages.

Defence attempted. The best charitable reading is "by (the proof of) Lemma 10.2.2": the object is lci because it is étale over 𝔛_{Kli}(p). That reading does not hold up. Lemma 10.2.2 is stated and proved only for ℭ^1 and ℭ^2, and its only input is "étale morphisms ℭ^i(p^m) → 𝔛_{Kli}(p) by construction". ℭ(p^m) is a fibre product, not one of the ℭ^i. Its natural map through ℭ^1 is not étale in characteristic p: r'_1 has μ_p-torsor fibres. Its map through ℭ^2 is étale only because q_2 is étale. The author version never states that q_2 is étale or that r_1 is flat. HAL v3 did prove r_1 finite flat, but that argument was removed in the rewrite. A fibre product of lci formal schemes is not lci in general. So the citation does not justify the step. The missing step is small but not a slip of notation, so "gap" (PROTOCOL §18) is the right kind, not "misprint".

The conclusion is true. I checked both routes:
- (a) q_2 is étale, because source and target are étale over 𝔛^{m-et}_par. That uses the open-closed component of 𝔛_{Kli}(p)|_{𝔛^{m-et}_par} where C = K(λ')^m, which p_2 maps isomorphically onto 𝔛^{m-et}_par.
- (b) r_1 is finite flat of degree p over the interior, as a splitting torsor.

The degrees are consistent: q_1 has degree p^3 (p^3+p^2+p+1 − (p^2+p+1) = p^3), r_1 has degree p, and t_1 has degree p^4. This matches the normalisations 1/p^2 (Lemma 10.3.3) · 1/p (Lemma 10.3.4) = 1/p^3 (Lemma 10.3.2). It also matches the rank-p^3 local rings on p. 60 times the p components of footnote 16. The other inputs of miracle flatness in Matsumura, CRT Thm 23.1 (printed as "chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1") are fine: 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is étale over the smooth 𝔜, so it is regular, and t_1 is finite between equidimensional schemes.

Consequences. Lemma 10.3.1 is used only in Lemma 10.3.2, the normalized trace (1/p^3)Tr_{t_1} over the interior. Neither lemma is cited by number later. U = U_1∘U_2 is built from Lemmas 10.3.3 and 10.3.4, which rely on Lemma 10.2.2 only for ℭ^i and are unaffected. So only this proof is affected, and no stated result changes.

On "affects": since the printed justification does not cover the object and a new argument is needed, "the proof" is more accurate than "nothing". The underlying facts are solid. Confidence is medium only because the omission is small, and a reviewer could treat it as an implicit extension of Lemma 10.2.2.

The quasi-finiteness follows from the fact that an abelian surface over a field of characteristic $p$ and of $p$-rank at least 1 has only finitely many subgroups of order $p$. sourceIssues.locator: §10.3, proof of Lemma 10.3.1, p. 60 (author version, 17 June 2019); bibliography entry [53] = H. Matsumura, Commutative ring theory, Cambridge university press (p. 112)
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. The map is proper. The quasi-finiteness follows from the fact that an abelian surface over a field of characteristic p and of p-rank at least 1 has only finitely many subgroups of order p. Therefore the map is finite. We prove the flatness. The formal scheme 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is regular and ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is Cohen-Macaulay by lemma 10.2.2. Flatness follows from [53], chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1.
sourceIssues.correction: "Flatness follows from [53], §23, Thm. 23.1", i.e. Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, §23 "Flatness and fibres", Theorem 23.1 (miracle flatness): a local homomorphism A → B of Noetherian local rings with A regular, B Cohen–Macaulay and dim B = dim A + dim B/m_A B is flat. Most likely "thm. 23.1" was mistyped as "thm. 2.3.1".
sourceIssues.reason: I rendered p. 60 at 110 dpi. The image reads "Flatness follows from [53], chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1." with a bold [53], so this is not a text-layer artefact. [53] is Matsumura's Commutative Ring Theory. That book has chapters 1–11 and numbered sections §1–§33, and its theorems are numbered by section (Theorem 23.1, 23.2, …). No result anywhere in it is numbered with three parts like "2.3.1". "Chap. 23" is loose wording for §23 "Flatness and fibres", which sits in Chapter 8 "Flatness revisited". Theorem 23.1 is the miracle-flatness criterion, and a web search agrees: the standard citation for miracle flatness is "Matsumura, CRT, §23, Theorem 23.1". This is exactly the tool the proof needs: a finite (so quasi-finite) map from a Cohen–Macaulay source to a regular target. So the citation as printed points to a theorem that doesn't exist, and the intended one is Theorem 23.1. The paper has no numbering convention of its own that would make "thm. 2.3.1" correct. The bibliography names CRT, and Matsumura's other book, Commutative Algebra, uses (n.X)/Theorem-N numbering, so it doesn't match either. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018, p. 50, Lemma 10.3.1) does not have this text. There the flatness is proved directly, by showing that the fibres of q1 are torsors under a group étale-locally isomorphic to the finite flat H1^⊥ and that r1 is finite flat. Matsumura ([49] in v3) is listed in the v3 bibliography, but I found no citation of it in the text layer. So the misprint was introduced when this proof was rewritten for the 2019 version. The published Duke text could not be checked. Side remarks, not part of this item: Theorem 23.1 also needs dim O_{ℭ,x} = dim O_{𝔜,y}, which the paper leaves implicit. Lemma 10.2.2 as stated covers ℭ^1(p^m) and ℭ^2(p^m) (lci over Spf Z_p), not the composite ℭ(p^m) directly. Neither point bears on the citation misprint.

review.reason: Confirmed, and I verified the exponents independently by calibrating against the paper's own analogous computation. Page 60 prints the ring as $W(\bar\F_p)[[X,Y,Z,X',Y',Z']]/((1+X')^p-1-X,(1+Z')^{p^2}-1-Z,Y'-Y)$, and the diagram at the top of p.\u202f61 has left vertical $\mathrm{diag}(p^2,p)$ and right vertical $\mathrm{diag}(1,p)$. Writing the Serre\u2013Tate parameter as a matrix $M$ and the commutativity as $\alpha\circ q=q'\circ\beta$ with $\alpha=\mathrm{diag}(1,p)$ on the target and $\beta$ the left vertical, the $(1,1)$ entry gives $1+X=(1+X')^{p^2}$ and the $(2,1)$ entry gives $1+Z=(1+Z')^{p}$. The same computation applied to the corresponding diagram on p.\u202f39, where $\beta=\mathrm{diag}(p,p)$, reproduces the relations printed there, $(1+X')^p-1=X$ and $(1+Z')^p-1=Z$, which confirms the convention. So the two exponents are interchanged on p.\u202f60 and the diagram on p.\u202f61 is right as printed, exactly as the finding says. The conclusion, that division by $p^3$ preserves integrality of the trace, is unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: §10.3, proof of Lemma 10.3.3, p. 61 of the author version. HAL v3 (p. 50) instead says "since the intersection of the boundary and the non-ordinary locus is of codimension 2", which is correct for the special fibre. The "codimension 1 in the special fiber … boundary is flat" wording was introduced in the revision.
sourceIssues.printed: Actually, it is enough to see that it is well defined over the entire ordinary locus since the intersection of the boundary and the non-ordinary locus is of codimension 1 in the special fiber and the boundary is flat over Spf Z_p (in other words, in the spectrum of the local rings Spec O_{ℭ^1(p^m),x} at closed points x of ℭ^1(p^m), the intersection of the boundary and the non-ordinary locus is of codimension at least 2).
sourceIssues.correction: "… is of codimension 1 in the special fiber of the boundary (codimension 2 in the special fiber of ℭ^1(p^m)), and the boundary is flat over Spf Z_p …"
sourceIssues.reason: Printed text confirmed. Dimension count: the special fibre of ℭ^1(p^m), finite over X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) away from the boundary, has dimension 3. Its boundary D_s has dimension 2. On the toric-rank-1 stratum, p-rank = 1 + p-rank of the elliptic abelian part, so non-ordinary means that elliptic curve is supersingular, a codimension-1 condition in D_s. The toric-rank-2 strata are ordinary. So D ∩ (non-ordinary) has dimension 1: codimension 1 in D_s but codimension 2 in the ambient special fibre. Read as the special fibre of ℭ^1(p^m), which is the natural reading, "codimension 1" is false. The appeal to flatness of the boundary shows the author meant D_s: codimension 1 in D_s and D flat give codimension 2 in D, hence at least 2 in Spec O_{ℭ^1(p^m),x} (in fact 3). The parenthetical conclusion, codimension ≥ 2 in the 4-dimensional local rings, is true either way, so the Hartogs-type extension of Θ is unaffected. This is a wording slip, not an error. Confidence is only medium because a charitable reader can take "the special fiber" to mean the boundary's.

sourceIssues.printed: Author version p. 67, transcribed from the page image at 250 dpi. (a) Paragraph after Lemma 11.1.1.1: "The second projection g_2 : 𝔇 → 𝔜^{ord} actually lifts to g_2 : 𝔇 → 𝔜^{ord}_{Kli}(p) by mapping (G, L) to (G/L, G[p]/L)." (b) Proof of Lemma 11.1.1.3: "L′ ⊂ (G/L)[p^2] is of type (1, p, p, p^2) and L′ ∩ (G[p]/(L ∩ G[p])) ≠ {0}. We have two projections s_1(G, H, L, L′) = (G, H), s_2(G, H, L, L′) = ((G/L)/L′, (G/L[p])/L′). This correspondence is associated to the operator U ∘ F. We observe that G[p]/L ⊂ L′. As a result, the map s_2^⋆Ω^{(1,0)} → s_1^⋆Ω^{(1,0)} factors through p s_1^⋆Ω^{(1,0)}. It then follows easily that the non normalized cohomological correspondence Θ : s_2^⋆Ω^{(k,r)} → s_1^!Ω^{(k,r)} factors through p^{6+2r+k} p_1^!Ω^{(k,r)}."
sourceIssues.correction:
1. Replace "p^{6+2r+k} p_1^!Ω^{(k,r)}" with "p^{6+2r+k} s_1^!Ω^{(k,r)}".
2. The second component of s_2 should be ((G/L)[p])/L′, meaning the image of (G/L)[p] in (G/L)/L′, that is ((G/L)[p]+L′)/L′.
3. Every "G[p]/L" (in the lift of g_2, in the second projection of T‴, and in "G[p]/L ⊂ L′") should read (G[p]+L)/L ≅ G[p]/(L∩G[p]). This is the image of G[p] in G/L, and it is the notation the author himself uses in the condition on L′. On the mod-p ordinary locus this group is G[p]^m/L^m ≅ μ_p, so it is multiplicative of order p, as the Klingen datum requires.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked each part against the page image and redid the reasoning.

(1) The correspondence 𝔥 in the proof of Lemma 11.1.1.3 is defined only with the projections s_1 and s_2, and the same sentence gives Θ the target s_1^!. So "p_1^!" is a leftover from the notation of §7.1 (Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 use p_1, p_2). This part is an unambiguous misprint.

(2) L is an extension of Z/p⊕Z/p^2 by μ_p. Its étale quotient has exponent p^2, so L is not contained in G[p], and G[p]/L is not literally defined. The intended group is the image of G[p] in G/L. On the mod-p ordinary locus (X_1^{ord}, where the reduced base forces L[p] = L∩G[p] to be flat of order p^3), I recomputed:
- L[p] maps onto G[p]^{et}, and L[p] ∩ G^m = L^m, which is μ_p.
- Hence G[p]/L[p] = G[p]^m/L^m ≅ μ_p, which is multiplicative of order p.
The author's revisions support this reading. HAL v3 wrote "L′ ∩ G[p]/L ≠ {0}" and "G[p] ⊂ L+L′". The author version changed these to "L′ ∩ (G[p]/(L∩G[p])) ≠ {0}" and "G[p]/L ⊂ L′", but left the other occurrences of "G[p]/L" unchanged.

(3) "(G/L[p])/L′", read literally as G/(L[p]), is an abelian scheme, not a subgroup of (G/L)/L′. The intended group is the image of (G/L)[p]. HAL v3 already wrote "G/L[p^2]" for (G/L)[p^2]. The author version added the parentheses in "(G/L)[p^2]" but not here.

The mathematics works with the intended meanings:
- H′ is the image of G[p] and has order p. Since L′∩H′ ≠ 0, we get H′ ⊂ L′.
- So the composite G → G/L → (G/L)/L′ kills G[p] and factors through [p].
- Its multiplicative kernel has order p^2, so on ω it is p times an isomorphism. This gives p^{k+2r} on Ω^{(k,r)}.
- With p^6 from the fundamental classes and the normalization p^{-(3+r)} twice, the normalized operator is divisible by p^k. It is therefore 0 mod p for k ≥ 1, exactly as stated.

A caveat: "G[p]/L" is used consistently (three times) and its meaning is clear, so one could call it an abuse of notation rather than a misprint. The p_1^! and the missing parentheses are genuine misprints either way.

HAL v3 (p. 56) has the same "(G/L, G[p]/L)", "(G/L[p])/L′" and "p_1^!", with further sloppiness ("G/L + L′", "G/L[p^2]").

sourceIssues.locator: §11.1.1, proof of Lemma 11.1.1.4, p. 68 (author version, 17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: (we have T^{1,et} = T′). We now observe that any isogeny G → G/L occuring in T^{n,m} will factor through multiplication by p on G. So we deduce, reasoning as in the proof of lemma 11.1.1.3, that T^{n,et} = T^n mod p^k. It is clear that Tr ∘ U^n ∘ i = pT^{n,et} and the factor p arises from the fact that given L_n, we can find p different subgroups H of order p and multiplicative type such that H ∩ L_n = {0}.  [Lemma 11.1.1.4 as printed: "For all n ≥ 0, we have Tr ∘ U^n ∘ i = pT^n mod p^k as endomorphisms of H^0(𝔛^{ord}, Ω^{(k,r)})."]
sourceIssues.correction:
Replace "will factor through multiplication by p on G" with "has kernel L ⊇ G[p]^m, the multiplicative part of G[p]". Then do the count step by step instead of copying Lemma 11.1.1.3.

Why L ⊇ G[p]^m holds for every chain in T^{n,m}:
- A T1^m step has H1 ⊇ G_i[p]^m.
- A T1^et∘T2^m step has kernel G_i[p].
- A chain made only of T′ = T1^et∘T2^et steps whose L^m is not cyclic already contains G[p]^m.
- If L^m is cyclic, then |L^m| = p^n and L is Lagrangian, so L has the T^{n,et} type (μ_{p^n}; Z/p^n ⊕ Z/p^{2n}).

The count uses Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2. Write M_i for a step's multiplicative-order exponent, F_i for its fundamental-class exponent, and δ = F_i + rM_i − 3 − r. The four step types give:
- T1^et T2^et: δ = 0
- T1^et T2^m: δ = r−1
- T1^m T2^et: δ = r−2
- T1^m T2^m: δ = 2r−3

A chain's normalized coefficient is then divisible by p^{Σδ + k·min(j1,j2)}, where (p^{j1}, p^{j2}) are the elementary divisors of L^m, and min(j1,j2) ≥ 1 on T^{n,m}. So T^{n,et} ≡ T^n mod p^k when r ≥ 2. That is the standing hypothesis of §11.1.1, and the lemma should state it.

An equivalent alternative correction:
- T ≡ T′ mod p^k when r ≥ 2, since the other three pieces carry p^{k+r−1}, p^{k+r−2} and p^{k+2r−3}.
- Inside T′^n the printed claim is literally true: L ⊇ L_1[p], and L_1[p] + G[p]^m = G[p].

How this compares with another proposed correction:
- The equivalent fix above is right and complete.
- The other proposed correction names the right fact (L ⊇ G[p]^m) but understates the rest: it takes divisibility of the differential by p to be all that the argument of Lemma 11.1.1.3 uses. Lemma 11.1.1.3 also takes p^3 per step from fundamental classes, and T1^m and T2^m steps do not supply that. Only det^r makes up the difference, and that needs r ≥ 2.

Aside: the lemma itself only needs pT^{n,m} ≡ 0 mod p^k. The same count seems to give this already for r = 1, because each T1^m step makes the whole differential divisible by p. So r ≥ 2 is needed for the proof's intermediate claim, not necessarily for the lemma. The requirement n ≥ 1 (the lemma fails at n = 0) is a separate item, sourceIssues E85.
sourceIssues.reason:
The page image of p. 68 matches the quoted text. Read literally, the sentence is false. I checked the counterexample myself. Take an ordinary G, for example the canonical lift, with G[p^∞] = μa ⊕ μb ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)e ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)f, where a pairs with e and b pairs with f. Let L = μ_{p²}a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ (Z/p)f.
- L is isotropic for e_{p²}: e_{p²} is trivial on G[p]×G[p], ⟨a,f⟩ = 0, and the annihilator of L^m in G^et[p²] is exactly (Z/p)f. Its order is p^4, so L is Lagrangian.
- L[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f has order p^3, with K = L[p]^⊥ = μ_p a. So L is the T_{p,1} chain T1^m ∘ T2^m, and it lies in T^{1,m}.
- G[p] ⊄ L, since e is missing.
There are other counterexamples: the T1^m T2^et chains H1 + ⟨e + αã⟩ with α ≠ 0 also lie in T^{1,m} and do not contain G[p].

The true statement is weaker: every T^{n,m} chain satisfies L ⊇ G[p]^m, so the differential is still divisible by p. But the appeal to "reasoning as in lemma 11.1.1.3" does not transfer. That proof gets p^6 from two T‴-type steps, each with fundamental class p^3. On T1^m and T2^m steps the fundamental class is an isomorphism (Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2). The missing powers are recovered only through extra det^r factors, which needs r ≥ 2. For example, T1^m T2^et has normalized coefficient p^{k+r−2}, and that hypothesis is not in the lemma.

I recomputed the coefficients p^{k+r−1}, p^{k+r−2}, p^{k+2r−3} of the pieces T1^et T2^m, T1^m T2^et and T1^m T2^m of T and confirmed them. I also found that T1^et T2^m consists only of the T_{p,0} chains L = G[p]. The corrected argument is sound.

The conclusion holds for n ≥ 1 and r ≥ 2. Its only use is Corollary 11.1.1.2 (r ≥ 2, k ≥ 2, n large), which then feeds Proposition 11.1.3/Theorem 11.2.1, so no stated downstream result is affected.

HAL v3 does not have this lemma. There, Corollary 11.1.1.2 (r ≥ 2, k ≥ 1) proves injectivity by a different argument, a local representation-theoretic p-stabilisation. So this passage is new in the 2019 version. The printed claim is false even for n = 1. Take an ordinary G with G[p^∞] = μ a ⊕ μ b ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)e ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)f, where a pairs with e and b with f.

First counterexample: L = μ_{p²}a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ (Z/p)f.
- L is Lagrangian in G[p²], and L[p] = (μ_p a)^⊥.
- It is the chain T1^m∘T2^m. This is the same L as in the counterexample above.
- Its multiplicative part is μ_{p²} ⊕ μ_p, so it lies in T^{1,m}.
- The e-direction is missing from G[p], so G → G/L does not factor through [p].

Second family: the T1^m∘T2^et chains (μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f) + ⟨e + αã⟩ with α ≠ 0 also lie in T^{1,m} and do not contain G[p].

I checked this by a short computer enumeration with p = 3, over all 40 order-p lines H, with H1 = H^⊥ and H1 ⊂ L ⊂ p^{-1}H:
- 108 T1^et T2^et chains, each with L^m = μ_p. These are exactly T^{1,et}.
- 36 T1^et T2^m chains, all with L = G[p].
- 12 T1^m T2^et chains: 4 with L = G[p] and 8 with G[p] ⊄ L.
- 4 T1^m T2^m chains, each with |L^m| = p³ and G[p] ⊄ L.
- All 48 chains of T^{1,m} contain G[p]^m. Of these, 12 do not contain G[p].

The defence fails.
- If T meant T′, the claim would be true. But the proof itself writes T^{1,et} = T′, so T^{1,m} = T − T′ is nonzero over 𝔛^ord.
- The paper identifies T with T′ only on H^0(X_1^ord), that is mod p, through Lemma 11.1.1.1. It never does so mod p^k.

sourceIssues.correction: Replace "For all n ≥ 0" with "For all n ≥ 1". At n = 0 the correct identity is Tr ∘ i = (p+1)·Id. Other hypotheses the lemma may need, such as r ≥ 2 for T^{n,et} ≡ T^n mod p^k, are a separate issue and not part of this correction.

I checked the page image at 220 dpi, and the statement reads "n ≥ 0". Take n = 0. Then U^0 = Id and T^0 = Id, so the left side is Tr ◦ i. Here i is pullback along 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord, and the paper says just above the lemma that this map is finite étale of rank p+1. This matches §9.1.1: H ⊂ G[p] is étale-locally μ_p, and on the ordinary locus G[p]^mult ≅ μ_p^2 has p+1 such lines. The trace of a pullback along a finite étale map of degree p+1 is multiplication by p+1, so Tr ◦ i = (p+1)·Id. The right side is p·T^0 = p·Id. The difference is Id. That is not ≡ 0 mod p^k for k ≥ 1, the standing range in §11.1.1 (Lemmas 11.1.1.1–3 need k ≥ 1, Corollary 11.1.1.2 needs k ≥ 2), because H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)) is a nonzero p-adically separated module. The printed statement is therefore false at n = 0. No normalisation convention rescues it: T^0 = Id whatever the normalisation of T, and renormalising Tr by 1/(p+1) would break the case n ≥ 1. The proof's count fails at the same place. L_0 ⊂ G[p^0] is 0, so all p+1 multiplicative H satisfy H ∩ L_0 = {0}, not p of them. For n ≥ 1 the count p is right: L_n ∩ G[p]^mult is the line μ_p ⊂ μ_p^2, and H must avoid it, which leaves p of the p+1 lines. The lemma is used only in the proof of Corollary 11.1.1.2, "Applying lemma 11.1.1.4 for n large enough"; a grep finds no other citation. So the fix to n ≥ 1 changes nothing downstream. HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3) does not contain this lemma or the rank-(p+1) sentence. Its §11.1.1 stops at Lemma 11.1.1.3 and Corollaries 11.1.1.1–2 (Corollary 11.1.1.2 there assumes k ≥ 1), and it proves injectivity by a p-stabilisation / Hecke-polynomial argument. The published Duke version could not be checked. On 'affects': I would record 'a stated result', not 'nothing'. The printed Lemma 11.1.1.4 is itself a stated result that is false in its n = 0 case, and its proof fails there too. The reach stops at that lemma: no later result depends on the n = 0 case. I checked this against the page image at 250 dpi. The statement reads "n ≥ 0".

**Why n = 0 fails.** U^0 = Id and T^0 = Id, so the claim at n = 0 says Tr ∘ i ≡ p·Id mod p^k. Here i is pullback along 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord. The paper says in the sentence just before the lemma that this map is finite étale of rank p+1.
