sourceIssues.locator: §13.4 (The spectral variety), displayed formula in the second paragraph, just before Proposition 13.4.1, p. 91 (author version). HAL v3 has the same text on printed p. 79 (PDF p. 80).
sourceIssues.printed: "Moreover, for all κ : Spa(C_p, O) → Spa(A_l[1/p], A_l) and α^{−1} ∈ C_p^× providing a point (κ, α^{−1}) : Spa(C_p, O) → Spa(A_l[1/p], A_l) × G_m , we have isomorphisms :  H^i((κ, α^{−1})^⋆ C_cusp(A_l)) = H^i_cusp(κ, r)[U = α]." (checked on the rendered page image, author version p. 91)
sourceIssues.correction: There are two faults. (i) Notation: 'H^i_cusp(κ, r)' should read 'H^i_cusp(†, κ, 2)'. The complex is built from C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), and r is not defined in §13.4. (ii) Mathematics: the fibre at the point does not compute the eigenspace. The correct statement localises at α^{−1} instead of taking the fibre there: H^i(Lκ^*C_cusp(A_l))_{(α^{−1})} ≅ H^i_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}, the generalised α-eigenspace of U. Equivalently, for the support: (κ,α^{−1}) lies in Supp H^•(C_cusp(A_l)) iff α is a U-eigenvalue on H^•_cusp(†,κ,2). That support statement is all the definition of Z_l needs. If a pointwise formula is wanted, for x = (κ,α^{−1}) there is an exact sequence 0 → coker(U−α | H^i_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}) → H^i(Lx^*C_cusp(A_l)) → ker(U−α | H^{i+1}_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}) → 0. Another proposed reading gives the same correction, but with the exact sequence shifted by one (that is the x^! form); its example (α only on H^0) fails only in degree −1 under the standard derived x^*. The passage is a false statement, not just an unproved one, so it is an error, not a gap.
sourceIssues.reason:
I transcribed the formula from the page image, and HAL v3 prints the same formula. In §13.1.2 the G_m/A^1 coordinate X is inverse to the eigenvalue (det(1−XŨ)), and the sheaf over the spectral variety is the slope part N^• with X acting as U^{−1}. My own check: the derived pullback along κ is N^•_κ, which computes the generalised eigenspaces (base change, since N^• is perfect over O_V). Pulling back further to X = α^{−1} tensors with the Koszul complex in degrees −1 and 0. That gives the long exact sequence above: H^i(fibre) is an extension of ker(U−α | H^{i+1}) by coker(U−α | H^i). So the printed equality fails in general. If α is a U-eigenvalue on H^0_cusp, then H^{−1}(fibre) = ker(U−α|H^0) ≠ 0, while the right side is 0 in degree −1. If α occurs on H^1 but not on H^0, then H^0(fibre) ≠ 0 = H^0[U=α]. The underived, termwise reading also fails. It depends on the representative Ũ. Explicit counterexample: N^0 = C_p^2 with U a Jordan block at α, N^1 = C_p with U = α, and d(e2) = 1. Then H^0 = ⟨e1⟩ with U = α, but the termwise fibre is acyclic. Another proposed reading has a long exact sequence with an index shift: the cocone/x^! version, 0 → coker(H^{i−1}) → H^i → ker(H^i) → 0. With the standard derived tensor, its example (α on H^0 only) gives H^{−1}(fibre) ≠ 0 rather than H^1(fibre) ≠ 0. The conclusion still holds, in degree −1. What the text actually uses does hold. By derived Nakayama, the support of H^•(C_cusp(A_l)) is the set of pairs (κ,α^{−1}) with α a U-eigenvalue on H^•_cusp(†,κ,2), so the definition of Z is fine. Proposition 13.4.1 ('corollary of the discussion above and proposition 13.1.3.1') needs only Prop 13.1.3.1 with h = 0 applied to C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), plus independence of n,ε,w. It does not use the fibre formula. Its only later use is in Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102), where it enters only through local constancy of the Euler characteristic. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED. In §13.1.2 (p. 84) the paper sets up a complex of coherent sheaves 𝓜^• over Z̃ ⊂ A^1 × Spa(A,A^+), 'the universal eigenspace of M^• for the action of Ũ'. The coordinate X satisfies P̃(X) = det(1 − XŨ), so X acts as U^{−1}, and the point (κ,α^{−1}) corresponds to the eigenvalue α. Nothing in §13.1–13.2 or in the cited sources ([14] Coleman, [9] Buzzard, [81] Urban) identifies the fibre at a point with an eigenspace. Buzzard's machine gives the fibre as the eigenspace quotient coker(U−α), not the eigenspace itself. I tested every reading of '(κ,α^{−1})^⋆':
(a) Derived fibre. Lx^*N = N ⊗^L O/(X−α^{−1}) = cone(U^{−1}−α^{−1} : N → N), where N = Lκ^*C_cusp(A_l) is the finite-slope part of C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ,2). This gives the exact sequence in the correction. Toy check, computed by hand: take N = C_p in degree 1 with U = α. The map U^{−1}−α^{−1} is 0, so the cone is N[1] ⊕ N and H^0(fibre) = C_p. But H^0[U=α] = 0. In general, in degree 0 the fibre has dimension dim H^0[U=α] + dim H^1[U=α]. So the formula fails at every α that is a U-eigenvalue on H^1_cusp(†,κ,2), which is the case the paper is about. It also fails in degree −1 whenever α occurs on H^0. Another way to see it: every derived fibre has Euler characteristic 0, while dim H^0[U=α] − dim H^1[U=α] is not 0 in general.
(b) Termwise fibre of the complex. This depends on the representative Ũ and fails the same way.
(c) Fibre x^*H^i(C) of the cohomology sheaves. For i = 1 this is coker(U−α | H^1_{(α)}), whose dimension equals that of H^1[U=α]. For i = 0 base change fails wherever H^1(C) has κ-torsion, i.e. where the dimensions jump. Lemma 14.8.4 exists precisely to rule out such jumps.
(d) '[U=α]' read as the generalised eigenspace. This is right only for the localisation, not for the fibre at the point.
So no faithful reading makes the display true. Separately, the r is a leftover of the general-r notation H^i_cusp(†,κ_A,r) (p. 83), and the † is missing.
CONSEQUENCES. 'Z_l' is defined as the support of H^•(C_cusp(A_l)). That, and 'quasi-finite and locally finite', need only the support description and Z_l ⊂ Z̃; the support description holds by derived Nakayama. Proposition 13.4.1 ('corollary of the discussion above and proposition 13.1.3.1') follows from Prop. 13.1.3.1 with h = 0, applied to C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), together with Cor. 13.2.4.2 (independence of n,ε,w on the finite-slope part). Neither step uses the display. The only later reference to §13.4 is Lemma 14.8.4 (author p. 102: 'by theorem 11.3.1 and proposition 13.4.1'), and it uses only the local constancy of the Euler characteristic. I searched the text: the glued Z → W and H^•(C_cusp) are never used again. Remark 1.2 mentions the finite-slope theory in passing, but no numbered result depends on this display. So the mathematics as intended (support, generalised eigenspaces) is right, and no result or proof is damaged.

review.reason: Confirmed as an error, and the sign and the shift are both decidable. The displayed formula in §13.4 reads $H^i((\kappa,\alpha^{-1})^\star C_{\mathrm{cusp}}(A_l))=H^i_{\mathrm{cusp}}(\kappa,r)[U=\alpha]$, in a paragraph whose complex is built from $C_{\mathrm{cusp}}(n,\varepsilon,w,\kappa_{A_l},2)$ and in which $r$ never appears, so the notational half is right. The mathematical half is right too. Derived pullback along $X-\alpha$ is the Koszul cone, so the long exact sequence gives $0\to\mathrm{coker}(U-\alpha\mid H^i)\to H^i(Lx^\star C)\to\ker(U-\alpha\mid H^{i+1})\to0$, which is not the eigenspace $H^i[U=\alpha]$ in either degree unless $U-\alpha$ is semisimple. Localising at $\alpha^{-1}$, as the correction does, gives the generalised eigenspace and is what the definition of $Z_l$ actually uses, since only the support of $H^\bullet(C_{\mathrm{cusp}}(A_l))$ enters. Proposition 13.4.1 and everything after it are unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.2 (The correspondences C_n), definition of C_n|_{𝒴_Kli(p)}, p. 92 of the author version (HAL v3: same passage, printed p. 80 = PDF p. 81)
sourceIssues.printed: where (G, H) ∈ 𝒴_{Kli}(p) and L_n ⊂ G[p^n] is a totally isotropic subgroup which is locally for the étale topology isomorphic to (ℤ/p^nℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n}ℤ and L_n ∩ H = {0}.
sourceIssues.correction: L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] (a Lagrangian subgroup: its order p^{n}·p^{n}·p^{2n} = p^{4n} is half the order p^{8n} of G[p^{2n}]).
sourceIssues.reason: I checked this on page 92 rendered at 110 and 220 dpi. The page really prints "L_n ⊂ G[p^n]" next to "(ℤ/p^nℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n}ℤ", so this is not a text-layer artefact. The printed text contradicts itself. A group scheme locally isomorphic to (ℤ/p^n)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n} has sections of order p^{2n}, so for n ≥ 1 it cannot lie in G[p^n]. For n = 1 it would require a ℤ/p^2 inside G[p]. The paper's own later text uses G[p^{2n}]: (1) the same paragraph says C_1 is the correspondence C of §13.2.1 (p. 85), which reads "L ⊂ G[p^2] ... isomorphic to (ℤ/pℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^2ℤ", and G[p^2] matches G[p^{2n}] at n = 1. (2) The proof of Corollary 14.3.1 (p. 94) says "L_i locally isomorphic to ℤ/p^{2i} ⊕ (ℤ/p^i)^2 and totally isotropic in G[p^{2i}]". (3) The proof of Lemma 14.6.1 (p. 97) says "|m_i|_x ≥ |p^{2n}|_x since L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}]". (4) The ordinary-case analogue in the proof of Lemma 11.1.1.4 (p. 68) says "L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] is a totally isotropic subgroup". The order count also works: L_n has order p^{4n}, exactly Lagrangian in G[p^{2n}], which fits the double coset diag(1, p^n, p^n, p^{2n}) = U^n that comes from iterating C_1 n times. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018) has the same wording on printed p. 80 (PDF p. 81), which I checked on the page image. The proposed correction L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] is right.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.1, proof of Lemma 14.1.1, p. 92 (author version, 17 June 2019); same sentence in HAL v3, p. 80 (PDF p. 81)
sourceIssues.printed: "The group H_n has degree at least n − 2(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)). Morover the maps p^{k−1} : H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] → H_n[p^{n−1}] = H_1 are morphisms which are isomorphisms on the generic fiber. Therefore, using [20], coro. 3 on p. 13, we deduce that deg H_1 ≥ (1/n) deg H_n ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1))." (checked on the page image at 110 and 250 dpi, author version p. 92)
sourceIssues.correction: p^{k−1} : H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] → H_n[p] = H_1 (the same as p^{n−1}H_n on the generic fiber)
sourceIssues.reason:
This is a real misprint. By §12.7.1 (p. 77), X_Kli(p^n, ϵ) parametrizes pairs (x, H_n), where H_n ⊂ G_x[p^n] is locally isomorphic to Z/p^nZ and is generated by e_1. The map to X_Kli(p) sends H_n to its subgroup of order p. So H_1, the Klingen subgroup whose degree is v_x(δ_H), is H_n[p] = p^{n−1}H_n, which has order p. H_n[p^{n−1}] has order p^{n−1}, and it is the level-p^{n−1} group H_{n−1}, not H_1. The two agree only when n = 2.

Checking the step myself: on the generic fiber, H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] ≅ Z/p. Multiplication by p^{k−1} maps it isomorphically onto H_n[p], which is also ≅ Z/p. For n ≥ 3 it cannot be an isomorphism onto H_n[p^{n−1}], a group of order p^{n−1}. So the sentence as printed is false.

With H_n[p] the argument works. Fargues [20], coro. 3 says that a morphism of finite flat group schemes that is a generic isomorphism does not decrease degree. Hence deg(H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}]) ≤ deg H_1 for each k. Since degree is additive along the filtration 0 ⊂ H_n[p] ⊂ … ⊂ H_n[p^n] = H_n, we get deg H_n ≤ n·deg H_1. Also deg H_n + deg H_n^D = n and deg H_n^D ≤ 2(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)). Together these give deg H_1 ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)), exactly as printed.

The error is only the exponent in one target group. The rest of the proof, the statement of Lemma 14.1.1 and Remark 14.1.1 are unaffected, and later uses of the lemma depend only on the bound, which is correct. HAL v3 (p. 80) has the same "H_n[p^{n−1}] = H_1", there with the phrase "are generic isomorphisms". It also has the separate slip "deg H_1 ≥ (1/n) deg H_n^D", which the author version fixes to deg H_n.

sourceIssues.reason: I checked both arXiv versions. In arXiv:1205.3463v2 (the Forum Pi paper), §9 'Miscellany' has 'Theorem 9.1. (i) The category of coherent O_{X0}-modules is equivalent to that of coherent O_X-modules. (ii) … R^i f_* F is coherent and equal to the analytification of R^i f_{0*} F_0'. This is relative GAGA for proper morphisms (Köpf), exactly the comparison and GAGA theorem the text uses. In arXiv:1111.4914v1 (Perfectoid spaces, = [69]), §9 is 'The weight-monodromy conjecture', and its 9.1 is 'Proposition 9.1', Grothendieck's quasi-unipotence theorem. sourceIssues.printed: 14.4.2 (p. 95), checked on the rendered page: "We normalize this map by dividing by the factor p^{n(3+r)} and call it U^n. This normalization is consistent with section 10.4. Restricting this map to 𝓕^{++} provides a map U^n : (t_{n,1})_⋆ t^⋆_{n,2} 𝓕^{++} → p^{−3n} 𝓕^{++}. The reason the map lands in p^{−3n}𝓕^{++} instead of p^{−3n−nr}𝓕^{++} is that the kernel L_n of the isogeny G → G_n has degree at least one by lemma 14.3.1, 2."
sourceIssues.correction: "... is that the kernel L_n of the isogeny G → G_n has degree at least n." Justification to add: C_n is C_1 iterated n times (p. 92). So G → G_n factors through the filtration L_1 ⊂ ... ⊂ L_n used in the proof of Cor. 14.3.1. Each graded piece L_i/L_{i−1} is the kernel of a C_1-point of G/L_{i−1}. δ_{L_n} is the product of the δ_{L_i/L_{i−1}}, so deg L_n = Σ deg(L_i/L_{i−1}). For each piece, deg = deg p(·) + deg (·)[p]/p(·) + deg (·)/(·)[p] ≥ 1, by Lemma 14.3.1(2) and non-negativity of the degree. Hence deg L_n ≥ n. Equivalently: prove the case n = 1 as printed, then use U^n = U∘···∘U, which the paper states a few lines later.
sourceIssues.reason:
I re-did the computation. F = Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G (p. 43 / §3). The unnormalized correspondence uses the differential Ω^+_{G_n} → Ω^+_G of G → G_n = G/L_n. On Sym^k this map is integral. On det^r it is multiplication by δ_{L_n}^r, where v_x(δ_{L_n}) = deg L_n|_x (§14.3, v_x(p) = 1, no division by n). The factor p^{3n} in the normalization belongs to the trace, as in §10.4, where the trace is normalized by p^{−3} and ω^r by p^{−r}. So after dividing by p^{n(3+r)}, the image lies in p^{r·deg L_n − nr − 3n}F^{++}. For r > 0, landing in p^{−3n}F^{++} needs deg L_n ≥ n. The printed reason, "degree at least one by lemma 14.3.1, 2", covers only n = 1: Lemma 14.3.1 is stated for points of C_1 only (p. 93). For n ≥ 2 it gives only p^{r−3n−nr}F^{++}, which is not p^{−3n}F^{++}. So the justification as printed falls short for n ≥ 2. The claimed conclusion is still true, via the filtration (additivity of the degree is already used in the proof of Corollary 14.3.1, p. 94) or via iteration. This is not a text-layer artefact: I checked the page image, and "one" and "lemma 14.3.1, 2" are printed that way. It is also not a convention issue: deg L_n is defined unnormalized, and on the relevant component deg L = 1, so the bound deg L_n ≥ n is exactly what is needed. Nothing later depends on the slip. Prop. 14.5.1 uses U^n only on F, not F^{++}. Prop. 14.6.1 gets its integrality from Lemma 14.6.1 directly. Cor. 14.6.1 and Remark 14.6.1 use only the n = 1 bound U: F^{++} → p^{−3}F^{++}. This correction is right, and nothing is affected. Two side notes, outside this issue: (1) for r < 0 the det^r map is δ^r with negative valuation, so the p^{−3n} claim implicitly assumes r ≥ 0. (2) On p. 92 the definition of C_n reads "L_n ⊂ G[p^n]", which should be G[p^{2n}] (compare p. 94 and Lemma 14.6.1). I tried to defend the text; it fails.

(1) The degree is not normalised by n. §14.3 (p. 93) defines deg L_n|x = v_x(δ_{L_n}) with v_x(p) = 1.

(2) What the claim needs. On 𝓕 = Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω ⊗ det^r ω (pp. 24, 30), the unnormalised correspondence has three parts:
- the differential of G → G_n, which is integral on Sym^k Ω^+;
- the factor δ_{L_n}^r on det^r;
- the integral trace on 𝒪^{++}.
The factor p^{3n} in the normalisation belongs to the trace. That matches §10.4, where the trace is normalised by p^{-3} and ω^r by p^{-r}. After dividing by p^{n(3+r)}, the image lies in p^{r·deg L_n − nr − 3n}𝓕^{++}. For r > 0, landing in p^{−3n}𝓕^{++} therefore needs deg L_n ≥ n. The reason as printed only gives deg L_n ≥ 1, hence only p^{r−nr−3n}𝓕^{++}. That is not enough once n ≥ 2.

(3) Lemma 14.3.1 is stated only for points of C_1 (p. 93). So "by lemma 14.3.1, 2" does not by itself bound deg L_n for n ≥ 2.

(4) No charitable reading rescues the sentence. It speaks explicitly of "the kernel L_n of the isogeny G → G_n". The parallel n = 1 statement on p. 88 ("ξ^⋆ : t_2^⋆(ω^{++})^r → p^r t_1^⋆(ω^{++})^r by lemma 14.3.1, 2") is correct. This suggests the sentence was written for n = 1 and not updated when n was introduced.

The conclusion itself is true. It follows from the filtration/additivity argument that the paper already uses in the proof of Cor. 14.3.1 (p. 94), or from "Obviously, U^n is the n-th iterate of U = U^1" (p. 95) together with the n = 1 case. So this is an inadequate justification for n ≥ 2, i.e. a gap. It is not a false statement. One could also call it a misprint ("one" for "n"). But changing that one word would still leave the n ≥ 2 case without a proof, because Lemma 14.3.1(2) alone does not give deg L_n ≥ n. So I classify it as a gap. The correction above is correct and minimal.

What later uses this passage:
- Prop. 14.5.1 and 14.5.2 use U^n only on 𝓕, not on 𝓕^{++}.
- Prop. 14.6.1 gets its integrality on V from Lemma 14.6.1. On W it only needs the image in 𝓕(U).
- Cor. 14.6.1 and Remark 14.6.1 use only the n = 1 bound U : 𝓕^{++} → p^{−3}𝓕^{++}, which the printed reason does cover.
- A search of the whole text finds no other use of p^{−3n}𝓕^{++} for n ≥ 2.
So nothing depends on the gap.

Two side remarks outside this issue:
- The bound implicitly needs r ≥ 0. For r < 0, δ^r has negative valuation.
- On p. 92, "L_n ⊂ G[p^n]" should read G[p^{2n}], because L_n ≅ (Z/p^n)^2 ⊕ Z/p^{2n}.

sourceIssues.correction:
Assume r ≥ 0 throughout §14. The simplest fix is to open §14.4.2 with "Let F be any of Ω^(k,r) or Ω^(k,r)(−D) with (k,r) ∈ Z≥0 × Z≥0". That covers every statement listed in the locator, and the printed statements and proofs are then correct.

Refinements, if a sharper fix is wanted:
- Lemma 14.6.1 and Proposition 14.6.1 are true exactly when k + r ≥ 0.
- For r < 0 the §14.4.2 bound p^{−3n} must be weakened, for example to p^{−n(3−2r)}. The shift "n−3" in Remark 14.6.1 and the "p^{−3}" in the proof of Corollary 14.6.1 then change the same way.
- Theorem 14.7.1 very likely holds for every r ∈ Z, so it needs no hypothesis in its statement.
- Corollary 14.7.1 needs r ≥ 0 anyway, because it uses Corollary 13.3.3.1 and Proposition 13.3.1.1, which are proved under the r ≥ 0 of §13.3.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page images. The text is as quoted, with no condition on r in §14. Ω^(k,r) is defined for r ∈ Z (§6.2.1, restated in §13.3.2), and §14.4.2 says "any of Ω^(k,r)". Only §13.3 says r ≥ 0. The sentence "instead of p^{−3n−nr}F^{++}" in §14.4.2 shows that the author implicitly takes r ≥ 0.

I redid the computation. In the diagonal basis the normalized map on Sym^k⊗det^r has entries m1^{a+r}m2^{k−a+r}·p^{−n(3+r)}. Here d = v(m1m2) = deg L_n lies in [n,3n], since deg L[p]/pL = 1 and pL, L/L[p] have order p. Also 0 ≤ v(m_i) ≤ 2n. For r ≥ 0 every step of the paper is fine. For r < 0 the factor (m1m2)^r has valuation rd ≤ r(3n−α), so the proof step "multiply v(m1m2) ≥ 3n−α by r" goes the wrong way.

The extreme case d = 3n does occur. Take G ordinary with multiplicative part ⟨e1,e2⟩ and Weil pairing e1↔e4, e2↔e3. Take H = ⟨e3/p⟩ and L = ⟨e2/p^2, e1/p, e4/p⟩. The lattice T+⟨e2/p^2, e1/p, e4/p⟩ is self-dual for p^2⟨,⟩, so L is totally isotropic of type (Z/p)^2⊕Z/p^2. Also L∩H = 0, L∩G^m ≅ Z/p^2⊕Z/p, deg L = 3 and ξ* = diag(p,p^2). With the other labelling e1↔e3, e2↔e4, the subgroup ⟨e2/p^2, e1/p, e3/p⟩ with H = ⟨e4/p⟩ does the same job. A brute-force count for p = 2 found 30 such L at an ordinary point. Their multiplicative parts are Z/2 (24 of them), (Z/2)^2 (3) and Z/4⊕Z/2 (3), so d = 3 does occur.

For (k,r) = (0,−1) and n = 1:
- The normalized map on this component is p^{3r}·p^{−(3+r)} = p^{−5}. The trace on ++-sections is integral. So the claim "lands in p^{−3}F^{++}" in §14.4.2 fails.
- Lemma 14.6.1 with α = 1 predicts p^{r(3n−α)} = p^{−2}, but the actual factor is δ^{−1} = p^{−3}. So the lemma is false as printed.
- Proposition 14.6.1 predicts n(−5+2ε'), but the V-part at d = 3n gives only −5n.

HAL v3 has the same text: §14.4.2 on p. 83 and Lemma 14.6.1 on p. 84 are verbatim the same, Theorem 14.7.1 on p. 87 has no r condition, and §13.3 and §13.3.2 read the same.

On 'affects': this affects a stated result, since printed statements are false for parameters the paper allows: the §14.4.2 bound and Lemma 14.6.1, and Proposition 14.6.1 when k+r < 0. The proofs of Theorem 14.7.1 and Corollary 14.7.1 do not cover r < 0. Nothing downstream is affected, though. The only later use is Theorem 14.8.1 with r = 2, which feeds Theorem 1.1. Corollary 14.7.1 is not cited anywhere else. I checked the page images (author pp. 88, 89, 93–100 and 62; HAL v3 p. 84). There is no condition on r anywhere in §14.

The defence partly succeeds. The author clearly means r ≥ 0:
(a) §13.3 opens with "(k,r) ∈ Z≥0×Z≥0", and §14 continues it. Corollary 14.7.1 combines Theorem 14.7.1 with Corollary 13.3.3.1, which is proved under that hypothesis.
(b) The §14.4.2 sentence "lands in p^{−3n}F^{++} instead of p^{−3n−nr}F^{++} ... degree at least one" only makes sense for r ≥ 0.
(c) §14 is only ever used with r = 2: Theorem 14.8.1, which feeds Theorem 1.1. HAL v3's Theorem 14.8.1 assumes r ≥ 2.
(d) §10.4, whose normalisation §14.4.2 cites, is not the source of the problem. There the det map is exactly p, so (1/p^r) works for every r.

But the statements as printed are not restricted. Ω^(k,r) is defined for all r ∈ Z (§6.2.1), §13.3.2 repeats "(k,r) ∈ Z≥0 × Z", and §14.4.2 says "any of Ω^(k,r)". For r < 0 the numbered statements are false.

Computation. Let d = v(δ_{L_n}), which lies in [n, 3n], and let 0 ≤ v(m_i) ≤ 2n. The entries of the map on Sym^k ⊗ det^r are m1^{a+r}·m2^{k−a+r}. Their smallest valuation is r·d + k·min v(m_i), and min v(m_i) ≥ d − 2n. So the entries have valuation at least (k+r)d − 2kn. Compared with the lemma's k(n−α) + r(3n−α), the difference is (k+r)(d − (3n−α)). Hence Lemma 14.6.1 holds iff k + r ≥ 0 (for α > 0). A grid check in python agrees.

Explicit counterexample. Use the symplectic basis ⟨e1,e4⟩ = ⟨e2,e3⟩ = 1. Take an ordinary point with multiplicative part ⟨e1,e2⟩ and H = ⟨e3/p⟩, which is étale. Let n = 1 and L = ⟨e2/p², e1/p, e4/p⟩.
- L is totally isotropic in G[p²]: the only nonzero pairing is e1/p with e4/p, and p²·(1/p²) = 1 ∈ Z.
- L ≅ Z/p² ⊕ (Z/p)² and L ∩ H = 0.
- L ∩ G^m ≅ Z/p² ⊕ Z/p, so d = 3 and ξ* = diag(p, p²).
For (k,r) = (0,−1):
- The normalised factor is p^{−3}·p^{−(3+r)} = p^{−5}, not p^{−3}. So the §14.4.2 claim fails.
- Lemma 14.6.1 with α = 1 predicts p^{−2}, but the actual factor is p^{−3}.
- Proposition 14.6.1 fails for any 0 < ε < ε'. Near x, t_1 is étale, so a section p^a·e with 0 < a < 2ε', supported on the branch through y = (G,H,L), is valid. Its restriction to t_2^{−1}(X_ε) vanishes, because (H+L)/L is étale of degree 0 < ε. Its U-image p^{−5+a}e does not lie in p^{−5+2ε'}F^{++}.

The main theorem very likely survives:
- If r < 0 ≤ k + r, Lemma 14.6.1 and Proposition 14.6.1 hold as printed. Corollary 14.6.1 then needs only some fixed constant c with U(F^{++}) ⊂ p^{−c}F^{++}, and c = 3 − 2r works because d ≤ 3n.
- If k + r < 0, the smallest normalised valuation is n(k+2r−3), attained at d = 3n. So slopes are at least k + 2r − 3, and Theorem 14.7.1 holds vacuously.
So only the auxiliary statements (§14.4.2, Lemma 14.6.1, Proposition 14.6.1, Remark 14.6.1) are false for some r < 0. The proofs of Corollaries 14.6.1–14.6.2 and Theorem 14.7.1 do not cover r < 0, and Corollary 14.7.1 is unproved for r < 0. Nothing downstream is affected.

I set 'affects' to "a stated result" because numbered statements are literally false for parameters the paper allows. It could be argued down to "nothing", since the intended r ≥ 0 is evident. In HAL v3 the passages are verbatim the same.

I checked the printed text on the rendered pages. §14.1 (p. 92) defines 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε = {|δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|} with no range for ε, and recalls that v_x(δ_H) = deg H_x ∈ [0,1] at rank-1 points. This holds at boundary points too, where the degree is computed through the semi-abelian part G^0, as on p. 93. So for ε′ > 1 no rank-1 point satisfies v(δ_H) ≥ ε′. A condition |f| ≤ |p^ε′| survives passing to the rank-1 generization, so 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε′ = ∅ and H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε′, ℱ) = 0. Nonzero finite slope classes exist (for example classical small-slope forms in H^0), so they cannot be "thought of" as sections there. The remark is therefore literally false for ε′ > 1.

At ε′ = 1, p. 100 says "By definition 𝒳^{≥1}_Kli(p) = 𝒳_Kli(p)_1". The argument the remark cites does not reach this case. Prop. 14.5.1 and Prop. 14.5.2 assume ε < 1 and continue classes only to ε′ ∈ ]0,ε[, and the dynamics in Cor. 14.3.2 needs [a,b] ⊂ ]0,1[. §14.8 compares with 𝒳^{≥1} separately: Lemma 14.8.2 gives only injectivity in H^0 and surjectivity in H^1, and only for the ordinary part f.

So the correct range is ε′ ∈ ]0,1[, and the context makes this clear. The remark says "using ... the above proposition", which works with ε′ < ε < 1. Every use of the remark takes ε′ < 1: Theorem 14.7.1 with ε ∈ [0,1[, Cor. 14.7.1 (which cites the remark), and Lemma 14.8.2 with ε ∈ ]0,1[. I therefore class this as a misprint (a slip in the quantifier range) rather than a gap. No step of any proof fails in the intended range. Restricting ε to ]0, n−1/(p−1)] is not needed: that is only the definitional range of 𝒳_Kli(p^n,ε) from §12.7.1 (p. 77), so "for any ε > 0" is not a mistake. My confidence is medium because a reader could count this as harmless informal phrasing rather than a recordable slip; the mathematics above is not in doubt. I checked the rendered pages 76–77, 91–102 of the author version and pages 79, 83–84 of HAL v3.

Conventions (p. 92): X_Kli(p)_ε is the locus where |δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|, and at rank-1 points v_x(δ_H) = deg H_x ∈ [0,1]. So a larger ε gives a smaller space. Nothing on p. 92 bounds ε. On p. 100 the paper itself says: "By definition X^{≥1}_Kli(p) = X_Kli(p)_1". Under the paper's own conventions, then, ε' = 1 is a legitimate value, and so is any ε' > 1.

What the cited results give: Prop. 14.5.2, "the above proposition", assumes ε < 1 and extends a class only to ε' with ε > ε' > 0. It relies on Cor. 14.3.2, where [a,b] ⊂ ]0,1[. Lemma 14.1.1 places X_Kli(p^n, ε) inside X_Kli(p)_{ε''} with ε'' = max{0, 1 − (2/n)(n − ε + 1/(p−1))}. This ε'' is always below 1, because n − ε + 1/(p−1) ≥ 2/(p−1). Together these ingredients reach every ε' ∈ ]0,1[, and no others.

Where the printed range fails:
(a) ε' > 1. The degree of an order-p group is at most 1, and at bad-reduction points it is computed through G^0 (p. 93). So v(δ_H) ≤ 1 at every rank-1 point. X_Kli(p)_{ε'} is a rational open subset, so if it were non-empty it would contain rank-1 points. Hence it is empty and H^i = 0. Read literally, the remark would then identify non-zero finite-slope classes (for example classical small-slope eigenforms in H^0) with sections of the zero group, which is false.
(b) ε' = 1. The space is X^{≥1}_Kli(p), where Prop. 14.5.2 does not apply. The paper handles this space separately in §14.8, and only for the slope-0 part in weight (k,2). There, Lemma 14.8.2 gives only injectivity on H^0 and surjectivity on H^1. Bijectivity comes later, from the dimension count in Lemmas 14.8.3–14.8.4. If the remark were meant to cover ε' = 1, that machinery would be unnecessary. So ε' = 1 is not intended, and the cited results do not cover it.

Defence (why this is a slip, not an error or gap): the intended range ]0,1[ is clear from context. The remark itself cites a proposition that works only on ]0,1[. The paper also habitually writes "ε > 0" when it means ε ∈ ]0,1[ (for example Cor. 14.6.1, "Let ε > 0", whose proof calls Prop. 14.5.1, which needs ε < 1). Every downstream use takes ε' < 1:

- Lemma 14.8.2: uses Prop. 14.5.2 for ε, ε' ∈ ]0,1[ ∩ Q.
- Lemma 14.8.4: compares d_i^{†'}(k) with d_i^†(k), where d_i^† is defined for ε ∈ [0,1[ ∩ Q.
With ε' restricted to ]0,1[, the remark follows from the cited ingredients. So the printed text is genuinely too broad, but nothing in the paper depends on the excess range. That fits PROTOCOL §18's definition of a misprint better than that of a gap.

sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this on rendered page images, not just the text layer. The misprint is real.

1. The definition on p. 92 (§14.1) reads: "We let X_Kli(p)_ε ⊂ X_Kli(p) be the locus where |δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|". Since v_x(δ_H) = deg H_x, this is the locus where deg H ≥ ε. Raising ε shrinks the locus, and X_Kli(p)_0 is the whole space. So ε′ ≥ ε gives X_Kli(p)_{ε′} ⊂ X_Kli(p)_ε.

2. The rest of the author version uses the same convention:
- Lemma 14.1.1 and its proof conclude deg H_1 ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n−ε+1/(p−1)), which says the map lands in X_Kli(p)_{index}, a set bounded below in deg H.
- Prop 14.5.1 and Prop 14.5.2 (p. 96) take ε > ε′ > 0, g ∈ H^i(X_Kli(p)_{ε′}, F) and res_{ε′,ε} g = f ∈ H^i(X_Kli(p)_ε, F), so the restriction goes from the larger space X_{ε′} to the smaller X_ε.
- The uniqueness argument factors H^i(X_{ε′}) → H^i(X_ε) → H^i(X_{ε′}), with res as the first arrow.
- Cor 14.6.2 and Thm 14.7.1 (p. 99) restrict from X_Kli(p) = X_0 to X_Kli(p)_ε.
- The proof of Lemma 14.7.1 needs closure(U_{i,ε′}) ⊂ U_{i,ε} for ε < ε′.

3. The two composition rules on p. 96 also fit these source and target spaces.

So the stated source, target and condition ε′ ≥ ε are right. The restriction RΓ(X_ε) → RΓ(X_{ε′}) is pulled back along the inclusion X_{ε′} ↪ X_ε. The printed map X_ε ↪ X_{ε′} does not exist in general, and even if it did, pulling back along it would give a map in the opposite direction.

HAL v3 (PDF p. 84, printed p. 83) has the same sentence word for word. However, HAL v3 (PDF p. 81, printed p. 79) defines X_Kli(p)_ε as the locus where |δ_H| ≥ |p^ε|. Under that definition the inclusion X_ε ↪ X_{ε′} is literally correct, and the inconsistency is in the definition instead. The author version fixed the definition to "≤" but did not update this clause, so the misprint is new in the 2019 author version. The published Duke text could not be checked.

Nothing later relies on the wording of this clause. Every later use (Props 14.5.1–14.5.2, §14.6, Lemma 14.7.1, Thm 14.7.1, §14.8) uses res with the correct source and target.

sourceIssues.correction: In Corollary 14.6.1 replace "Let ε > 0" with "Let 0 < ε < 1". In Corollary 14.6.2 and Lemma 14.7.1 add "ε ∈ ]0,1[" (ε = 0 is trivial there, so [0,1[ also works, matching Theorem 14.7.1). This is the right and minimal fix. The only non-vacuous case it removes is ε = 1: X_Kli(p)_ε = {deg H ≥ ε}, deg H ≤ 1, so X_ε is presumably empty for ε > 1. It is also the hypothesis the paper itself uses in Prop. 14.5.1/14.5.2 (ε < 1), Thm. 14.7.1 (ε ∈ [0,1[) and Lemma 14.8.2 (ε ∈ ]0,1[).
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the rendered pages 91–100. By §14.1 (p. 92), 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε = {|δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|} = {deg H ≥ ε}, with deg H ∈ [0,1]. By p. 100, 𝒳_Kli(p)_1 = 𝒳^{≥1}_Kli(p), the non-empty locus where p-rank ≥ 1 and H is multiplicative, so ε = 1 is a real case of the printed statement "Let ε > 0".

The proof's first step shrinks ε below ε′ using Prop. 14.5.1, which explicitly requires ε < 1. It cannot use a larger ε′ instead: ε′ must satisfy 2ε′(r+k) < 2r+k−3−v(a), so ε′ < 1. If ε′ ≥ 1, then α < 0 and Prop. 14.6.1 gives no convergence. Nothing in the proof handles ε = 1.

The analytic-continuation method also cannot be adapted at ε = 1:
- The dynamics of Cor. 14.3.2 need [a,b] ⊂ ]0,1[.
- Lemma 14.3.1(5) shows the correspondence only preserves deg H = 1.
- For every ε′ < 1, the space 𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′} contains points with supersingular (p-rank 0) reduction. For example, take G with p-divisible group that of E1×E2 (supersingular reduction, small Hasse valuation w) and H = can(E1), so deg H = 1−w. Isogenous quotients G/L_n keep p-rank 0, so they have no multiplicative H′. Hence no U^n maps 𝒳_{ε′} into 𝒳_1.
- In Lemma 14.7.1, U is not compact on H^i(𝒳_1, 𝓕), so the factorisation through a strictly smaller 𝒳_{ε′} is unavailable, and even the ≤h part is not defined by the paper's slope theory.

For i = 0, the statement at ε = 1 would say that every U-eigenform on 𝒳^{≥1}_Kli(p) of slope < 2r+k−3 is classical. The paper proves nothing like this. It treats ε = 1 only for weight (k,2) and slope 0, by the separate argument of Thm 14.8.1 (Lemmas 14.8.2–14.8.4). The analogue for modular curves (Katz forms on the ordinary locus) is false. I could not prove the Siegel statement false at ε = 1, so this is a gap rather than a proven error.

Downstream, all uses have ε < 1 (Thm 14.7.1 with ε ∈ [0,1[, then §14.8), so no later result is affected. Only the three over-stated results are unproven, at ε = 1. Checked on rendered pages 92, 96–101 (author version) and 84–88 (HAL v3).

1. The proof fails at ε = 1. The corollary's α > 0 forces 2ε′(r+k) < 2r+k−3−v(a). With v(a) ≥ −3 (Prop. 13.3.1.1), this gives ε′ < (2r+k)/(2r+2k) ≤ 1. So for ε ≥ 1 we have ε ≥ ε′, and the step "We can assume 0 < ε < ε′ … by proposition 14.5.1" needs analytic continuation from X_ε to a smaller ε. Prop. 14.5.1 (p. 96) explicitly requires "ε < 1". Its proof uses Cor. 14.3.2, which only covers [c,d] ⊂ ]0,1[. The torsion-coefficient map of Prop. 14.6.1 cannot replace it either, because it needs ε < ε′ with α > 0.

2. The case ε = 1 is real, not vacuous. Page 92 defines X_Kli(p)_ε as the locus |δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|, i.e. deg H ≥ ε with deg H ∈ [0,1]. Page 100 says "By definition X^{≥1}_Kli(p) = X_Kli(p)_1", the generic fibre of the non-overconvergent p-rank ≥ 1 formal locus. On this locus the correspondence gives no improvement. The new subgroup is H′ = (H+L)/L = (G[p]+L)/L, and Lemma 14.3.1(5) gives deg H′ ≥ deg H = 1, so X_1 maps to itself and no neighbourhood X_ε′ (ε′ < 1) is pushed into it.

3. At ε = 1 the statement is probably false, not just unproved. In degree 0, H^0(X_1, F^{++}) is p-adically separated, and lim_n H^i(X, Ω/p^n Ω^+) = H^i(X, Ω) (Prop. 3.2.1, as used in the proof of Thm. 14.7.1). So the conclusion would make every U-eigenform on X^{≥1} with v(a) < 2r+k−3 classical. The analogous statement for modular curves is false. On the ordinary-canonical locus of X_0(p), take any g with Ug = 0 (for example f − VUf). Then F = Σ a^m V^m g converges for v(a) > 0 and satisfies UF = aF. This gives an infinite-dimensional a-eigenspace, whereas the classical eigenspace is finite-dimensional. I have not built such a counterexample for the Siegel–Klingen case, so I record this as a gap rather than an error.

4. The paper itself treats ε = 1 as separate. Theorem 14.7.1 is stated only for ε ∈ [0,1[, and this bound was added after HAL v3. Remark 14.8.1 keeps a slope > 0 part of H^i(X^{≥1}). Theorem 14.8.1 proves only slope-0 classicity at ε = 1, by a dimension count through colim_{ε<1} (Lemmas 14.8.2–14.8.4). That detour would be unnecessary if 14.6.2 + 14.7.1 held at ε = 1.

5. Lemma 14.7.1 has the same problem. Its proof needs U to be compact on X_ε, via some ε′ > ε with the correspondence mapping X_ε into X_ε′. At ε = 1 this is impossible, so the slope decomposition "(M^•)^{≤h}" is not even available.

Consequences: the passage is used only in Thm. 14.7.1 (ε ∈ [0,1[; ε = 0 is trivial because the restriction is the identity), Cor. 14.7.1 (overconvergent, i.e. ε < 1, via Remark 14.5.1), and §14.8 (ε ∈ [0,1[ or ]0,1[). No later result invokes ε ≥ 1, so the main theorems stand once the hypothesis is added. Only the printed statements of 14.6.1, 14.6.2 and 14.7.1 overreach.

Middle row: H^i(X_Kli(p)_ε, p^{-3-v(a)}F^{++}|_{X_Kli(p)_ε}) --a^{-n-1}U^{n-1}_{ε,0}--> H^i(X_Kli(p), F/p^{(n-1)α-3-v(a)}F^{++}). Bottom row: H^i(X_Kli(p), F^{++}|_{X_Kli(p)_ε}) --a^{-n-1}U^{n-1}_{ε,0}--> H^i(X_Kli(p), F/p^{(n-1)α}F^{++}). Just before the diagram the paper sets f_n = a^{-n}U^n_{ε,0} f; just after it, it concludes "f_n = f_{n-1} in H^i(X_Kli(p), F/p^{(n-1)α-3-v(a)}F^{++})".
sourceIssues.correction: Label both the middle and bottom horizontal arrows a^{-(n-1)}U^{n-1}_{ε,0} = a^{1-n}U^{n-1}_{ε,0}. The exponent is -n+1, not -n-1.
sourceIssues.reason:
I redid the computation. Write β = 2r+k-3-2ε'(r+k), so α = β - v(a). By Proposition 14.6.1, U^m_{ε,0} sends F^{++}|_{X_ε} to F/p^{mβ}F^{++}. Multiplying by a^{-m} then gives a well-defined map to F/p^{mβ-m·v(a)} = F/p^{mα}.
(1) Top row: a^{-n}U^n_{ε,0} lands in F/p^{nα}. This matches the print.
(2) Commutativity of the upper square. On the left, a^{-1}U sends f to a^{-1}Uf = f in p^{-3-v(a)}F^{++}, because Uf = af in p^{-3}F^{++}. So the middle arrow x has to satisfy x∘(a^{-1}U) = a^{-n}U^n_{ε,0}. That forces x = a^{-(n-1)}U^{n-1}_{ε,0}. With the printed label the composite is a^{-n-2}U^n_{ε,0}, which is wrong.
(3) Targets. With a^{-(n-1)}, the middle row sends p^{-3-v(a)}F^{++} to F/p^{(n-1)β-3-v(a)-(n-1)v(a)} = F/p^{(n-1)α-3-v(a)}, and the bottom row lands in F/p^{(n-1)α}. Both match the printed targets exactly. With a^{-n-1} they would be F/p^{(n-1)α-3-3v(a)} and F/p^{(n-1)α-2v(a)}, so each is off by 2v(a), as the reader said.
(4) The deduction needs the bottom row to produce f_{n-1} = a^{-(n-1)}U^{n-1}_{ε,0}f. With the printed label it would produce a^{-2}f_{n-1}, and "f_n = f_{n-1}" would not follow.
So the printed targets and the conclusion both agree with a^{-(n-1)}. The author's own conventions show this is a typo (-n-1 written for -n+1), not a different normalisation. It is also not a text-layer artefact: the page image shows a^{-n-1}. HAL v3 (PDF p. 86, printed p. 85) has the identical diagram with the same two labels, so the typo survived the 2019 revision; the Duke text could not be checked. Once the labels are read correctly the argument is complete, and the rest of the proof uses only the correct f_n = a^{-n}U^n f. That includes the second diagram (a^{-n}U^n, U) and the projective system in F/p^{nα-3-v(a)}. Corollary 14.6.1 and later results in §14.6 do not depend on the label.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.6, Corollary 14.6.2 and its proof, p. 99 (author version, 17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same proof word for word (printed p. 86 = PDF p. 87); its statement says "roots a of P in Q̄_p" where the author version says "in ℂ".
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. We let Q = −a_0^{−1}(X^m + a_{m−1}X^{m−1} + ··· + X). Then Q(U)f = f and we let f_n = Q(U)^n f as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1. □   [The statement just above reads: "Let P = X^m + a_{m−1}X^{m−1} + ··· + a_0 ∈ O[X] be a polynomial of degree m. We assume that P(U)f = 0 and that for all the roots a of P in ℂ, we have v(a) < 2r + k − 3."]
sourceIssues.correction:
(i) Misprint: read Q = −a_0^{−1}(X^m + a_{m−1}X^{m−1} + · · · + a_1X). This is what Prop. 14.5.2 on p. 96 prints ("+ · · · + a_1X"). With it, P(U)f = 0 is equivalent to Q(U)f = f. Also, a_0 ≠ 0 follows from the root hypothesis, since v(0) = ∞, so Q is defined.
(ii) Missing estimate, to add to "as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1":
- Let s_max be the largest valuation of a root of P. Choose ε′ so that β := 2r+k−3−2ε′(r+k) > s_max. The hypothesis on the roots makes this possible, and it is where that hypothesis enters.
- Write Q = Σ_{i=1}^m b_i X^i with b_i = −a_i/a_0. Each a_i is ± the elementary symmetric function of degree m−i in the roots, so v(a_i) ≥ v(a_0) − i·s_max, i.e. v(b_i) ≥ −i·s_max.
- Hence Q^n = Σ_{j=n}^{mn} c_j X^j with v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max.
- By Prop. 14.6.1, U^j_{ε,0}f is defined in H^i(X_Kli(p), F/p^{jβ}F^{++}). So f_n := Σ_j c_j U^j_{ε,0}f is well defined in H^i(X_Kli(p), F/p^{n(β−s_max)}F^{++}).
- The rest goes exactly as in Cor. 14.6.1 with α = β − s_max. After rescaling, Q(U)f = f integrally in p^{−C}F^{++}|X_ε. Then f_n ≡ f_{n−1} and P(U)f_n ≡ 0, each up to a bounded loss p^{−C′}.
The statement of Cor. 14.6.2 is correct as printed.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the page image at 250 dpi: the last term inside the bracket is a bare "X", not "a_1X". With a bare X, Q(U)f = f does not follow from P(U)f = 0 unless a_1 = 1. The intended a_1X is clear from Prop. 14.5.2's proof on p. 96, which prints "+ ··· + a_1X".

The substantive point is a gap. Cor. 14.6.1 (p. 98) sets f_n = a^{−n}U^n_{ε,0}f ∈ H^i(X, F/p^{nα}F^{++}) with α = β − v(a) > 0. The gain p^{nβ} comes from Prop. 14.6.1 (p. 97) and is set against a single denominator a^{−n}. Copying this literally for Q(U)^n bounds the coefficients only by a_0^{−n}O. That gives the modulus p^{n(β−v(a_0))}, which needs v(a_0) = Σ v(root) < β. That is much stronger than the hypothesis "every root has v < 2r+k−3" as soon as m ≥ 2. I checked an example with p = 3 and P = (X−3)^2, taking β = 1.5, so each root has valuation 1 < β. The naive exponent n(β − v(a_0)) = −0.5n goes to −∞. The true exponent min_j(jβ + v(c_j)) = 0.5n goes to +∞. A short computer check over 60 random products of linear factors and n ≤ 6 found no violation of v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max.

So "as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1" does not cover the step. The needed Newton-polygon bound on the coefficients of Q(X)^n (or a reduction to generalized eigenvectors, which also needs its own argument) is not stated. The hypothesis being on the roots rather than on a_0 shows the author intended the correct estimate. The statement is therefore true and only the proof is incomplete.

Downstream: Cor. 14.6.2 is used only in Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 99). That theorem concerns slope < k+2r−3, where P can have several roots whose valuations add up to more than β, so the refined estimate is really needed there. Since the corrected proof gives the statement as printed, no stated result changes. HAL v3 has the identical proof text, including the bare "X". Defence first. The paper is right about the statement but not about the proof as written.
(a) The bare "X" is a genuine slip. If a_1 ≠ 1, then Q(U)f = f does not follow from P(U)f = 0. The intended a_1X is clear from Prop. 14.5.2, p. 96.
(b) The step "as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1" does not go through on its own. In Cor. 14.6.1 (p. 98), f_n = a^{−n}U^n_{ε,0}f ∈ H^i(X, F/p^{nα}F^{++}) with α = β − v(a) > 0: one scalar a^{−n} is set against the gain p^{nβ} from Prop. 14.6.1 (p. 97). For Q(U)^n = Σ c_jU^j, the only bound visible from the data is b_i ∈ a_0^{−1}O, which gives v(c_j) ≥ −n·v(a_0). That yields the modulus p^{n(β−v(a_0))}, which needs v(a_0) = Σ v(roots) < β. For m ≥ 2 this is much stronger than the hypothesis. Example: P = (X−p)^2 and β ∈ (1,2). Each root has v = 1 < β, but the naive exponent n(β−2) goes to −∞. The coefficient of X^n in Q^n is (2/p)^n, of valuation −n, so the true exponent is ≥ n(β−1), which goes to +∞.
(c) The printed proof never uses the hypothesis on the roots, and any correct proof must. A charitable reading takes α = β − s_max, which gives the right modulus, but it still leaves the key bound v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max unstated.
(d) No nearby result supplies it. Prop. 14.5.2 works in characteristic 0 and needs no estimate. [38] (Kassaei) is cited only for the idea. Reducing to generalised eigenvectors would need the same kind of estimate for (X−a)^k, which the paper does not prove either.
Checks:
- The bound v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max is correct. A short computer check (p = 3, 300 random polynomials with integer roots of mixed valuations, repeated roots included, n ≤ 6) found no violation.
- In 178 of those cases the naive condition v(a_0) < β fails while the refined exponent min_j(jβ + v(c_j)) is positive.
- The terms c_jU^j_{ε,0}f are well defined mod p^{j(β−s_max)}; they need not vanish there.
Consequences:
- The only later use of Cor. 14.6.2 is the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 99: "we obtain (f_n) … by corollary 14.6.2"). There f lies in the slope < k+2r−3 part and P can have several roots, or a repeated root, whose valuations add up to more than β. So the refined estimate is really needed there.
- Cor. 14.7.1 and Theorem 14.8.1 depend on Cor. 14.6.2 through Theorem 14.7.1 (checked by grep; 14.8.1's reduction is on p. 100).
- The corrected proof gives Cor. 14.6.2 exactly as stated, so no stated result changes.
- The proposed correction (a_1X, plus choosing ε′ with β > s_max and the elementary-symmetric-function bound) is right and minimal.
- Judgement call: one could argue the estimate is routine and file this as a misprint with nothing affected. But a required estimate is missing, the hypothesis is never used, and the literal analogy fails, so "gap" fits better.

review.reason: Confirmed, and both halves check against the page. (i) The printed proof is `We let $Q=-a_0^{-1}(X^m+a_{m-1}X^{m-1}+\dots+X)$', with the last coefficient dropped; since $P=X^m+a_{m-1}X^{m-1}+\dots+a_1X+a_0$, the identity $P(U)f=0\iff Q(U)f=f$ forces $\dots+a_1X$, so the misprint is internally decidable. That $a_0\neq0$ follows from the hypothesis on the roots, as the correction notes, since $v(0)=\infty$. (ii) The rest of the proof is the single sentence `and we let $f_n=Q(U)^nf$ as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1'. In 14.6.1 the single eigenvalue gives one valuation to track; here the coefficients of $Q^n$ grow, and the hypothesis $v(a)<2r+k-3$ on the roots is precisely what makes $\beta-s_{\max}>0$ after choosing $\varepsilon'$, so it has to be used and is not. The correction's estimate is the routine one ($v(b_i)\geq-i\,s_{\max}$ from the elementary symmetric functions, hence $v(c_j)\geq-j\,s_{\max}$ in $Q^n$) and reduces the case to 14.6.1 with $\alpha=\beta-s_{\max}$. The statement of the corollary is correct as printed.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.7, proof of Lemma 14.7.1, p. 99 (author version, 17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same text at §14.7, Lemma 14.7.1, p. 86. It has the same U_{ε,ε′}, the same Ũ_{ε′,ε}, the same condition U(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε and the same parenthetical. The only difference is that v3 says 'Let 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h}) ⊂ M^i.' without 'be the cocycles of slope less than h'.
sourceIssues.printed: Transcribed from the rendered image of p. 99. "Let ε < ε′ be such that U(𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε. [...] The U operator is defined as the composite RΓ(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε, 𝓕) --res--> RΓ(𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′}, 𝓕) --U_{ε,ε′}--> RΓ(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε, 𝓕). We can represent RΓ(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε, 𝓕) by the Čech complex M^• = Čech(𝒰_ε, 𝓕) and RΓ(𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′}, 𝓕) by N^• = Čech(𝒰_{ε′}, 𝓕). The map U can be represented by Ũ : M^• --res--> N^• --Ũ_{ε′,ε}--> M^• which is compact. [...] Let 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h}) ⊂ M^i be the cocycles of slope less than h. This is a finite dimensional vector space. We denote by M^{+•} the Čech complex Čech(𝒰_ε, 𝓕^+). Then M^{+i} is bounded in M^i. It follows that M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h}) is bounded and thus a lattice. As a result, its image in H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε, 𝓕)^{≤h} (which is H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε, 𝓕)^{≤h} ∩ V′) is bounded. □"
sourceIssues.correction:
Replace the last sentence with this argument. Let c ∈ H^i(𝒳_ε,𝓕)^{≤h} ∩ V′. Then c = [z] with z ∈ 𝒵^i(M^{+•}). The slope projector π_{≤h}: M^• → (M^•)^{≤h} is a chain map and is the identity on H^{≤h}, so c = [π_{≤h}(z)]. The projector is continuous (the paper states this for the analogous complex in the proof of Prop. 13.3.1.1, p. 89) and M^{+i} is open and bounded, so π_{≤h}(M^{+i}) ⊂ p^{-N}M^{+i} for some N. Hence H^{≤h} ∩ V′ lies in the image of p^{-N}(M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h})), which is bounded. The parenthetical should therefore say "whose p^{-N}-multiple contains H^{≤h} ∩ V′", not "which is H^{≤h} ∩ V′".

There is also a separate index slip, a misprint. In the §14.5 convention, U^n_{ε,ε′}: RΓ(𝒳_ε) → RΓ(𝒳_{ε′}) is defined when t_{n,2}t_{n,1}^{-1}(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε. So the second arrow should be U_{ε′,ε}, which matches the Ũ_{ε′,ε} in the next display. The hypothesis should be U(𝒳_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{ε′}, that is t_{1,2}t_{1,1}^{-1}(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′}. By Cor. 14.3.2 such an ε′ > ε exists for ε ∈ ]0,1[. For ε = 0 one may take ε′ = 0, since compactness then comes from Ū′_i ⊂ U_i alone, and the case is trivial in Thm 14.7.1 anyway. Both fixes are minimal and use only facts stated in the paper.
sourceIssues.reason:
1) The parenthetical equality is false in general. The image of M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i is always contained in H^{≤h} ∩ V′, but the reverse inclusion can fail, because π_{≤h} need not preserve M^{+•}. Counterexample, with a U-stable integral lattice and h = 3/2. Take M^0 = Ky and M^1 = Ka ⊕ Kb with d(y) = b, Ua = pa, Ub = p²b and Uy = p²y. Take M^{+0} = Oy and M^{+1} = O(a+b)/p ⊕ Ob. This is a subcomplex and U-stable, since U((a+b)/p) = p·(a+b)/p + (p−1)b. Then (M^•)^{≤h} = Ka in degree 1, so H^1 = H^{≤h} = K[a]. V′ = image of M^{+1} = p^{-1}O[a]. But M^{+1} ∩ Ka = Oa, whose image O[a] is strictly smaller than H^{≤h} ∩ V′. So as written, the proof only bounds a subset of the set it needs to bound. The lemma is still true, via continuity of π_{≤h} as in the correction; that continuity is stated and used in the proof of Prop. 13.3.1.1. 2) Notation. §14.5 writes the source first: U^n_{ε,ε′}: RΓ(𝒳_ε) → RΓ(𝒳_{ε′}). The §14.7 map goes RΓ(𝒳_{ε′}) → RΓ(𝒳_ε), yet it is labelled U_{ε,ε′}, while the next display writes Ũ_{ε′,ε}; the proof is inconsistent with itself. With ε < ε′ we have 𝒳_{ε′} ⊂ 𝒳_ε. By Lemma 14.3.1(5) the correspondence never lowers deg H, since (G[p]+L)/L = (H+L)/L, both of order p. So the printed condition U(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε always holds and says nothing. What is actually needed is t_2t_1^{-1}(𝒳_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{ε′}, which Cor. 14.3.2 provides. Effect on later results: Lemma 14.7.1 is used only in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 ('Using lemma 14.7.1, we deduce that res∘ext = id'), which feeds Corollary 14.7.1 and §14.8. The lemma's statement is true once the fix is made, so no stated result changes. The earlier HAL version v3 (p. 86) has the identical text. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(1) The parenthetical. The image of M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i(M^{≤h}) is always contained in H^{≤h} ∩ V′, but equality is not a formal consequence and fails in general. A class [z] with z ∈ 𝒵^i(M^+) has representatives in 𝒵^i(M^{≤h}) exactly of the form π(z) + d(M^{≤h,i-1}). None of these need lie in M^{+i}, because π_{≤h} need not preserve M^{+•}. It does not help that M^+ is Ũ-stable, since π is only a limit of K-polynomials in Ũ.

I checked a counterexample by hand. Take h = 3/2, M^0 = Ky and M^1 = Ka ⊕ Kb, with dy = b, Ua = pa, Ub = p²b and Uy = p²y. Take M^{+0} = Oy and M^{+1} = O(a+b)/p ⊕ Ob. This is a U-stable subcomplex, since U((a+b)/p) = p(a+b)/p + (p−1)b. Then:
- H^1 = H^{≤h} = K[a];
- V′ = p^{-1}O[a];
- M^{+1} ∩ Ka = Oa, whose image O[a] is strictly smaller than H^{≤h} ∩ V′.
So, as written, the proof bounds only a subset of the set it has to bound.

No nearby statement fills the step directly. The missing ingredient, continuity of the slope projector, is stated and used by the paper itself in the proof of Prop. 13.3.1.1 (p. 89: "Its image (C^{•,++})^{=a} under the continuous projection C^• → (C^•)^{=a} is again open and bounded"). With it the lemma follows. Boundedness of H^{≤h} ∩ V then gives injectivity, because the kernel of the map to lim_n H^i(𝓕/p^n𝓕^+) is H^{≤h} ∩ ⋂_n p^nV.

I classify this as a gap rather than an error because the intended claim, boundedness of H^{≤h} ∩ V′, is true with a short fix. One could argue for "error", since the parenthetical identity is false in general.

(2) The indices. X_ε is the set where deg H ≥ ε (p. 92), so 𝒳_{ε′} ⊂ 𝒳_ε for ε < ε′. By Lemma 14.3.1(5), deg H′ = deg(G[p]+L)/L ≥ deg H, because (H+L)/L = (G[p]+L)/L, both of order p. So the printed hypothesis U(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε always holds and is not the one needed. Neither reading of U(S), as t_2t_1^{-1}(S) or t_1t_2^{-1}(S), makes it the needed condition t_2t_1^{-1}(𝒳_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{ε′}. The label U_{ε,ε′} contradicts both §14.5 (source index first; see also U^n_{ε,0} on p. 98) and the Ũ_{ε′,ε} printed two lines later. The intent is clear from context, so this part is a misprint.

(3) Consequences. Lemma 14.7.1 is cited only once: in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 100, "Using lemma 14.7.1, we deduce that res∘ext = id"). Corollary 14.7.1 and §14.8 (Thm 14.8.1) depend on it through Theorem 14.7.1. The lemma's statement is true with the fix, so no stated result is affected.

review.reason: Confirmed, and both parts are printed as reported. The proof of Lemma 14.7.1 ends `It follows that $M^{+i}\cap Z^i((M^\bullet)^{\leq h})$ is bounded and thus a lattice. As a result, its image in $H^i(\mathcal X_{\mathrm{Kli}}(p)_\varepsilon,\mathcal F)^{\leq h}$ (which is $H^i(\mathcal X_{\mathrm{Kli}}(p)_\varepsilon,\mathcal F)^{\leq h}\cap V')$ is bounded.' The parenthetical equality is what fails: a class in $H^{\leq h}\cap V'$ is represented by an integral cocycle, not by an integral cocycle of slope $\leq h$, and reaching one costs the slope projector. The correction's repair keeps the conclusion — the projector is a continuous chain map and is the identity on $H^{\leq h}$, so a $p^{-N}$-multiple of the lattice suffices — and the paper states the continuity it needs for the analogous complex on p. 89. The index slip is real too: the composite is printed with $U_{\varepsilon,\varepsilon'}$ as its second arrow while the Čech-level version two lines later is $\tilde U_{\varepsilon',\varepsilon}$, and Cor. 14.3.2 gives $t_{1,2}(t_{1,1}^{-1}(\mathcal X_{\mathrm{Kli}}(p)_\varepsilon))\subset\mathcal X_{\mathrm{Kli}}(p)_{\varepsilon+r}$, so the hypothesis should be $U(\mathcal X_\varepsilon)\subset\mathcal X_{\varepsilon'}$ with $\varepsilon<\varepsilon'$, not the printed inclusion.

sourceIssues.printed: Proof. We let Q = −a_0^{−1}(X^m + a_{m−1}X^{m−1} + · · · + X). Then Q(U)f = f and we let f_n = Q(U)^n f as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1.
sourceIssues.reason: P(U)f = 0 means U^m f + a_{m−1}U^{m−1} f + ... + a_1 U f + a_0 f = 0. Hence f = −a_0^{−1}(U^m + ... + a_1 U) f. So Q(U)f = f holds exactly for Q = −a_0^{−1}(P − a_0), whose linear coefficient is −a_1/a_0, not −1/a_0. We have a_0 ≠ 0 because 0 is not a root: every root has v(a) < 2r + k − 3. The same construction in the proof of Prop. 14.5.2 (p. 96) prints '+ · · · + a_1X' correctly. The dropped a_1 is a typo.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.9 (Estimates on Satake parameters), Proposition 14.9.1, p. 102 (proof §14.9.1, p. 103)
sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 14.9.1. — For all k ≥ 0, the Hecke operators T_{p,2} and U_{Kli(p),2} acting on H^i(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗_{Z_p} C and H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗_{Z_p} C respectively only have eigenvalues of positive p-adic valuation.
sourceIssues.correction: "... respectively only have eigenvalues of non-negative p-adic valuation", i.e. every eigenvalue α satisfies v(α) ≥ 0 (is p-adically integral). "Positive" here is the French usage (≥ 0), not the strict inequality.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered image of p. 102, and it reads exactly as quoted. (1) What the proof shows (p. 103): "We assume that U_{Kli(p),2} f = αf with v(α) < 0 ... We want to deduce that f = 0." It uses v(α) < 0 in the step "there exists n' such that p^n ∈ α^{-n'}O". So the proof gives only v ≥ 0 and says nothing when v(α) = 0.

(2) The strict reading is false under the paper's own normalisations.
- Lemma 5.1.5.1: T_{p,2} acts on the spherical line by α+β+γ+δ.
- Prop. 5.1.5.1: on the 4-dimensional Klingen invariants of a generic spherical π_p, the U_{Kli,2}-eigenvalues are the Weyl orbit of α+β, namely α+β, α+γ, β+δ, γ+δ.
- Corollary 14.9.1: a π_p contributing to eH^i has valuations (0,0,k+1,k+1). The Klingen eigenvalue α+γ then has v(α)=0 and v(γ)=k+1 ≥ 1, so it is always a p-adic unit.
- For k=0, a weight-2 form attached to an abelian surface of p-rank ≥ 1 has T_{p,2}-eigenvalue a_p, which is a unit.

(3) The paper's own usage points to ≥ 0. Elsewhere it writes "non-negative" for ≥ 0 (Remark 13.3.1.1 "only non-negative slopes"; proof of Lemma 14.8.4 "non-positive"/"non-negative").

(4) Later results only use v ≥ 0. I redid the Newton-polygon step behind Corollary 14.9.1.
- Spherical case: take e1 = α+β+γ+δ (v ≥ 0 by the proposition). T-ordinarity with k ≥ 1 forces v(e2) = 0, since e2 = Θ(T) − p^{-1}(1+p)αδ. Also v(e3) = v(e1)+k+1 and v(e4) = 2k+2. The slopes are therefore (0,0,k+1,k+1).
- Klingen case: αβ is a unit (f-ordinary, U = p·U_{Kli,1}) and v(α+β) ≥ 0, which forces v(α) = v(β) = 0 for all k ≥ 0.
Both cases need only v ≥ 0, and Lemma 14.8.3 cites only Corollary 14.9.1. So nothing downstream breaks; only the statement of Prop. 14.9.1 is misworded.

(5) HAL v3 has no §14.9 and no such proposition: §14.8 is followed directly by §15. Its counterpart, in §11.1.1 (HAL v3 p. 58), says instead "The roots are p-adic integers ... It can be proved in an elementary way (by an analysis of the integral properties of the Hecke operators)". That is the v ≥ 0 statement, which confirms what was intended.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.8, proof of Lemma 14.8.4, p. 102 (author version, 17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. Let us denote by d_i^{†,′}(k) = dim_ℂ H^i_{cusp}(†, k, 2). We have d_0^{†,′}(k) = d_0^†(k) for all k ≥ 0, and d_1^{†,′}(k) ≥ d_1^†(k) for all k ≥ 0, with equality if k ≥ 3 by corollary 13.3.3.1. The Euler characteristics d_1(k) − d_0(k) and d_1^{†,′}(k) − d_0^{†,′}(k) are locally constant functions of k ∈ Z_{≥0} by theorem 11.3.1 and proposition 13.4.1.
sourceIssues.correction: d_i^{†,′}(k) = dim_ℂ H^i_{cusp}(†, k, 2)^{=0}, the slope-0 part for U, which is the same as dim_ℂ f H^i_{cusp}(†, k, 2) with f the ordinary projector attached to U. HAL v3 writes it the second way.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page image at 200 dpi. The formula is printed as "d_i^{†,′}(k) = dim_ℂ H^i_cusp(†, k, 2)", with no ordinary projector f and no =0 superscript.

By §12.8.1, p. 79, H^i_cusp(†, κ_A, r) is the whole overconvergent locally analytic cohomology, colim_{n,ε,w} H^i(X_Kli(p^n, ε), F^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r(−D)). This is a colimit of cohomologies of Banach complexes (Prop. 12.8.2.1). It is not a finite-slope or ordinary part, so its dimension is not finite in general. The ordinary part is finite-dimensional, as p. 102 itself says.

Taken literally, the definition breaks every later step of the proof:
(a) "d_0^{†,′}(k) = d_0^†(k)" would compare the dimension of the whole space with d_0^† = dim f H^0(X_Kli(p)_ε, ·), a finite number.
(b) The appeal to Cor. 13.3.3.1 only makes sense on the slope-0 part. Slope 0 < k+1 always holds, which gives the isomorphism in degree 0 and the injection in degree 1. Slope 0 < k−2 holds exactly when k ≥ 3, and the proof says "with equality if k ≥ 3".
(c) Prop. 13.4.1 (p. 91) is explicitly about k ↦ dim_ℂ H^1_cusp(†, k, 2)^{=0} − dim_ℂ H^0_cusp(†, k, 2)^{=0}.
Remark 14.8.1 identifies f H^i with H^i^{=0}. So the intended definition is clear, and the proof holds once the =0 (equivalently f) is added. This correction is right.

HAL v3 does not have the same text. There the matching argument sits inside the proof of Theorem 14.8.1 (HAL v3 p. 87, PDF p. 88), which I checked on the page image. It defines "d_i^†(k) = dim f H^i_cusp(†, k, r)" with the projector f. So the omission appeared when the argument was rewritten for the 2019 author version.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.9: Proposition 14.9.1, statement p. 102; its proof in §14.9.1, pp. 103–104 (the quoted sentence is on p. 103); Lemma 14.9.2, p. 103 (author version, 17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: p. 103 (§14.9.1): "Let i ∈ {0, 1}. Let f ∈ H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗ ℂ be an eigenclass. We assume that U_{Kli(p),2} f = αf with v(α) < 0, …" The statement being proved, p. 102: "Proposition 14.9.1. — For all k ≥ 0, the Hecke operators T_{p,2} and U_{Kli(p),2} acting on H^i(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗_{ℤ_p} ℂ and H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗_{ℤ_p} ℂ respectively only have eigenvalues of positive p-adic valuation." The lemma the proof rests on, p. 103: "Lemma 14.9.2. — For any n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} ∪ {∞}, the maps H^i(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)/p^n) → H^i(𝔛^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)/p^n) and H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D) ⊗ 𝓘^{−3}/p^n) → H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D) ⊗ 𝓘^{−3}/p^n) are isomorphisms for i = 0 and injective for i = 1." I checked all three against the rendered pages 102–104.
sourceIssues.correction: Restrict the statement to i ∈ {0,1}: "For all k ≥ 0 and i ∈ {0,1}, the Hecke operators T_{p,2} and U_{Kli(p),2} acting on H^i(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗ C and H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗ C … only have eigenvalues of valuation ≥ 0." Add the same restriction to Corollary 14.9.1. For the fH^i part of the corollary the restriction costs nothing: once Theorem 14.8.1 is proved, fH^i(X_{Kli}(p)) ⊗ Q_p = 0 for i ≥ 2. This is the minimal correction, and it is all that is ever used. The only citation is in the proof of Lemma 14.8.3 (p. 102). There Corollary 14.9.1 is applied to eH^i(X) and fH^i(X_{Kli}(p)) inside the claim that eH^i → fH^i "are isomorphisms for i ∈ {0,1}". Lemma 14.8.4, Theorem 14.8.1 and everything after them depend only on those degrees and are unaffected.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed text is confirmed on the page images. In the statement of Proposition 14.9.1, i is free. The only paper-wide restriction is a sentence of focus in §5.3, p. 25: "Our main focus will be on the case r = 2, i ∈ {0, 1}". It is not a standing convention, since §14 does treat other degrees (for example, Lemma 14.8.2 proves that complexes are concentrated in degrees 0 and 1).

1. **The proof cannot be extended to i ≥ 2.** It needs the restriction map from H^i(X_{Kli}(p), ·) to H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, ·) to be injective. In degrees ≥ 2 the target is zero. The image of these opens in the minimal compactification is covered by two affines, as in the proof of Lemma 14.8.2, and the cuspidal sheaves have no higher direct images to the minimal compactification (the paper cites [50], thm. 8.6 in the proof of Theorem 11.3.1). So the restriction maps vanish in degrees 2 and 3. Lemma 14.9.2 is correct as stated: codimension-2 complement in a Cohen–Macaulay scheme gives an isomorphism in degree 0 and injectivity in degree 1 only.
2. **Degrees 2 and 3 are not vacuous.** The canonical bundle is Ω^{(0,3)}(−D). By Serre duality, H^3(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) is dual to H^0(X, Ω^{(k,1−k)}). For k = 0 this is H^0(X, det ω), the scalar Siegel forms of weight 1. These can be non-zero at suitable prime-to-p level (for example, products of theta constants θ_mθ_n at level Γ_2(4,8)). So the i = 3, k = 0 case of the proposition, as printed, is a real claim that the paper does not prove.
3. **The i ≥ 2 case is probably true, but not shown here.** It should follow from Newton-above-Hodge for the attached crystalline Galois representations, whose Hodge–Tate weights are {0, 0, k+1, k+1}. In the weight-1 example the parameters of the dual system have valuations (0, 0, 1, 1). So this is a scope gap, not a false statement. The intended meaning is probably i ∈ {0,1}.

'affects' = "a stated result" is appropriate only in the narrow sense that the printed scope of Proposition 14.9.1 (and of Corollary 14.9.1) has to be restricted; no later result depends on i ≥ 2.

Side note: "positive p-adic valuation" means ≥ 0 (French usage); the proof only rules out v(α) < 0.

HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018) has no §14.9: §14.8 is followed directly by Part IV. The whole section, including Proposition 14.9.1 and Lemma 14.9.2, was added after v3, so there is nothing to compare. The published Duke version could not be checked. I checked pp. 102–104 on rendered page images; the printed text is as quoted.

The defence fails, for three reasons.
(a) No convention restricts i. The paper's only general remark is in §5.3, p. 25: "Our main focus will be on the case r = 2, i ∈ {0, 1}". That states a focus; it sets no convention. The sentence that opens §14.9 defines the Hecke action on H^i for every i, and the proposition then quantifies only over k.
(b) The method cannot reach i ≥ 2. Lemma 14.9.2 is correct: a codimension-2 complement in a Cohen–Macaulay scheme gives depth 2, so H^0 is an isomorphism and H^1 is injective, via SGA2 exp. III. It says nothing in higher degrees, and in fact the restriction maps vanish there. As the proof of Lemma 14.8.2 shows, the image of the p-rank ≥ 1 locus in the minimal compactification is covered by two affines. The paper also uses (citing [50]) that cuspidal sheaves have no higher direct images to the minimal compactification. So H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, ·) = 0 for i ≥ 2, and the injectivity the argument needs fails as soon as H^i(X_{Kli}(p), ·) ≠ 0.
(c) The unproved cases are not vacuous. By Kodaira–Spencer, K_X = Ω^{(0,3)}(−D). Serre duality then makes H^3(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) dual to H^0(X, Ω^{(k,1−k)}). For k = 0 this is M_1, the scalar forms of weight 1. It is non-zero at suitable neat prime-to-p level: by Igusa, θ_mθ_n is a weight-1 form for Γ_2(4,8), for p odd. So the case i = 3, k = 0 of the printed statement is a real claim, and the paper does not prove it.

The mistake is still mild. The missing degrees are probably true: the attached Galois representations would have Hodge–Tate weights {0,0,k+1,k+1}, and Newton-above-Hodge would give the bound. So I found no counterexample, and I class this as a scope gap rather than an error. The proof's first line, "Let i ∈ {0,1}", shows what the author intended. A reader could therefore reasonably call it a misprint, in which case affects = nothing. I keep it as a gap because the printed statement asserts unproved cases, and a formaliser must use the restricted statement. 'affects' = "a stated result" only in that narrow sense: the printed scope of Proposition 14.9.1 and Corollary 14.9.1 shrinks, and no later result changes.

Side note, not part of this issue: "positive p-adic valuation" is French usage for ≥ 0. The proof only rules out v(α) < 0.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap, and the printed proof restricts itself twice over. Proposition 14.9.1 is stated for $H^i$ with no bound on $i$; §14.9.1 opens `We will only give a full proof of the proposition for classes at Klingen level', then proves Lemma 14.9.2 only `for $i=0$ and injective for $i=1$', and then says `Let $i\in\{0,1\}$' before the eigenclass argument. sourceIssues.locator: §14.8, proof of Lemma 14.8.3, p. 102 (author version, 17 June 2019), using Lemma 5.1.5.2 on p. 22. HAL v3 does not have this text: it has no Lemma 14.8.3 and no Lemma 5.1.5.2. At the corresponding point (v3 p. 57), v3 argues through "the projection to the ordinary line", citing [23] coro. 3.2.2 and 3.2.4, with no distinctness hypothesis.
sourceIssues.printed: p. 102, proof of Lemma 14.8.3: "The Hecke parameters (α, β, γ, δ) of an irreducible smooth admissible representation π_p of GSp_4(Q_p) contributing to either eH^i(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) or fH^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) have p-adic valuations (in a suitable order) 0, 0, k + 1, k + 1 by corollary 14.9.1. The claim follows from proposition 5.1.5.2 and lemma 5.1.5.2." Lemma 5.1.5.2 on p. 22 reads: "Assume that the set {αβ, βδ, αγ, γδ} has 4 distinct elements. The map π_ℓ^{GSp_4(Z_ℓ)} ↪ π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)} →^{π_{αβ}} (π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)})_{αβ} is an isomorphism."
sourceIssues.correction: The other natural approach, verifying the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.5.2, cannot work because that hypothesis can genuinely fail. The minimal fix is to weaken Lemma 5.1.5.2 so that it only needs αβ ∉ {αγ, βδ, γδ}, and to take (π^{Kli})_{αβ} to be the generalized ℓ^{-1}αβ-eigenspace of U_{Kli(ℓ),1}, with the projection taken along the other generalized eigenspaces. That space is 1-dimensional. In the proof of Lemma 14.8.3, add that the valuations (0, k+1, k+1, 2k+2) of (αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ) make αβ a simple eigenvalue. The ordinary projector f for U = p·U_{Kli(p),1} is then exactly this projection.
sourceIssues.reason:
Page images of pp. 21, 22 and 102 checked. Conventions (p. 21): αδ = βγ. The Weyl group W (order 8) permutes positions while keeping the pairs {α,δ} and {β,γ}, so the W-orbit of αβ is {αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ}. These are the eigenvalues of U = p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1} = pU_{Kli(p),1} for r = 2 (§10, "U corresponds to the operator p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1}"), and f is the ordinary projector of U (§14.8).

Corollary 14.9.1 gives valuations 0, 0, k+1, k+1. Because αδ = βγ, each pair must contain one unit, so after a Weyl move v(α) = v(β) = 0 and v(γ) = v(δ) = k+1. Then αγ and βδ both have valuation k+1. With δ = βγ/α, we get βδ = αγ exactly when β² = α², i.e. β = ±α. Nothing in the valuations or the other hypotheses rules this out.

Explicit case: α = β = u and γ = δ = p^{k+1}/u, with u a p-adic unit (e.g. a unit Weil number of weight k+1). This satisfies αδ = βγ = p^{k+1}. All ratios ξ^{-1}ξ' lie in {1, p^{±(k+1)}}, so none equals p for k ≥ 1, and Prop. 5.1.5.2 makes π_p generic spherical. Yet the set {αβ, βδ, αγ, γδ} = {u², p^{k+1}, p^{k+1}, p^{2k+2}/u²} has only 3 elements, so the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.5.2 fails. The same happens for β = −α (δ = −γ). The proof never checks this hypothesis. The set is W-stable, so a different "suitable order" cannot rescue it.

The stated result still holds. αβ is the only unit eigenvalue of U, so its generalized eigenspace is well defined and one-dimensional, and the spherical vector projects to it nontrivially. The relevant c-factors involve only the ratios α/γ, α/δ, β/γ, β/δ and their inverses, which have valuation ±(k+1), never 0 or 1. The Levi root α/β, where the degeneracy sits, does not enter. So this is a gap in the proof: a lemma is applied without checking its hypothesis, which can fail. It is easily repaired, and Lemma 14.8.3 is not affected. Conventions (p. 21): αδ = βγ, and U = p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1} with r = 2 (p. 38). By Proposition 5.1.5.1 the eigenvalues of U on π_p^{Kli(p)} are the W-orbit of αβ, namely {αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ}. This set is W-stable, so no reordering helps. e is the T-ordinary projector and f the U-ordinary projector.

The valuations (0, 0, k+1, k+1) are compatible with αδ = βγ only if one member of each dual pair is a unit. So after using W we may take v(α) = v(β) = 0 and v(γ) = v(δ) = k+1. Then v(αβ) = 0, v(αγ) = v(βδ) = k+1 and v(γδ) = 2k+2. Using δ = βγ/α, αγ = βδ ⟺ α² = β² ⟺ α = ±β. Neither the valuations, the hypotheses of Theorem 14.8.1 (which puts no condition on π) nor anything else in the paper excludes this. It would be a repeated Frobenius eigenvalue, or two opposite ones, among the unit roots. So the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.5.2 is neither checked nor implied, and the proof as written does not cover such π_p.

Defence attempted: the needed fact is still true, so only the proof is affected. The hypothesis of Proposition 5.1.5.2 (ξ^{-1}ξ' ≠ p) does hold for k ≥ 1, since valuation differences are 0 or ±(k+1). So π_p is generic spherical. Only αβ has to be a simple eigenvalue, and the valuations guarantee that. The argument: π^{Kli} ≅ (π_N)^{M(Z_p)} (Borel–Casselman, Klingen parabolic P = MN). The summand σ of π_N whose central character gives the αβ-eigenvalue splits off as a direct summand because that character differs from the other three. By Frobenius reciprocity π embeds in Ind_P^G σ. The spherical vector v0 goes to a nonzero spherical function F, and F(1) ≠ 0 because G = P·GSp4(Z_p). F(1) is the image of v0 in σ^{M(Z_p)}, which is 1-dimensional, so v0 ↦ π_αβ(v0) is nonzero, hence an isomorphism of lines.

The T-ordinarity side is also consistent: Θ(T) = (αβ+αγ+αδ+βδ+γδ) + p^{-1}(1+p+p²)αδ is a unit iff αβ is a unit, because v(p^{-1}αδ) = k ≥ 1. So the claim that eH^i → fH^i is an isomorphism holds, and Lemma 14.8.3, Lemma 14.8.4 and Theorem 14.8.1 all stand. Downstream, Lemma 14.8.3 is used only in the proof of Lemma 14.8.4, which completes Theorem 14.8.1.

Aside: the p. 22 Klingen paragraph writes "αβ = γδ". This is inconsistent with αδ = βγ on p. 21. Read literally it would make αβ = γδ, so Lemma 5.1.5.2's set could never have 4 distinct elements. It is a separate misprint.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap, and the hypothesis genuinely fails to follow. Lemma 5.1.5.2 on p. 22 begins `Assume that the set $\{\alpha\beta,\alpha\gamma,\beta\delta,\gamma\delta\}$ has 4 distinct elements', and the proof of Lemma 14.8.3 on p. 102 invokes it having only the valuations `$0,0,k+1,k+1$' for $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$ from Corollary 14.9.1. Those give $v(\alpha\beta)=0$, $v(\alpha\gamma)=v(\beta\delta)=k+1$ and $v(\gamma\delta)=2k+2$, so $\alpha\gamma$ and $\beta\delta$ are not separated by valuation and can coincide; no other input in the proof separates them. The correction is the right minimal one: $\alpha\beta$ is separated from the other three for every $k\geq0$, so it is a simple eigenvalue of $U_{\mathrm{Kli}(\ell),1}$, its generalised eigenspace is one-dimensional, and the projection along the remaining generalised eigenspaces is defined without any distinctness among those three. That weakened form of Lemma 5.1.5.2 is what the ordinary projector gives.

sourceIssues.printed: Proof. This follows from [SGA], exposé III, section 3. The point is that 𝔛 and 𝔛_Kli(p) are Cohen-Macaulay and 𝔛^{≥1} and (𝔛_Kli(p))^{≥1} are opens of codimension 2.
sourceIssues.correction: … and 𝔛^{≥1} and (𝔛_Kli(p))^{≥1} are opens whose complements (the p-rank-0 loci, contained in the special fibre) have codimension 2 (≥ 2 suffices).
sourceIssues.reason: Read literally, the statement is false: a non-empty open subset has codimension 0. The SGA2 exp. III argument (H^0 iso and H^1 injective) needs depth ≥ 2 of the coefficient sheaves along the closed complement Z. That follows from Cohen–Macaulayness plus codim Z ≥ 2. The author uses the correct wording elsewhere, e.g. p. ~81/Cor. 11.2.1: 'the complement of 𝔛^{≥1} in X is of codimension 2'. The intended claim is also true for Klingen level. The p-rank-0 locus of X_Kli(p)_{F_p} is 1-dimensional: the supersingular curves, plus P^1-fibres over the finitely many superspecial points, where α_p ⊂ α_p^2. So it has codimension 2 in the 3-dimensional special fibre, which is what matters for the /p^n coefficients. This is a wording slip with clear intended meaning. Confidence is only medium because some readers would treat 'open of codimension 2' as acceptable shorthand rather than a misprint.

sourceIssues.locator: §14.9.1 ("proof of proposition 14.9.1 assuming lemma 14.9.1"), last paragraph, p. 103 last two lines continuing to p. 104 line 1 (author version, 17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: "Rescaling g further, we may assume that h = 0. For any n ≥ 0, there exists n′ such that p^n ∈ α^{−n′}𝒪 and we deduce that g′ = α^{−n}U^{n}_{Kli(p),2} g′ is zero in H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗ [p. 104] 𝓘^{−3}/p^n)⊗𝒪, and therefore g maps to zero in H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗𝓘^{−3}/p^n)⊗𝒪." I checked this on the page image (p. 103 at 300 dpi, last two lines; the sentence ends on p. 104). The membership is printed "p^n ∈ α^{−n′}𝒪", with the prime on n in the exponent of α. The next formula is printed "α^{−n}U^n_{Kli(p),2}", with no primes on either exponent.
sourceIssues.correction: "For any n ≥ 0, there exists n′ such that α^{−n′} ∈ p^n𝒪 (i.e. n′·|v(α)| ≥ n), and we deduce that g′ = α^{−n′}U^{n′}_{Kli(p),2} g′ is zero in H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗𝓘^{−3}/p^n)⊗𝒪". This contains two slips: the membership is reversed, and the unprimed exponent n in α^{−n}U^n should be n′.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked on the page image, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The setup is v(α) < 0, α^{−1}U g′ = g′ (h = 0), and U = U_{Kli(p),2} preserves the integral lattice H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗𝓘^{−3})⊗𝒪 (Lemma 14.9.1). The proof needs g′ to lie in p^n times that lattice.

(1) The inclusion is reversed. Because v(α) < 0, α^{−n′}𝒪 = {x : v(x) ≥ n′|v(α)|}. So "p^n ∈ α^{−n′}𝒪" means n ≥ n′|v(α)|, which n′ = 0 already satisfies, and it gives nothing. What the argument needs is α^{−n′} ∈ p^n𝒪, i.e. n′|v(α)| ≥ n, which some n′ satisfies. Then g′ = α^{−n′}U^{n′}g′ lies in p^n·(lattice), so it maps to 0 mod p^n.

(2) The printed formula α^{−n}U^n g′ uses n where n′ is meant. The identity itself is true, but it only puts g′ in α^{−n}·(lattice), of valuation n|v(α)|. That is ≥ n only when |v(α)| ≥ 1, which need not hold. The n′ just introduced is otherwise never used, so n′ is clearly intended.

With both fixes the argument goes through unchanged: Lemma 14.9.2 injectivity for i ∈ {0,1}, then the limit over n gives g = 0, hence f = 0. So Proposition 14.9.1 and Corollary 14.9.1, and anything later that uses them, are unaffected, so 'affects' = nothing.

sourceIssues.locator: §15.1, Proposition 15.1.1 and its proof, p. 106 of the author version; used in §15.2, p. 107 (the H^{Np}-action on fRΓ and the localisation at 𝔪), and hence in Theorem 15.2.1 and Theorem 1.1(3).
