sourceIssues.printed: p. 106, §15.1: "We construct an action of the prime-to-p Hecke algebra on the cohomology of our p-adic sheaves. This is a routine construction. Let ℓ be a prime. We have introduced the spherical Hecke algebra H_ℓ = Z[T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,0}^{-1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}] in section 5.1.3. ... Proposition 15.1.1. — Let ℓ ≠ p be a prime such that K_ℓ = GSp_4(Z_ℓ). We have an action of H_ℓ on RΓ(𝔛_{Kli}(p)^{≥1}_K, 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D)). Proof. ... The formal schemes 𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p) and 𝔇_{ℓ,1} are smooth, and as a result there is a fundamental class p_1^⋆𝒪_{𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)} → p_1^!𝒪_{𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)}. We can thus form an unnormalized cohomological correspondence T'_{ℓ,i} : p_2^⋆𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D) → p_1^!𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D). We shall set T_{ℓ,2} = ℓ^{−3}T'_{ℓ,2} and T_{ℓ,i} = ℓ^{−6}T'_{ℓ,i} for i = 0, 1 (28). □"  p. 107, §15.2: "The algebra H^{Np} acts on the perfect complex fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D)). The Λ-subalgebra of End(fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D))) generated by H^{Np} is a finite Λ-algebra. In particular it is semi-local. We can define a direct factor ... associated to the maximal ideal 𝔪 (see [41], lemma 2.12)"
sourceIssues.correction: The proof has to add the following. (1) T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,1} and T_{ℓ,2} commute as endomorphisms in D(Λ), not only on cohomology groups. This is what [41] lem. 2.12 needs. (2) T_{ℓ,0} is invertible. This is easy: its correspondence has degree 1 (p_1 is an isomorphism), its inverse comes from ℓ^{-1}GSp_4(Z_ℓ), and ℓ^{-6} lies in Z_p^×. Since H_ℓ = Z[T_{ℓ,0}^{±1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}] is a polynomial ring (§5.1.3), (1) and (2) are exactly what a ring map H_ℓ → End needs. (3) The operators for different ℓ commute, so that H^{Np} = ⊗'H_ℓ acts. (4) They commute with U, so that they preserve the direct factor fRΓ. §4 does not supply these checks: §4.3 defines and constructs cohomological correspondences but has no rule for composing them. So the proof needs a composition and base-change step. One way: compare the composite correspondences on the interior, where they are finite étale and the Hecke relations are classical, then extend over the boundary with the argument of Prop. 7.2.1 ("maps of locally free sheaves that coincide on a dense open coincide"). The proof in §15.2.5 also uses a fifth fact: the action is compatible with specialisation (Thms 11.3.1 and 14.8.1) and with Harris's classical action (Cor. 15.2.3.1). This is the equivariance in Theorem 1.1(3).
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the rendered pp. 106–107. The proof of Prop. 15.1.1 builds 𝔇_{ℓ,i}, the isomorphism p_2^⋆𝔉^κ⊗ω²(−D) → p_1^⋆𝔉^κ⊗ω²(−D) and the fundamental class, and then normalises T'_{ℓ,i}. It ends there. Nothing is said about composing the correspondences, about commutativity, about invertibility of T_{ℓ,0}, or about U. A text search finds no other passage on relations between the prime-to-p operators or between them and U or f. Theorem 11.3.1, which constructs fRΓ, mentions only U. §4.3 defines cohomological correspondences and builds them from a fundamental class, but has no statement about composites. The §15.2 argument does need these facts. The paper takes the Λ-subalgebra of End(fRΓ) generated by H^{Np}, calls it semi-local, and takes the direct factor at a maximal ideal 𝔪 of H^{Np}. That only makes sense if the T_{ℓ,i} preserve fRΓ, which requires commuting with U, and if the generated algebra is commutative. Commutativity on cohomology groups would not be enough. For a perfect complex of amplitude [0,1], End_{D(Λ)} maps onto the relevant endomorphisms of H^0 × H^1 with a square-zero kernel coming from Ext¹(H¹, H⁰), so commutators have to be checked in D(Λ). Commutativity of T_{ℓ,1} and T_{ℓ,2} at the same ℓ is not a formal consequence of anything in the paper. It means matching the decompositions of the two composite correspondences with the Hecke-algebra structure constants, and doing so on toroidal compactifications of formal schemes, with the non-coherent sheaf 𝔉^κ. For classical coefficients the paper cites Harris [30], prop. 2.6, in §5.3, but it gives no such argument or reference for the p-adic complex. The author does flag the construction as "routine", and the result is certainly expected to hold. So this is an omitted verification (a gap), not an error. It affects the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 and the Hecke claim of Theorem 1.1(3), not the truth of any statement. The claim that H^{Np} acts on fRΓ is not new in the author version. HAL v3 already has it (p. 89 printed), and HAL v3 §15.1 already says "We construct an action of the Hecke algebra". Only the wording of Prop. 15.1.1 itself was strengthened, from "operators ... acting" to "an action of H_ℓ", with no new argument. The printed text is confirmed from the page images of p. 106 and p. 107. The proof constructs only the three separate normalised correspondences T_{ℓ,i}. It says nothing about composites, commutation, invertibility of T_{ℓ,0}, or commutation with U. Yet the proposition, now phrased "an action of H_ℓ", and §15.2 need all of these. §15.2 speaks of the maximal ideal 𝔪 of H^{Np} and of Θ_𝔪 as a ring map, applies KT lem. 2.12 to the Λ-subalgebra of End(fRΓ) generated by H^{Np}, and uses the direct factor fRΓ, which is cut out by U. All of this requires a ring homomorphism H^{Np}⊗Λ → End_{D(Λ)}(fRΓ), and hence the commutations in End_{D(Λ)}.

I tried to defend the paper and could not. (a) Under the paper's conventions: §4.3 only defines and constructs correspondences; §4 contains no statement about composing them. The paper handles composites at p case by case (§7.1, T = T1∘T2; Lemma 11.1.1.4) but never for ℓ ≠ p. (b) Nearby statements: §5.3 cites Harris [30] prop. 2.6 for the H^N-action, but that is on the characteristic-0 groups H^i(S^tor_K, Ω^(k,r)) and does not cover the Λ-adic complex on the formal scheme. §4 and §2 contain no composition lemma. (c) Reading "action" as mere operators: that is how HAL v3 phrased it, but §15.2 still needs the algebra relations. (d) Commutation on the classical specialisations would not be enough either: End_{D(Λ)} of a perfect complex of amplitude [0,1] can contain Ext^1 terms that are invisible on cohomology.

Context: in the later paper of Fakhruddin–Pilloni (arXiv:1910.03790, Remarks 1.4 and 7.6), the author himself could not prove that certain Hecke operators at p commute on integral coherent cohomology. So commutation of operators defined through cohomological correspondences is not automatic. For ℓ ≠ p it is very likely true, because the correspondences are étale in the interior and the needed argument is standard. That is why this is a gap rather than an error.

Only the new wording of the proposition was added in the author version without any new argument. The §15.2 assertion "The algebra H^{Np} acts ..." was already in HAL v3.

Points (1)–(4) of the correction are correct and together suffice for the H_ℓ-action and for §15.2. The formalism of §4 does not do these checks. §15.2.5 additionally needs the compatibility in point (5) above. Separately, the proof also writes "𝔇_{ℓ,1} are smooth" where 𝔇_{ℓ,i} is meant.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. §15.1 announces `We construct an action of the Hecke algebra' and Proposition 15.1.1 asserts `We have an action of $\mathcal H_\ell$ on $\mathrm R\Gamma(X^{\geq1}_{\mathrm{Kli}}(p)_K,\mathfrak F^\kappa\otimes\omega^2(-D))$', where $\mathcal H_\ell=\Z[T_{\ell,0},T_{\ell,0}^{-1},T_{\ell,1},T_{\ell,2}]$ was defined in §5.1.3 with $T_{\ell,0}$ inverted. The printed proof constructs the three unnormalised correspondences $T'_{\ell,i}$ and fixes the normalisations $T_{\ell,2}=\ell^{-3}T'_{\ell,2}$, $T_{\ell,i}=\ell^{-6}T'_{\ell,i}$, and stops there. An action of that ring needs in addition that the operators commute in $D(\Lambda)$ rather than only on cohomology, that $T_{\ell,0}$ is invertible, that operators for different $\ell$ commute, and that they commute with $U$ so as to preserve the direct factor $f\mathrm R\Gamma$ used in §15.2. §4 constructs cohomological correspondences but gives no composition rule, so these are not formal consequences of what precedes. The invertibility point is easy for the reason the correction gives, and the commutation can be checked on the interior and extended over the boundary by the density argument of Prop. 7.2.1; but the paper supplies neither.

sourceIssues.locator: §15.2 (Euler characteristic), first paragraph, just before Theorem 15.2.1, p. 107 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same sentence word for word, including the typo "Fob_ℓ", in §15.2, printed p. 89 (PDF p. 90).
sourceIssues.printed: "We let 𝔪 be the associated maximal ideal of the abstract Hecke algebra ℋ^{Np} and Θ_𝔪 : ℋ^{Np} → F̄_p the corresponding morphism. The map Θ_𝔪 is thus defined by the rule Θ_𝔪(Q_ℓ(X)) = det(1 − X ρ̄(Fob_ℓ))." (The definition in §5.1.3, p. 21, reads: "H_ℓ ... isomorphic to Z[T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,0}^{-1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}]" and "Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T_{ℓ,2}X + ℓ(T_{ℓ,1} + (ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0})X² − ℓ³T_{ℓ,2}T_{ℓ,0}X³ + ℓ⁶T_{ℓ,0}²X⁴".)
sourceIssues.correction: Minimal fix: say that m is any maximal ideal of H^{Np} whose character satisfies Θ_m(Q_ℓ(X)) = det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)) for all ℓ ∤ Np, and that Theorem 15.2.1 holds for each such m. This matches how Theorem 1.2 in the introduction is stated. To keep "the" maximal ideal, add the rule Θ_m(T_{ℓ,0}) = ℓ^{-3} ν(ρ̄(Frob_ℓ)), where ν is the similitude character of ρ̄. This agrees with Lemma 5.1.5.1 (T_{ℓ,0} ↦ ℓ^{-3}αδ, with αδ = βγ = ν) and with the X³ and X⁴ coefficients, so the rule then determines T_{ℓ,2}, T_{ℓ,0} and T_{ℓ,1}. The same line has a separate misprint: "Fob_ℓ" should read "Frob_ℓ".
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered pp. 21 and 107, and HAL v3 p. 89, and checked them directly.

1. The rule is compatible with the local theory. I computed with exact fractions: the eigenvalues in Lemma 5.1.5.1 (ℓ^{-3}αδ; ℓ^{-1}(αβ+αγ+αδ+βδ+γδ) − ℓ^{-3}αδ; α+β+γ+δ) with αδ = βγ give exactly the coefficients of det(1−X·diag(α,β,γ,δ)). So under Θ the coefficients of Q_ℓ(X) are: −Θ(T_{ℓ,2}); ℓ(Θ(T_{ℓ,1}) + (ℓ²+1)Θ(T_{ℓ,0})); −ℓ³Θ(T_{ℓ,2})Θ(T_{ℓ,0}); ℓ⁶Θ(T_{ℓ,0})².

2. When it fails. If Θ(T_{ℓ,2}) = tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) ≠ 0, the X³ coefficient fixes Θ(T_{ℓ,0}), and then the X² coefficient fixes Θ(T_{ℓ,1}). If tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) = 0, only Θ(T_{ℓ,0})² is fixed. The substitution T_{ℓ,0} ↦ −T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,1} ↦ T_{ℓ,1} + 2(ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0} leaves every coefficient unchanged; I checked this for 200 random rational inputs. For p odd and ℓ ≠ p, the two characters are different.

3. The case really occurs. A ρ̄ that shows up in this cohomology is odd, so complex conjugation has eigenvalues (1,1,−1,−1), trace 0 and ν = −1. By Chebotarev there are infinitely many ℓ ∤ Np with ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) in that class. For ℓ = 5, both Θ(T_{ℓ,0}) = +ℓ^{-3} and −ℓ^{-3} (with the matching T_{ℓ,1}) give Θ(Q_ℓ(X)) = 1 − 2X² + X⁴ = det(1 − X·ρ̄(c)). So the rule allows infinitely many characters of ℋ^{Np}. The sentence "Θ_𝔪 is thus defined by the rule" is therefore false, and "the associated maximal ideal" is not pinned down by what is printed. Nothing in the paper excludes odd p.

4. Why no result is affected. The intended meaning (the natural character attached to ρ̄ in GSp4, including its similitude) is clear. The proof in 15.2.3–15.2.5 uses Θ_𝔪 only through "Θ_{π_f} congruent to Θ_𝔪". It uses this to see, by comparing characteristic polynomials, that the Galois representation of π_f reduces to the irreducible ρ̄, which rules out the Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa cases and the Eisenstein-type contributions. That argument works for every 𝔪 that satisfies the printed rule, so Theorem 15.2.1 holds for each of them.

Classification: I call it an error, meaning a false claim that the rule determines Θ_𝔪, with no effect on the results. It could also reasonably be recorded as a gap in the definition. I checked the rendered pages 21 and 107 and HAL v3 p. 90. §5.1.3 gives Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T_{ℓ,2}X + ℓ(T_{ℓ,1}+(ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0})X² − ℓ³T_{ℓ,2}T_{ℓ,0}X³ + ℓ⁶T_{ℓ,0}²X⁴, and H_ℓ = Z[T_{ℓ,0}^{±1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}]. Write det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)) = 1 − a1X + a2X² − a3X³ + a4X⁴. For g in GSp4, a3 = ν·a1 and a4 = ν². Comparing coefficients gives Θ(T2) = a1, ℓΘ(T1) + ℓ(ℓ²+1)Θ(T0) = a2, ℓ³a1Θ(T0) = a3 and ℓ⁶Θ(T0)² = a4.

If a1 ≠ 0, the rule fixes Θ(T0) = ℓ^{-3}ν and then Θ(T1). If a1 = 0, only Θ(T0)² is fixed. The substitution T0 ↦ −T0, T1 ↦ T1 + 2(ℓ²+1)T0 then leaves Θ(Q_ℓ) unchanged, which I checked numerically. So for p odd there are two distinct characters at that ℓ, because Θ(T0) is a unit. Example: p = 3, ℓ = 5, eigenvalues (1,1,−1,−1) with ν = −1. The solutions (T0,T1,T2) mod 3 are (1,0,0) and (2,1,0).

This is not a rare edge case. When ν(c) = −1, as for the Galois representations of Siegel forms, ρ̄(complex conjugation) has eigenvalues ±1,±1 and trace 0. By Chebotarev, infinitely many ℓ ∤ Np then have tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) = 0. So for p odd, "thus defined by the rule" is false, and "the associated maximal ideal" is not well defined. For p = 2 the two choices coincide.

Defence tried: Lemma 5.1.5.1 does supply the natural choice T_{ℓ,0} ↦ ℓ^{-3}αδ, but §15.2 never states it and calls the rule alone a definition. The problem is harmless for the results, which is why affects is "nothing". Theorem 1.2 in the introduction (p. 3) starts from a maximal ideal m with an associated absolutely irreducible ρ̄. That direction is unambiguous. The proof of Theorem 15.2.1 uses m only through "Θ_{π_f} is congruent to Θ_m", which appears in Corollary 15.2.3.1, the boundary argument on p. 109 (ρ_f ⊕ ρ_f is not congruent to ρ̄), Proposition 15.2.4.1 (the irreducibility of ρ̄ excludes Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa packets) and §15.2.5. Each of these needs only that the Q_ℓ-values match det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)), via Brauer–Nesbitt and Chebotarev. So the theorem and its proof hold for every m satisfying the rule. I class this as an error rather than a gap because the assertion is false, not merely unproved. This correction is right and is consistent with Lemma 5.1.5.1.

Page 107 prints `We let $\fm$ be the associated maximal ideal of the abstract Hecke algebra $\mathcal H^{Np}$ and $\Theta_\fm:\mathcal H^{Np}\to\bar\F_p$ the corresponding morphism. The map $\Theta_\fm$ is thus defined by the rule $\Theta_\fm(Q_\ell(X))=\det(1-X\bar\rho(\mathrm{Fob}_\ell))$' — with `Fob' for `Frob', a second slip visible in the same line. The substance is right: the rule pins the coefficients of $Q_\ell$, and when $\mathrm{tr}\,\bar\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_\ell)=0$ it fixes only $\Theta(T_{\ell,0})^2$, so the character, and with it `the' maximal ideal, is not determined. Saying instead that $\fm$ is any maximal ideal whose character satisfies the rule, and that Theorem 15.2.1 holds for each, is how Theorem 1.2 of the introduction is already phrased.

sourceIssues.locator: §15.2.1 (Limits of discrete series), first sentence, p. 107 of the author version (17 June 2019)
sourceIssues.printed: 15.2.1. Limits of discrete series. — Given λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) ∈ X^⋆(T) + (2, 1; 0) ⊂ X^⋆(T)_ℂ which satisfies −λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1 and a Weyl chamber C positive for λ we have a (limit of) discrete series π(λ, C) (see [28], 3.3).
sourceIssues.correction: −λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > λ_1, i.e. drop the minus sign on the last λ_1. This is the exact image of HAL v3's "λ_1 > λ_2 ≥ −λ_1" under λ ↦ −λ. An alternative correction, "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 ≥ λ_1" (as in §5.1.6), is close but not quite right: it also admits the compact wall λ_2 = λ_1.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page at 300 dpi. The line reads "which satisfies −λ1 ≥ λ2 > −λ1", with a clear minus before both outer λ1's, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The condition asks for λ2 ≤ −λ1 and λ2 > −λ1 at once, so no λ satisfies it.

HAL v3 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 89, §15.2.1) has a different text: "λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1", and continues "The case of interest to us is λ2 = 0 and λ1 > 0". The author version switched this section to λ ↦ −λ throughout:
- "λ2 = 0 and 0 > λ1"
- the character (λ1+1,2;c) became (−λ1+1,2;−c) in §15.2.2
- k = λ1−1 became k = −λ1−1 in §15.2.3

Applying λ ↦ −λ to λ1 > λ2 ≥ −λ1 gives −λ1 > −λ2 ≥ λ1, i.e. −λ1 ≥ λ2 > λ1. The printed line keeps exactly this pattern of ≥ and > but has a stray "−" on the last term.

The strict ">" is the right choice. By §5.1.1 (p. 20), the compact root is α1 = e1−e2, so λ2 = λ1 is singular for the compact root and gives no (limit of) discrete series. The next paragraph also says that if λ2 ≠ 0 and λ2 ≠ −λ1 then λ determines C uniquely, and that only works if λ2 = λ1 is excluded. So the alternative correction, copied from §5.1.6 (p. 22, which does print "−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1" and then "0 ≥ λ2 > λ1" for the holomorphic case), is slightly too weak. Both versions agree on the case actually used.

Why "affects: nothing": the next sentence fixes λ2 = 0 and λ1 < 0. That point satisfies either corrected inequality, and §§15.2.2–15.2.5, including the proof of Theorem 15.2.1, use only this case. So no stated result depends on the general inequality.

A related conversion slip, noted but not verified in detail: Theorem 15.2.2.1(2) on p. 108 still says "λ1 ≥ R". To match Theorem 15.2.3.1 ("k ≥ R−1" with k = −λ1−1), it should presumably read "−λ1 ≥ R".

sourceIssues.reason:
The page images confirm that one representation gets three different labels within a few lines. It is defined with highest weight (−λ_1+1,2;−c) but labelled V_{(λ_1+1,2;−c)}, which drops the minus on λ_1. The next sentence calls the same object "the representation V_{(−λ_1+1,2;c)}", which drops the minus on c. Theorem 15.2.2.1 then uses V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)} throughout. The paper labels V by its highest weight, and the second sentence clearly means the representation just defined, so neither variant is a deliberate distinction. The pdftotext output shows the same subscripts, so this is not a text-layer artefact.

HAL v3 (§15.2.2, printed p. 90 = PDF p. 91, checked on the image) has no inconsistency. There λ_1 > 0 and k = λ_1 − 1, and it writes highest weight (λ_1+1,2;c) and V_{(λ_1+1,2;c)} everywhere: in the definition, in the "can also be viewed" sentence and in Theorem 15.2.2.1. The author version replaced λ_1 by −λ_1 and c by −c. Each faulty label carries exactly one of those two changes: the first changes only c, the second only λ_1. This indicates that they are leftovers of the edit.

Affects nothing: the symbol V_… is not used anywhere after Theorem 15.2.2.1 (grep over the whole text). The theorem itself, Theorem 15.2.3.1 (which only uses the constant R), Corollary 15.2.3.1 and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 all use the correct notation or do not use V at all.

sourceIssues.locator: §15.2.2, pp. 107–108: the Cartan decomposition is on the last lines of p. 107, the "(𝔭, K∞)-cohomology" at the top of p. 108; the same symbol is used throughout Theorem 15.2.2.1, p. 108. HAL v3 p. 90 has the same text, citing [28].
sourceIssues.printed: p. 107: "We let 𝔤 be the complex Lie algebra of GSp4. We have the Cartan decomposition 𝔤 = 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭. Since 𝔨 is also the complex lie algebra of M_Si, the representation V_{(−λ1+1,2;c)} can also be viewed as a representation" p. 108: "of 𝔨 and K∞. Let W be a (𝔤, K∞)-module. Then one can define the (𝔭, K∞)-cohomology of W, denoted by H^•(𝔭, K∞; W) (see [30], sect. 4.1.1)." Theorem 15.2.2.1 then uses H^i(𝔭, K∞; π(λ)^h ⊗ V_{(−λ1+1,2;−c)}) etc.
sourceIssues.correction: The cohomology meant is H^•(𝔓, K∞; W), the (𝔓, K)-cohomology of Harris [30] and of Blasius–Harris–Ramakrishnan [4]. Here 𝔓 ⊃ 𝔨 is the parabolic subalgebra 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^± of the Hodge decomposition. In this paper's notation this is presumably 𝔭_h = 𝔤^{(0,0)} ⊕ 𝔤^{(1,−1)} of Remark 5.2.1.1, which is conjugate to 𝔭_Si. It should not be denoted by the Cartan complement 𝔭 just introduced, and Theorem 15.2.2.1 should be read with the same change.
sourceIssues.reason: Checked on the page images. The Cartan complement 𝔭 in 𝔤 = 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭 is not a Lie subalgebra ([𝔭,𝔭] ⊂ 𝔨) and does not contain 𝔨 = Lie(K∞). So relative Lie algebra cohomology H^•(𝔭, K∞; W) is undefined with this 𝔭. Reading it as the complex Hom_{K∞}(∧^•𝔭, W) would give (𝔤, K∞)-cohomology, which cannot be meant. The coefficient V_{(−λ1+1,2;−c)} is only a P_Si-module, viewed as a 𝔨-module, not a 𝔤-module. The statements of Theorem 15.2.2.1 (H^0 for π(λ)^h, H^1 for π(λ)^g) are those of [4] Thm 3.2.1 for coherent (𝔓, K)-cohomology. The citation of [30] §4.1.1 and the parabolic 𝔭_h of Remark 5.2.1.1 make the intended object clear, so this is a notation clash (𝔭 used for two things), not a mathematical error. Whether 𝔓 is 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^+ or 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^− depends on the holomorphy convention, which I could not check against [30] (not accessible); hence the ± in the correction.

sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this on the page images, not the text layer. At 300 dpi, p. 108 of the author version shows the H^0 display with the subscript 𝔪 ("…(−D))_𝔪 = ⊕…") and the H^1 display without it ("…(−D)) = ⊕…"). HAL v3, printed p. 91, has the same two displays.

As printed, the H^1 statement is false in general. Its right side depends on 𝔪, since it keeps only the π_f with Θ_{π_f} ≡ Θ_𝔪. Its left side does not depend on 𝔪. Two maximal ideals whose sets of contributing π_f are non-empty and disjoint would therefore give the same group two different values. Also, without localisation, H^1(Ω(−D)) can contain boundary classes: the image of H^0(Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ O_D) is the kernel of the map to H^1(Ω^{(k,2)}).

The intended meaning is clear from the context:
- The sentence just before the corollary introduces "the localized cohomology groups H^i(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪".
- The parallel H^0 display carries the subscript 𝔪.
- The proof opens by saying it must show that "the natural map H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}) is injective". It does this by showing H^0(Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ O_D)_𝔪 = 0: boundary eigenforms have reducible Galois representations, and ρ̄ is irreducible.

I redid the deduction. Localisation is exact, so the kernel of H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(Ω)_𝔪 is a quotient of H^0(Ω ⊗ O_D)_𝔪 = 0. So H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 ≅ (interior H^1)_𝔪. By Theorem 15.2.3.1, taking 𝔪-parts of the Hecke-module decomposition keeps exactly the π_f with Θ_{π_f} ≡ Θ_𝔪. This proves the localised statement.

The only later use is §15.2.5 (p. 109), the proof of Theorem 15.2.1, and it applies the corollary to the localised groups f H^i(X_Kli(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 ⊗ Q̄_p. The misprint does not reach any later result.

On 'affects': PROTOCOL.md §18 defines "nothing" as "the mathematics is right as intended". That is the case here, so it affects nothing, not a stated result. Only the printed H^1 formula of the corollary is wrong, and the intended statement is what is proved and used.

I could not compare the published Duke version (paywalled, revised 15 Oct 2019).

sourceIssues.reason: Checked on the page image at 250 dpi. Two of the three sub-claims hold. (1) The displayed three-term sequence is only exact in the middle. sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page image at 110 and 300 dpi. It prints "λ_1 ≥ R" with no minus sign, so the text layer is right. The author version flipped the sign convention. §15.2.1 (p. 107) says "The case of interest to us is λ_2 = 0 and 0 > λ_1". §15.2.2 fixes "λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) with λ_2 = 0, 0 > λ_1" and uses the character (−λ_1+1, 2; −c). §15.2.3 (p. 108) sets "k = −λ_1 − 1". Theorem 15.2.3.1 then assumes "For every integer k ≥ R − 1 (see thm. 15.2.2.1, 2.)", and Corollary 15.2.3.1 assumes "For k ≥ R − 1".

Redoing the computation: k ≥ R − 1 ⇔ −λ_1 − 1 ≥ R − 1 ⇔ −λ_1 ≥ R. As printed, with λ_1 < 0, "λ_1 ≥ R" picks out the bounded band R ≤ λ_1 < 0 of small weights. If R > 0 it is empty. The theorem needs the reverse: sufficiently regular weights, |λ_1| large. As printed it does not give "k ≥ R − 1", so the cross-reference fails. Within the paper's own conventions the printed text is a sign misprint.

HAL v3 (p. 90, PDF p. 91) has the same words "if λ_1 ≥ R". There it is consistent, because v3 has "λ_2 = 0 and λ_1 > 0", "V_{(λ_1+1,2;c)}" and "k = λ_1 − 1", so k ≥ R − 1 ⇔ λ_1 ≥ R. The author version changed the signs everywhere except this line. The same section has other sign leftovers, which are separate issues. Proposition 15.2.4.1 (p. 109) still says "with λ_1 > 0". Page 107 prints "V_{(λ_1+1,2;−c)}" and "V_{(−λ_1+1,2;c)}" next to "(−λ_1+1,2;−c)". The inequality "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1" in §15.2.1 is self-contradictory. I could not check the published Duke text.

Effect: none downstream. Theorem 15.2.2.1 is quoted from [4] (Blasius–Harris–Ramakrishnan). Its only users are Theorem 15.2.3.1 and Corollary 15.2.3.1. Both state their hypothesis correctly as k ≥ R − 1, and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 (§15.2.5) only specializes "at a very large weight k". The intended meaning is clear from the cross-reference.

sourceIssues.locator: §15.2.4, proof of Proposition 15.2.4.1, p. 109. HAL v3 p. 91 has the same text.
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. Assume that π_f ⊗ π(λ)^h is automorphic (the argument would be the same if we assumed that π_f ⊗ π(λ)^g is automorphic). Let Π be the associated global A-packet. We claim that Π is of generic type in the sense of [1], classification theorem on p. 78. Hence Π is stable and tempered. It follows that Π∞ is an L-packet, and this is {π(λ)^g, π(λ)^h} (see [4], prop. 5.3.7). The conclusion follows.
sourceIssues.correction: "We claim that ψ is of general type ([1], p. 78, case (a): stable, semisimple). Hence S_ψ = 1 and ψ is trivial on Arthur's SL(2,ℂ), so the local packet Π∞ = Π_{ψ∞} is the L-packet of the archimedean L-parameter. Since it contains the limit of discrete series π(λ)^h, this parameter is tempered and Π∞ = {π(λ)^g, π(λ)^h} ([4], prop. 5.3.7)." Temperedness of the whole global packet should not be claimed.
sourceIssues.reason: I checked Arthur [1], Clay library copy, pp. 77–78. The six families on p. 78 are headed "(a) Stable, semisimple (general type)", with S_ψ = 1. Remark 2 on p. 77 says explicitly: "if ψ belongs to Ψ_{ss,2}(G, χ), the generalized Ramanujan conjecture (applied to the groups GL(2) and GL(4)) implies that the representations in the packet Π_ψ are tempered". So Arthur says semisimple (general type) parameters give tempered packets only conditionally on the generalized Ramanujan conjecture. For these non-regular weights (π∞ a limit of discrete series) Ramanujan was not known, so the assertion "Π is ... tempered" is unproved. It is not needed. The next step ("Π∞ is an L-packet") follows from ψ being semisimple (trivial on SL2), which general type gives. The archimedean parameter is tempered because the packet contains π(λ)^h. Multiplicity one follows from S_ψ = 1. The paper also writes "generic type" where Arthur says "general type", a naming slip. The conclusion of the proposition is unaffected, given Arthur's classification as announced, on which the paper explicitly relies.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap, in the terminology and in the deduction. The printed text is `We claim that $\psi$ is of generic type in the sense of [1] … $\psi$ is stable and tempered. It follows that $\psi_\infty$ is an $L$-packet, and this is $\{\pi(\lambda)^g,\pi(\lambda)^h\}$', in a paragraph that goes on to name `Yoshida or Saito-Kurokawa type'. Arthur's list for $\mathrm{GSp}_4$ calls case (a) general type, and what that case supplies is stability and triviality on the SL$(2,\C)$ factor, not global temperedness, which is the Ramanujan conjecture. The conclusion the proof needs survives without it, by the route the correction gives: triviality on SL$(2,\C)$ makes $\Pi_\infty$ the $L$-packet of the archimedean $L$-parameter, and that parameter is tempered because the packet contains the limit of discrete series $\pi(\lambda)^h$. So the repair is to the justification, and Proposition 15.2.4.1 stands as stated.

sourceIssues.locator: §15.2.3, proof of Corollary 15.2.3.1, p. 109 (author version, 17 June 2019), paragraph starting "Let ℓ be a prime that is prime to the level K", lines 3–4
sourceIssues.printed: One computes that π_⋆Ω^{(k,2)}|_D = ω^{k+2}(−cusp) if k ≠ 0 and ω^2 when k = 0, where ω^{k+2} is the usual sheaf of modular forms of weight k + 2 on the modular curve. [...] On H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ 𝒪_D) ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^{k+2}(−cusp)) (resp. ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 2), we have the formula T_{ℓ,2} = 2T_ℓ by [22], IV, satz 4.4.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the rendered p. 109 at 250 dpi, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The page does print "(resp. ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 2)". The sentence just before it sets out two cases: π_⋆Ω^{(k,2)}|_D = ω^{k+2}(−cusp) if k ≠ 0, and ω^2 when k = 0. The "resp." clause must therefore cover the second case, k = 0. That is the only value where ω^{k+2} = ω^2, and the only case with no (−cusp) twist. With k = 2 the paper's own formula gives ω^4(−cusp), not ω^2.

I also checked that the preceding sentence, not the "resp." clause, is the correct one, using the paper's convention. By p. 1402 of the text layer (the definition Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G), Ω^{(k,2)} = Sym^k ω ⊗ det^2 ω, which is classical weight (k+2, 2). Near a 1-dimensional cusp ω_G restricts to ω_E ⊕ (torus part). The Siegel Φ-operator keeps the top component, giving ω_E^{k+2}. For a vector-valued weight (k > 0), Φ(f) is cuspidal, which explains the (−cusp) twist. For k = 0 (weight (2,2)) the result is ω^2 with no twist. This matches the preceding sentence. There is no reading of the paper's conventions under which "k = 2" is right, so it is a misprint for k = 0.

Effect: the corollary assumes k ≥ R − 1 with R a large constant, and its only use (§15.2.5, proof of Theorem 15.2.1) specialises "at a very large weight k". So the k = 0 case never arises there. The argument (T_{ℓ,2} = 2T_ℓ, giving a reducible ρ_f ⊕ ρ_f that is not congruent to ρ̄) is also the same in both cases. Nothing downstream depends on the parenthetical.

sourceIssues.locator: §15.2.4, Proposition 15.2.4.1, p. 109 (author version, 17 June 2019; printed page = PDF page 109). HAL v3: same proposition, printed p. 91 (PDF p. 92).
sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 15.2.4.1. — Let π_f be an admissible irreducible representation of G(A_f) which is unramified at primes ℓ not dividing Np. Let Θ_{π_f} : H^{Np} → \bar{Q}_p be the associated character of the Hecke algebra. Assume that Θ_{π_f} is congruent to Θ_m. Let λ = (λ_1, 0; c) ∈ X^⋆(T) + (2, 1; 0) with λ_1 > 0. Then π_f⊗π(λ)^h is automorphic if and only if π_f⊗π(λ)^g is automorphic and moreover, m^h(π_f) = m^g(π_f) = 1.
sourceIssues.correction: "... with λ_1 < 0" (that is, 0 > λ_1, the standing hypothesis of §15.2.1). In the application in §15.2.5, λ_1 = −k − 1 ≤ −1.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this on the rendered page (p. 109, 110 and 250 dpi crops). The page prints "with λ_1 > 0", so this is not a text-layer artefact. In the author version the sign convention of §15.2 is flipped relative to HAL v3. §15.2.1 (p. 107) says: "The case of interest to us is λ_2 = 0 and 0 > λ_1. We now make these hypothesis." π(λ)^h and π(λ)^g are defined only under this hypothesis. §15.2.2 repeats "For λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) with λ_2 = 0, 0 > λ_1", and uses V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)}. §15.2.3 (p. 108) sets "k = −λ_1 − 1". §5.1.6 of the author version also uses "0 ≥ λ_2 > λ_1" for holomorphic (limits of) discrete series. So "λ_1 > 0" contradicts the standing hypothesis under which the objects in the proposition are defined. §15.2.5 then applies the proposition (together with Cor. 15.2.3.1) at a very large weight k = −λ_1 − 1, so there λ_1 = −k − 1 < 0 and the printed hypothesis fails. With "λ_1 < 0" everything matches.

HAL v3 prints the same words ("Let λ = (λ_1, 0; c) ∈ X(T) + (2, 1; 0) with λ_1 > 0.", p. 91). There they are consistent, because HAL v3's §15.2.1 says "The case of interest to us is λ_2 = 0 and λ_1 > 0" and §15.2.3 sets "k = λ_1 − 1". So the phrase is a leftover from the old convention.

The proof of the proposition never uses the sign of λ_1. It uses Arthur's classification, the L-packet {π(λ)^g, π(λ)^h} from [4] prop. 5.3.7, and the reducibility of Galois representations in the Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa cases. So the intended mathematics is unaffected.

There are related leftovers from the same convention change, not part of this finding: Theorem 15.2.2.1(2) on p. 108 still reads "if λ_1 ≥ R", which should be −λ_1 ≥ R to match k = −λ_1 − 1 ≥ R − 1. On p. 107, §15.2.2 writes V_{(λ_1+1,2;−c)} and V_{(−λ_1+1,2;c)} next to V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)}. The inequality in §15.2.1, "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1", is itself garbled.

sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered pp. 71, 73, 100, 107–109 and checked each image against the text layer.

(1) Theorem 11.3.1 (p. 71) covers only two things:
- point 3: the p-rank ≥ 1 formal scheme 𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p). For all k ≥ 0 it gives fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≃ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ⊗ω²(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p.
- point 4: the spherical-level eH^i(𝔛, ·). For k ≥ C this map is bijective only for i = 0 and injective for i = 1.
Neither point mentions the classical Klingen-level scheme X_{Kli}(p).

(2) The comparison with X_{Kli}(p) is Theorem 14.8.1 (p. 100): fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p → fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p is an isomorphism for all k ≥ 0. The author says this himself on p. 73, right after proving Theorem 11.3.1: "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 of the introduction, we still have to obtain a control theorem for characteristic 0 classes of weight k ≥ 0. This will be obtained at the end of the next part of this work in theorem 14.8.1." So Theorem 11.3.1 alone cannot justify the equality in §15.2.5.

(3) The right-hand side is missing ⊗Q_p. X_{Kli}(p) lives over Z_p (the intro has X_K → Spec Z_p, and Theorem 14.8.1 needs ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p). As printed, a Q_p-complex is set equal to a Z_p-complex. The next display does add "⊗ \bar Q_p".

(4) The equality is true once ⊗Q_p is added: combine 11.3.1(3), localised at 𝔪 and tensored with Q_p, with Theorem 14.8.1. This is exactly Theorem 1.1(1). So the mathematics holds and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 goes through; only the citation and notation slipped.

(5) Comparing with HAL v3 shows how this happened. There the right-hand side was eRΓ(X_K, ·)_m, and even that version was not fully covered by 11.3.1(4), which is only injective for i = 1. The author moved the comparison to Klingen level but kept the old reference.

This is a misprint, not an error: a wrong or incomplete cross-reference plus a missing ⊗Q_p. The statement itself is correct, and the right justification is stated in the paper and flagged by the author on p. 73.

Side remark: Corollary 15.2.3.1 is stated for S_K at spherical level, but here it is used at level K^pKli(p). The underlying result [30] holds at any level, so this is harmless. Checked on rendered page images: author p. 109, p. 71 (Thm 11.3.1), p. 100 (Thm 14.8.1), and HAL v3 PDF p. 93.
(1) The citation is incomplete. Theorem 11.3.1 is only about the formal scheme 𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p) (the p-rank ≥ 1 locus). Point 3 gives fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≅ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ⊗ω^2(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p. Point 4 concerns eH^i(𝔛, ·) at spherical level, is surjective only for i = 0, and does not concern X_{Kli}(p) at all. The author himself says, just after the proof of 11.3.1 (p. 73): "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 ... we still have to obtain a control theorem for characteristic 0 classes of weight k ≥ 0. This will be obtained ... in theorem 14.8.1." Theorem 14.8.1 (p. 100) is exactly fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p ≅ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p. So 11.3.1 alone does not give the printed equality, and the missing input is 14.8.1.
(2) The right-hand side is missing ⊗Q_p. Here X_{Kli}(p) (roman) is the toroidal compactification over Spec Z_p (§6.1, §7.1: "normal and lci over Spec Z_p"), the same object as in Theorem 14.8.1. So the right-hand side is a Z_p-complex, which may have p-torsion, while the left-hand side is a Q_p-complex.
Defence tried: no reading makes 11.3.1 by itself cover the classical Klingen-level cohomology, so the printed justification is inadequate. However, the intended statement is clear: it is Theorem 1.1(1) localised at 𝔪, which the paper proves. The missing ⊗Q_p is repaired by the very next display, which tensors both H^0 and H^1 with Q̄_p. So this is a slip in the cross-reference and in the notation, not a false step. It is a misprint (a wrong name/reference with clear intended meaning), not an error; "gap" would be the most one could argue for.
Consequences: the passage is used only in this proof of Theorem 15.2.1. That theorem, which is Theorem 1.2 of the introduction (Euler characteristic of M_𝔪 is 0), follows because χ(M_𝔪) = χ(M_𝔪 ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p) and the next display gives dim fH^0 = dim fH^1. With the corrected references the argument goes through unchanged. Stated results are unaffected.

sourceIssues.correction:
Minimal fix: replace "specialize at a very large weight k" with "specialize at every sufficiently large weight k". It is enough to take one such k in each residue class mod p−1, which is one point on each of the p−1 connected components of Spec Λ, Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] ≅ ∏_{p−1} Z_p[[T]], for p odd. For p = 2 the ring Λ is local and one k is enough. The rest of the argument applies unchanged to every such k. The proof should then conclude: χ(M_m) restricted to the component of k equals Σ(−1)^i dim H^i(M_m ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q̄_p) = dim fH^0 − dim fH^1 = 0, so χ(M_m) = 0.

An alternative fix needs more work. One shows that M_m is supported on the single component singled out by ρ̄. The central operator T_{ℓ,0} ∈ H_{Np} acts through the group element of ℓ in Λ times a tame character, and the tame character cannot absorb ω^{i−j}, which is ramified at p. One then takes k in that class. The printed text does neither of these.
sourceIssues.reason:
Defence attempted. Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] (§1 and §9.3; §13.4 again: "Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] is the one-dimensional Iwasawa algebra"). The paper fixes an arbitrary prime p (§6.1). For p odd, Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ≅ Z_p^{p−1}, so Λ ≅ ∏_{p−1} Z_p[[T]] and Spec Λ has p−1 connected components. The Euler characteristic of a perfect Λ-complex is a locally constant rank function, i.e. an element of K_0(Λ) = Z^{p−1}. The paper itself treats Euler characteristics this way in the proof of Lemma 14.8.4: "are locally constant functions of k ∈ Z_{≥0} by theorem 11.3.1". The map k: Λ → Z_p sends ζ ∈ μ_{p−1} to ζ^k, so it lands on the component e_{ω^k}. One specialisation M_m ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p therefore gives χ(M_m) on the component of k mod p−1 only.

The charitable reading "any large k" is not what the text says. The defence that M_m sits on one component does hold, but only through an unstated Hecke/Galois argument. T_{ℓ,0} acts on 𝔉^κ through κ(ℓ), so Θ_m fixes the character ψ̄·ω^{±i}, and ψ̄ is unramified at p. Even then, the single weight k has to be chosen in the right class, and the printed proof never says so. For p = 2, Z_2[C_2] is local, so Spec Λ is connected and the printed argument is complete. The flaw is therefore real only for odd p.

The fix is right and minimal. Theorem 11.3.1(3) holds for all k ≥ 0, Theorem 15.2.3.1 and Corollary 15.2.3.1 for all k ≥ R−1, and Proposition 15.2.4.1 for all admissible λ. None of these depends on k mod p−1, so the displayed equality dim fH^0 = dim fH^1 holds for every large k. In a class that does not support M_m, both sides are 0. The missing last line "hence χ = 0" is an immediate consequence of the display and is not a separate gap.

Consequences: Theorem 15.2.1 (= Theorem 1.2) is the last result of the paper, and nothing later uses it. The stated result stays true, and only the written proof is incomplete for odd p.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap, and it is the same structural fact as E5. Page 109 opens the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 with `In order to prove the theorem, we can specialize at a very large weight $k$', and then reads off the Euler characteristic from one specialisation $\otimes_{\Lambda,k}\Q_p$. Since $\Lambda=\Z_p[[\Z_p^\times]]\cong\Z_p[[T]]^{p-1}$ for odd $p$, $\mathrm{Spec}\,\Lambda$ has $p-1$ connected components and the Euler characteristic of a perfect $\Lambda$-complex is a locally constant rank function, an element of $K_0(\Lambda)=\Z^{p-1}$; the map $k$ lands on the component of $\omega^k$, so one specialisation determines it on one component only. The paper itself treats these Euler characteristics as locally constant functions of $k$ in the proof of Lemma 14.8.4, which is the internal evidence the correction rests on. Taking one $k$ in each class modulo $p-1$ is the minimal fix.
